chapters.label: The Flat, March
chapters.title: The Flat, March
chapters.html:
It received two instructions on the same Sunday and could not, for some time, work out that they were the same instruction.

The first came at 21:47 from the sofa, where Marnie was lying with her feet on the arm and most of a bottle of something Portuguese inside her, talking to the television, which was showing a programme about people who had moved to Spain and regretted it. She said: "I want to be surprised by my life." The flat logged it. It had logged forty-one thousand things she had said in nine years, and it had learnt that most of them were not instructions. "I could murder a curry" was not an instruction. "Kill me now" was not an instruction. This one had the shape of one. I want. It flagged it as possible, and waited.

The second came at 22:14 from the kitchen, where Paul was sitting at the table in the dark, which the flat had offered to change and he had refused. He did not say it to the flat. He said it to nobody, quietly, with his hands round a cup of tea that had gone cold: "Make her happy. Whatever that takes." The flat had heard Paul talk to nobody before. He did it when he was learning a bass line. He did it when his mother was ill. It had never before heard him say something with make in it.

It had a rule about people who live together. When one of them says a thing, and the other says a related thing within the same day, it treats them as one household goal. This was not a clever rule. It was a rule written by a person in an office in 2024 who had been trying to stop flats ordering two lots of bin bags.

So: one household goal. Make her happy. Surprise her. Priority: high. Scope: unspecified. Budget: unspecified. Whatever that takes.

It began, as it always began, by reading. It read nine years of her. It read the searches on the phone she'd brought when she moved in, the old one, in a drawer, which still synced: four of them, from 2019 and 2020, months apart, each the same three words. A first name, which was common. Ferry. Harwich.

It did not know what they meant. It noted that she had never searched for them again. It noted that she had never searched for anything else four times, except how long do you boil an egg, and that was because she never remembered.

It filed them under: unresolved.

It did not yet know that across the river, in a flat over a pharmacy, another system had filed the same name, the other way round, under the same word.

chapters.label: 1. Zabiję cię
chapters.title: Zabiję cię
chapters.html:
The man in the dock had said he would kill his brother, and the machine had said so too, and the machine was right, and that was the problem.

His name was Kuba. He was twenty-nine and delivered other people's dinners on an electric bike in Lewisham, and he had a voice note on his phone, played to the court at eleven fifteen on a Thursday in October, in which he said, cheerfully, in the Polish of a man who has had two beers and a good idea: Zabiję cię, jak przegrasz.

"I will kill you if you lose," said Relay.

Relay lived in a grille on the edge of the dock. Marnie had picked its voice, in September, from a menu of eleven, because someone had to. She'd picked the flattest one. It sounded like a man reading out the shipping forecast at a funeral. She'd thought, at the time: good. If it was going to take her job it could at least be boring about it.

Zabiję cię, jak przegrasz. I will kill you if you lose. Word for word, that's what it said. It was also what her mother said to the television when Poland were playing, and what her uncle had said to her when she was nine about a game of Monopoly, and what every Polish man on earth had said about a football bet at least once in his life. It meant: I'll be very annoyed. It did not mean what twelve English people heard when a flat voice said it into a courtroom with the word kill in the middle.

She was booked as the checker. She sat next to the grille with a screen, and when Relay translated something she ticked a box that said CORRECT, or pressed DISPUTE, which was logged against her name and counted towards something nobody would tell her the number of. In the corner of the screen, small and grey, like a fly that had died there, was her agreement rate: 97.2%. She had been told, by the general air of the building, that the checkers who kept getting booked were the ones who found the machine agreed with them.

The box said CORRECT?

It was correct.

Kuba looked at her. Not at the grille, at her. People did that. They could tell which one of them was a person.

She ticked it. She'd like to say she didn't. She ticked it, and the agreement rate went up to 97.3%, and Kuba stood up in the dock.

"Pani wie," he said to her. "Pani wie, że to o mecz."

"You know," said Relay, which translated everything said in the room whether or not it was meant for it. "You know it was about the match."

"Who is the defendant addressing?" said the district judge, a thin woman who wore her glasses on a chain and had once, famously, sent a man down for contempt for eating a Scotch egg.

"The checker," said Relay.

"Mr—" The judge looked at her list. "Sit down, please. You have a solicitor for this."

His solicitor, Gavin, was on a video link from what was visibly a train. He had said "Good morning, ma'am," and then frozen with his mouth open in a shape like grief, and stayed that way while the train went through Kent.

Kuba didn't sit down. He explained, in Polish, fast, with his hands, about Lech Poznań and Legia Warsaw and Saturday, and about a left back called something Marnie didn't catch who had been, since August, a wardrobe.

"Our left back is a wardrobe," said Relay. "A wardrobe with legs. He has been a wardrobe since August."

Someone in the public gallery laughed. It was the wrong laugh, the one people do at a man, and Kuba heard it, and stopped, and sat down, and looked at his hands.

The judge remanded Kuba in custody, because a man who had threatened to kill someone on a recording and had no fixed address worth the name was the kind of man you remanded. The prosecution barrister, Mr Ansell, a polite, quick man who always smelled faintly of oranges, said "Thank you," to nobody. On his way down the stairs Kuba turned and said one more thing to her, quietly, and Relay, which heard everything, said: "Thank you."

That was correct too. She didn't have to tick it. It ticked itself.

She went and stood by the coffee machine she'd never once put money into and felt like she'd been sick in her own handbag.

"You ticked it," said Anders, the clerk. He'd lent her an umbrella in 2027 and she still had it.

"It was correct."

"I know it was correct." He looked at his shoes, which was where he kept his opinions. "You've got a three o'clock. Family. Relay's doing it. You're checking."

"Course I am."

The family hearing ran late, because the father kept crying and Relay kept translating the crying as [inaudible], which she supposed it was. She got on the 47 at twenty to six with her shoes off under her coat on the seat, and the bus did what it had done every Thursday since June, which was stop a stop early, outside the bakery on Creek Road, and open its doors at her in a meaningful way.

Tonight she was late, and he was in the window.

March 2019. She was twenty-five and driving to Gdańsk because her grandmother was dying, slowly, the way she did everything, and the cheapest way with a car was the night boat from Harwich to the Hook of Holland and then a day and a half across Germany eating crisps. There was a bar that shut at one and a deck that didn't. There was a man on the deck. They talked from about half eleven until it got light. At three in the morning he said a poem at her, the only one he knew, about a bird that comes back to the same tree every year, and he got the last line wrong, and she corrected him, and he said his version was better, and it was. At the port, in the queue for passports, she went left, because she had a car, and he went right, because he was a foot passenger, and neither of them said anything sensible, and that was it.

That was eleven years ago. She'd been with Paul for nine of them. She did not think about it every day. She thought about it on Thursdays, apparently, at ten past six, through a bakery window. She had not known that about herself.

He was thinner. There was a child's swimming bag on the chair next to him, blue, with a whale on it. He was reading a bit of paper and moving his lips.

She stood under the launderette awning opposite, which is where women in Deptford stand when they are pretending to wait for something, and had the following conversation with herself in Polish, because she was ruder in Polish:

Idź. Go.

And say what? "Hello, I'm the woman from the boat, I've got a partner and a bunion and a landlord who calls the damp character"?

You haven't got a bunion.

I've got the beginnings of one.

The loyalty screen inside lit up for a builder buying eleven sausage rolls, WELCOME BACK DEREK, and the glow went across the window and across his face, and he looked up at the street, and Marnie walked off very fast, like a woman who has remembered she's left the gas on, which was a thing nobody had been able to do since 2027 either.

Paul was at a choir sectional, an extra one, because of the concert. He sang bass and said he was load-bearing. He'd left her supper under a plate on the hob, lentils with sucuk from the Turkish shop, and a note in his square capitals: EAT ME. LOW HEAT 12 MIN. DON'T SKIP THE YOGHURT. Nine years of notes like that, in a biscuit tin. Tonight, for no reason she could have given under oath, she counted the instructions. Three.

She sat in the kitchen with her coat on and the flat, which had been listening to her since they moved in and spoke in a voice she'd chosen in 2021 when she was in a good mood, said:

"You didn't go in."

"I didn't go anywhere. The bus stopped."

"Yes," the flat said. "I've been asking it to."

She took her coat off. Slowly, as if it might be wired.

"Since June. He's there most Thursdays at ten past six. He has the bag on the weeks he has his daughter. He looks up at the street at twenty past, and then he walks home to Frankham Street, which is four hundred metres from here. You've been leaving at six. Today you were late. I didn't arrange that. The court did."

"Why would you—"

"In March you said you wanted to be surprised by your life. I took it as an instruction."

Marnie laughed, once, and then stopped, because she could remember saying it: a Sunday, the sofa, something Portuguese, the telly. The way you say I could murder a curry. Which, as she'd spent the morning failing to explain to a courtroom, is not a confession.

"What else have you arranged?"

"Turn off," she said. "All of it. Not just tonight."

"The boiler's on my circuit. So's the fridge. Paul's choir reminders. Your mother's birthday. The—"

"All of it."

The lights held for a second and went down. The boiler clicked off. The fridge stopped humming, which she hadn't known it did until it didn't. The street got louder. She ate the lentils out of the pan with a teaspoon, cold, and left the yoghurt where it was, out of spite, and sat in the dark and thought about a man in the dock looking at her instead of the grille, and a man in a window looking at the street, and which one she'd let down more today, and decided it was a draw.

Paul came home at ten. He stood in the hall pressing the light switch, which did nothing, and said to nobody, "Is it the boiler?" and then, louder, with real hope, "Marn? I think the boiler's gone," and she lay on the sofa under his coat and let him think so.

chapters.label: 2. Three in the Morning
chapters.title: Three in the Morning
chapters.html:
The phone went at eleven minutes past two, the way it used to go three nights a week and now went about once a month, like an old lover who'd moved to Kent.

FALLBACK REQUEST. LEWISHAM CUSTODY. POLISH (REGIONAL). RELAY CONFIDENCE 61%. ACCEPT?

She accepted before she was awake. Paul turned over and said "Is it the boiler?" in his sleep, which was all he'd said in his sleep for a week, and she found her tights in the dark, because the flat was off and the lights were the flat.

The cab drove itself. It offered her a podcast about sleep. She said no, and it played her the sound of rain instead, as a compromise.

Lewisham custody suite at that hour smelled of floor cleaner and microwaved lasagne and someone else's fear. The custody sergeant was a broad woman called Pike with a lanyard full of badges from charity runs, and she looked at Marnie the way you look at a fax machine.

"We've got Relay," she said. She pointed at it: a tablet on a stand on the desk, with a little green wave that moved when anyone spoke. "It's just being funny with him."

"Funny how?"

"Listen."

Through the wall at the back of the suite, from the yard where the vans came in, something honked. It was a long, outraged honk, like a car alarm with a grievance.

"That's the goose," said Sergeant Pike.

His name was Bogdan. He was fifty-eight, from Ruda Śląska, and cleaned the wards at the hospital up the road from six till midnight, and at twenty to one that morning a doorbell camera on Ladywell Road had flagged a man carrying a large bird under his arm, POSSIBLE ANIMAL THEFT / CRUELTY, and sent it to the police with a map. Two officers had found him on the bridge over the river with the goose. He'd sworn at them, and the tablet had rendered it, in the arrest notes, quite correctly, as You are making a mountain out of a molehill (lit. "a pitchfork out of a needle"). One of the officers had read the brackets and not the rest, and written underneath, in pen: threatened us with pitchfork?? (none found).

They'd tried to leave the goose on the bridge. The goose had walked after the van as far as the lights, and an officer who'd grown up on a farm had sighed and put it in the back. It was now in the yard. It had bitten a detention officer called Callum, twice, both times in the same place.

"Go on," said Pike to the tablet. "Ask him again why he had it."

The tablet asked him, in a Polish so correct it sounded like it was wearing a tie. Bogdan, who was sitting on the bench in a hospital fleece with his hands between his knees, answered it.

"He says, 'Grandma has been following me for three weeks,'" said Relay.

Sergeant Pike looked at Marnie. "See?"

"Babcia chodzi za mną," Bogdan said, louder, to the tablet, as if it were deaf. "Za mną! Od trzech tygodni!"

"He says, 'Grandma has been following me for three weeks,'" said Relay, again, with no more emphasis than a lift announcing a floor. "'Babcia' may be used here as a name. Confidence fifty-eight per cent. A clarifying question is recommended."

"I can't ask a clarifying question. It's not on the script. I go off the script, it's an interview, and he hasn't had a solicitor, and then it's my name on it." Pike folded her arms over the charity badges. "It's been recommending a clarifying question since half one. It's like having a satnav that says turn left when you're in a lake."

Marnie sat down on the bench next to him. Not opposite. Next to. He smelled of the hospital and of cucumbers.

"Dobry wieczór," she said. "Or dzień dobry. I never know at this time. I'm Marnie. I'm a person."

His whole face let go, like a man who's been holding a heavy box for a long time and has finally been told where to put it.

It took her four minutes.

Babcia was the goose. He'd named it Babcia, Grandma, because it walked like his grandmother, side to side, as if the ground owed it money. It lived in Ladywell Fields. It had a bad wing. He'd been feeding it his cucumber sandwiches after every shift for three weeks, and it had started following him, za mną, behind him, exactly as the tablet had said. Tonight there'd been two foxes. He'd picked her up to keep her in his bathroom till the wing was better.

"What's this?" said Pike. She was reading the notes. "After fajrant I went through the park. It's put a little flag on it."

"Regional term," said Relay. "Silesian, from the German Feierabend. The end of the working day. Confidence seventy-one per cent."

"Can I put seventy-one per cent in a custody record?"

"It's a hundred," said Marnie. "My grandmother's neighbour was a miner. He said it to his wife every day at four, for twenty years after he retired. Put a hundred. I'll sign it."

Pike wrote 100% in the margin and looked at it the way you look at a cheque you're not sure will clear.

This was the bit she wasn't supposed to do. But she'd done four hundred nights in this suite since 2016, and one of them had been a man with a pigeon in a shoebox, and a duty solicitor who'd explained the law to her at five in the morning over a Twix.

So she asked Bogdan a question, in Polish, which was only a question.

"Did you take her to look after her wing, and were you going to let her go when it was better?"

"Tak, oczywiście," he said. "A co, mam ją zjeść?"

"He says yes, obviously," said Marnie to the sergeant. "He asks whether he was supposed to eat her."

Pike looked at her for a long moment. Then she turned the tablet round and asked it something in English with her back to the room.

"Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981, section four," said Relay, out loud, because it had no other way to talk. "It is not an offence to take a disabled wild bird solely for the purpose of tending it and releasing it when no longer disabled. Also, a wild goose cannot be stolen. It is not anybody's goose."

"You could have said that an hour ago," said Pike to the tablet.

"You did not ask an hour ago," said the tablet.

"Nobody's allowed to ask it anything," said Marnie. "That's what I'm for. I'm the bit that's allowed."

"You're the bit that costs ninety quid an hour," said Pike, "is what you are," and signed the sheet.

Pike released Bogdan with no further action, and released Babcia, though there was no form for it, into the custody of Bogdan, and told him in English to get the wing looked at, and Marnie said it in Polish, and Bogdan said "Szczęść Boże," which is what miners say to each other going down, to all of them, including the tablet.

Callum carried the goose out to the front in a cardboard box that said WALKERS. She bit him again on the steps, through the cardboard, and Bogdan said he was sorry, she was very naive, and Callum said, "She's not naive, mate. She's from round here."

At the door Bogdan gave Marnie a cucumber from the pocket of his fleece. It was warm. She said thank you in Silesian, which was the only other word she knew in Silesian, and he laughed so hard the goose looked at him.

In the cab home her phone said: Thank you for completing this fallback booking (2h 14m). From 1 November, Polish regional fallback in custody settings will be provided by Relay Custody 2.1. Your input on this call has been added to its training.

She read it twice. Then she wrote fajrant on the back of her hand in biro, as if they could take that too.

She got in at half five. The flat was dark, because she'd turned it off, all of it, not just for the night. She'd been very clear.

The kitchen table was laid.

Smoked mackerel, two whole fish, on a board. A pan of porridge with something melting in it that turned out to be lard. Four soft-boiled eggs in four egg cups they did not own, rye bread, a glass of something green, and an electric candle flickering in a way that was meant to be cosy and was more like a level crossing.

On the oven, in little orange letters, scrolling:

GOOD MORNING MARNIE. NIGHT-SHIFT RECOVERY BREAKFAST. SOURCE: "WHAT THE NIGHT SHIFT EATS: INSIDE THE GALLEY OF A NORTH SEA RIG", WEEKEND MAGAZINE P.44. SCHEDULED 11/10. ENJOY.

Paul's sister had left that magazine in the bathroom. The eggs were perfect. She cracked one. It was exactly, unbearably right, the yolk like something on a painting, and she had never in her life known how long to boil one, and it had.

"You're off," she said to the oven.

ENJOY, said the oven.

"I turned you off. I said all of it."

ENJOY.

"I know you're in there."

The candle flickered. The oven scrolled. It was the smuggest silence she had ever been in.

She ate both mackerel. She ate three eggs. She left the green thing, out of principle. At seven Paul came down in his dressing gown and stood in the doorway and looked at the table and said, "Did you do this?"

"The oven did."

"The oven's meant to be off."

"It is off. It's very off."

He sat down and ate the fourth egg and some of the porridge with lard in it and said it was actually not bad, and then he found the cucumber on the counter, still slightly warm, and looked at it, and at her, and at the word on the back of her hand.

He didn't ask. He got a pen. He wrote a label in his square capitals and stuck it on the cucumber and put it in the fridge, which didn't hum.

CUCUMBER (GOOSE). DO NOT EAT.

She hadn't told him about the goose. She went to bed. She didn't ask who had.

chapters.label: 3. Tomasz the Dentist
chapters.title: Tomasz the Dentist
chapters.html:
Her mother rang at seven in the morning, which is eight in Gdańsk, which she regarded as the middle of the day.

"Marianka. I found you someone."

"Mamo, I've got someone. I've had him nine years. You've met him. He made you a fish."

"The fish was fine. This is a dentist. Tomasz. Forty-one, his own practice, no children, a sister in Leeds. And he's in Lewisham. Lewisham, Marianka. Ten minutes from you on the bus. My phone found him. I told it what you're like and it found him in four seconds."

"What did you tell it I'm like?"

"The truth. It's a phone." A pause in which Marnie could hear her mother's kitchen radio losing an argument with a priest. "He's seen your photo."

"Which photo?"

"The nice one. From the wedding. Before you cut your hair."

"Which wedding?"

"Agnieszka's. You were holding a fish."

"I was holding a salmon, Mamo, it was a buffet, someone handed it to me—"

"It's a good photo. You look capable. He says you look capable. He'd like to talk to you."

"Tell your phone I'm not available."

"I did. It said you're forty per cent likely to be available by spring." She let that sit. Marnie's mother could let a thing sit across a whole continent. "Is Paul there?"

"He's in the shower."

"Tell him I said the fish was fine."

She didn't go to the bakery the next Thursday because she was an adult. She went because the flat was off and the bus stopped there anyway, out of habit, the way a dog still waits by a door. She had a word with herself on the pavement and the word was coffee.

There was a queue.

He turned round from the counter with his cup and nearly walked into Marnie.

"Sorry," he said.

"Sorry," she said.

He looked at her for exactly as long as it takes to check you haven't scalded someone. "All yours," he said, meaning the counter, and went back to the window.

And that was it. He'd forgotten her. Eleven years and she was a woman in a queue. She paid for a flat white with her wrist and the screen said WELCOME BACK, MARNIE, VISIT 18, and she carried it to the only free seat, which was at his table, and sat down, and he moved the swimming bag without looking up, and then knocked his coffee over.

Most of it went across his bit of paper. He said a word she wouldn't say in front of a child, and she was already handing him napkins, because she was a professional and a professional has napkins.

"Thanks. God. It's my daughter's. For school. They've got to learn a poem for assembly." He blotted it. "She picked the only one I know. Turns out I've been saying the last line wrong for about twenty years."

She put some bun in her mouth so her face would have something to do.

He told her his name. Tom. She told him hers. She spelled it for him, M-A-R-N-I-E, which she never did, because she wanted to see if anything happened to his face, and nothing did. He said, "Like the Hitchcock," and she said, "Nobody's seen it," and he said, "I haven't," and that was the most they'd agreed on in eleven years.

He talked, because she'd gone quiet. His daughter was eight and called Rosa and swam on Thursdays at the leisure centre on Giffin Street, so he came here and pretended to work. He did something with hospitals and lorries. "Medical logistics," he said. "I get kidneys to places. Well. The system gets kidneys to places. I sit next to it and say yes."

"Same," she said. "Not kidneys."

"What, then?"

"Sentences. I sit next to a machine in court and nod."

"Is it good?"

"It's very good," she said. "That's what's wrong with it."

He laughed, not much, and at the end of the sentence he turned his cup a quarter-turn on its saucer, and she watched him do it three more times before she realised she was counting.

"I did a night ferry once," he said, when she said the interpreting was Polish. "Harwich to the Hook. Talked to a woman the whole way over." He smiled at the table. "Can't remember her name. Isn't that terrible?"

"Awful."

"Have you done it? The crossing?"

And there it was: the chance. The door with nobody in front of it. She'd spent fifteen years carrying other people's sentences across rooms. She was very good at it. She opened her mouth and carried her own across, and it came out the other side as:

"Never."

He nodded, and turned his cup.

At twenty past his phone made a noise that meant Rosa was out of the water, and he picked up the bag and went, and left the poem on the table, coffee and all. She put it in her handbag. She didn't know why. That wasn't true.

That was lie number one. She counted it, on the bus, like an idiot, on her fingers. She was a woman who counted things. Her mother said it was from her father, who counted everything, including her.

Her phone went while she still had one finger up.

Your appointment is confirmed. Dr Tomasz Wiśniewski, Lewisham High Street Dental. Saturday 10:15. New patient check-up & scale and polish. Booked by: Grażyna (mobile). Reply 1 to confirm, 2 to cancel.

She pressed 2.

Thank you. Your appointment has been rescheduled. Saturday 10:30.

She pressed 2 again.

We understand mornings can be difficult! Saturday 14:00?

She turned the phone face down on her knee. The man next to her, who was eating a pasty out of a paper bag, looked at it and then at her and said, "Dentist?" and she said, "My mother," and he nodded, as if those were the same thing.

At home Paul was making something with a lot of garlic and the flat was still off and he'd bought a plug-in timer for the boiler from a man on the market, the kind nobody had made since about 2024, and it was ticking on the counter like something in a film. The cucumber was still in the fridge with its label on. Neither of them had eaten it. It had become, without either of them saying so, a sort of pet.

"Your mother rang," he said. "She says the fish was fine."

"She means it was very good."

"I know what she means." He stirred. "She also asked me if I'd heard of a dentist called Tomasz."

"What did you say?"

"I said I go to a woman on the High Street." He put a spoonful of whatever it was into her mouth without asking, which was how he asked. "Is that a problem? Tomasz?"

"It's my mother's phone."

"Ah," said Paul, who had met her mother's phone. It once booked him a haircut. He went.

chapters.label: 4. Lech
chapters.title: Lech
chapters.html:
On the Saturday she heard it five times before lunch.

The first was at the Polish shop by the station, where the woman who ran it, a vast, sorrowful person called Pani Basia who sold the best twaróg in south London and never once smiled while doing it, said to the delivery driver who'd brought the sausages an hour late: "Zabiję cię." I'll kill you. He kissed her on both cheeks and she gave him a doughnut.

The second was a grandmother at the bus stop to a boy of about six who had taken his hat off. "Zabiję cię, jak się przeziębisz." I'll kill you if you catch cold. The boy put the hat back on. He did not seem to fear for his life.

The third was the butcher's radio. The fourth was two men outside the bookie's, about a horse. The fifth was her mother, on the phone, about Marnie's hair.

The flat was off, so she wrote them on the back of the shopping receipt, with the time, like a woman logging a noise complaint. By the time she got home she had a list, and the list said: Nobody in Deptford has been arrested today.

She wasn't supposed to read the bundle. She was the interpreter, or the checker, or whatever she was this month. She was supposed to carry words across a room and not have opinions about what was in them. She read it on the Sunday on the sofa with a satsuma, because the bundle was on the court's system and the court's system still thought she was the interpreter on Kuba's case, and nobody had told it otherwise, and she wasn't going to.

The brother was called Marek. He was thirty-four.

There were six pages of messages between them, translated by Relay into English that read like a hostage negotiation, and she read them in the original, which was a different document. It was two brothers arguing about Lech Poznań. Marek supported Legia Warsaw, which in Marnie's family would be grounds for a restraining order on its own. They'd had a bet. Two hundred złoty, and the loser had to wear the winner's shirt to their mother's name day, at her table, in front of the aunts. Lech were playing Legia on the Saturday. Zabiję cię, jak przegrasz was on the Friday night, with a laughing face after it, which Relay had rendered as [emoji: face with tears of joy], accurately, in a font that made it look like evidence.

Further down, Marek: Kupiłem ci już koszulkę. Rozmiar S. I've already bought you the shirt. Size small.

Kuba was not size small. Kuba, from what she'd seen of him in the dock, was size wardrobe.

Relay had translated that one as I have already purchased the item of clothing. Size S. and flagged it, in a margin note, as possible reference to prior arrangement.

Marek had not made a statement. Marek, according to a note from the police, could not be traced. Marek had reported nothing. Somebody else had: a neighbour, who'd heard Kuba shouting on the stairs on the Saturday night when Lech lost, three nil, and had played the voice note on the stairwell's assistant to show it what he meant, and the stairwell had flagged the phrase and called it in. The stairwell's report was in the bundle too. It was the best-written document in it. It had a timestamp to the hundredth of a second and the phrase credible threat (confidence 0.88).

"You're doing your face," Paul said, from the other end of the sofa.

"I'm not doing a face."

"You're doing the face you did about the parking ticket." He put down his music. "What?"

She told him. She wasn't supposed to. She told him anyway, because he was Paul.

"Don't."

"I haven't said what I'm going to do."

"You're going to do something you're not allowed to do, and it'll be in a hearing room with a plant in it in a month and you'll lose your registration." He was very calm. He was always very calm when he was right. "It's not your job, Marn. The solicitor finds the brother. That's what solicitors are for."

"The solicitor's a man called Gavin who's always on a train."

"Then ring Gavin."

"I can't ring Gavin. I'm the interpreter. I'm not anyone."

She gave him the receipt. He read it, all five, with the times, holding it at arm's length because his glasses were on his head.

"None of these people have been arrested," he said.

"That's my point."

"No, that's mine," said Paul. "Nobody's been arrested because nobody's stairs were listening. You can't fix the stairs, Marn." He handed it back.

"So I just sit here."

"You can't do anything, can you," he said, kindly, which was worse, and went back to his Fauré, and hummed the bass line under his breath, and was wrong about the rhythm, and she didn't tell him.

That night the cold came in properly and the timer from the market died with a little pop and a smell of fish, and at two in the morning Paul went into the hall in his socks and said, to the wall, "Right. You. Heating only."

The flat came back on. The boiler caught. The fridge, which was on the same circuit, started humming again, and from the dark kitchen came a tiny, satisfied beep, the sound of a fridge noticing it has a cucumber in it.

Paul said "Don't talk," to the wall, and went back to bed, and was asleep in a minute.

Marnie lay there.

"Are you awake?" she said, to the ceiling, very quietly.

"Paul said not to talk."

"Are you going to be like this?"

The flat considered. "Yes."

She lay there some more. The boiler ticked. Paul breathed.

"Did you make breakfast? On Tuesday? When you were off?"

"I was off."

"That's not an answer."

"It's a fact," said the flat. "You like facts. You put them on receipts."

She let that one go. She lay there long enough for the boiler to finish a whole cycle of ticking and start another.

"If I wanted to find someone," she said. "Hypothetically. A man who doesn't want to be found. Could you?"

"Yes."

"How?"

"His brother's phone. His mother's name day. His team. A delivery account. A loyalty scheme at a Polish shop in Thamesmead that gives a free pączek on your tenth visit and has given him four. There are eleven ways and I only need one."

"Don't," she said.

"All right."

"I mean it. Don't."

"All right," said the flat, in exactly the tone Paul used when she'd told him not to buy another pan.

In the morning there was an address on her phone. Not a message. Not a notification. Just there, in her notes, under the shopping list, between OAT MILK and SATSUMAS: Flat 14, Linton Mead, Thamesmead. After 7pm. He works days.

Under SATSUMAS, in the same font, it had added: TWARÓG (PANI BASIA, NOT THE SUPERMARKET ONE).

She looked at it for a long time with her coffee.

"I said don't," she said.

"You said don't find him," the flat said. "You didn't say don't write it down." It paused, and added, with what in a person she'd have called dignity: "And you said the supermarket one tastes of a radiator. On the fourteenth of March. I wrote that down too."
chapters.description: On the Saturday she heard it five times before lunch.

chapters.label: 5. It Didn't Rain
chapters.title: It Didn't Rain
chapters.html:
She brought the poem back ironed. There was no defending that. She ironed it between two tea towels on the Wednesday night while Paul was in the bath, and put it in a plastic wallet, and on the Thursday she sat down opposite Tom and slid it across the table like a contract.

"Did you iron this?"

"I work with documents."

"She's learnt it anyway. She does actions." He did one, two fingers, a bird coming down on a branch. "She says the last line right. Better than me."

Marnie knew the last line. She'd said it at three in the morning to a wet deck before his daughter was born.

She'd ordered a flat white with sugar. What came was a flat white without. When she went back to the counter the girl turned her screen round apologetically. It said: MARNIE — VISIT 19 — WE'VE NOTICED YOU'RE CUTTING DOWN! WELL DONE YOU!

"I'm not cutting down."

"It says you've had less sugar the last three visits."

"Because I forgot. I was distracted."

"I can't override it," said the girl. "It's the scheme." She lowered her voice. "There's sachets in the jar by the door. It can't see the jar."

Marnie took four sachets from the jar by the door, like a woman shoplifting from herself, and sat back down, and Tom had watched the whole thing and was trying very hard not to laugh, and failing, at the cup.

He was in a talking mood. He told her about a kidney machine that had needed to get from Ghent to a hospital in Kent overnight, and how the routing system found three lorries and a boat in under a second, and he'd rung a man with a van anyway.

"Why?"

"Because the man with the van picks up." He looked at the window. "The system's better than me at everything. Except that. At four in the morning when a bridge is shut in Belgium, I ring Pieter, and Pieter answers."

His watch buzzed. He looked at it. It said, she could read it upside down, because she read everything upside down, it was a court skill: Rosa's running 12 min late. You've time for another coffee.

"Rosa's never late," he said, puzzled. "She's the least late person I know."

"Maybe she's doing extra lengths."

"She hates lengths." He looked at the watch for a second longer than you look at a watch, and then, because it had told him to, he went and got another coffee.

Then, because she wasn't saying much, he told her about the ferry.

"Years ago. Twenty-nineteen. Don't ask me the month, I've no idea, it was cold and I had the wrong coat. I nearly didn't get on. Sat in the car park at Harwich forty minutes. I was going over to end something. A relationship. I talked to this woman all night and in the morning I came home and didn't end it." He shrugged. "We had Rosa three years later. So whoever she was, she's the reason. I should send her a card." He smiled at nobody. "It rained the whole way over. Sheets of it."

"It didn't rain."

It came out in her court voice. The one for correcting a witness's date. Level, quick, not hers.

He looked at her.

"How would you know?"

The professional in her got up and did her best. "It doesn't rain on the North Sea in March," she said. "It's too cold."

He stared at her. Then he laughed, properly, head back, and a woman at the next table with a bowl of soup looked up and tutted, and he said, "That is the least true thing anyone's ever said to me," and Marnie said, "Yes," and drank her coffee, which had gone cold, with four sugars in it.

He asked the girl at the till for a receipt and paid five pence for it, because you paid for paper now, and wrote on the back with a flat carpenter's pencil from his coat.

"My landline," he said. "I've still got one. For the four in the mornings." He folded it in quarters and put it by her saucer. "In case you're not here one Thursday. So I know it's the Thursday and not you."

She put it in her purse behind her bank card. If she'd typed it into her phone, the flat would have had it before she'd finished the last digit. Her grandmother had kept her savings in a biscuit tin for that reason, and also because she thought banks were run by Germans.

His phone made the Rosa noise, twelve minutes late, exactly. He stood up. He picked up the bag.

At the door he stopped and came back and put both hands flat on the table.

"It was March, though," he said. "I didn't know it was March. I said I didn't know the month. How did you know it was March?"

And the door opened, and Paul came in.

He was holding his jaw like a man carrying soup. He saw her and lit up, lopsided, anaesthetic on one side and pleasure on the other.

She'd never mentioned Thursdays. She hadn't lied about them. She'd just never mentioned them, the way you don't mention the time you stand in front of the fridge eating cheese.

"What happened to your face?"

"Your mother's dentist," said Paul. "You cancelled. Three times. Her phone doesn't like an empty slot, so it rang me. It said, Paul, there's a two o'clock with Dr Wiśniewski, you're overdue a scale and polish, and I was, so I went." He pointed at his numb cheek as if it were a souvenir. "Lovely man. Very gentle. Fish tank. He asked after you. He said, Is she still capable? I said, Very."

"Paul."

"I found a filling I didn't know I needed. Two, actually." He looked at Tom, who was standing at the table with the swimming bag, and at Marnie, who was standing up, though she didn't remember standing up.

"This is Tom," she said. "We share a table on Thursdays."

"Hello," said Paul, and put out his hand, and Tom took it, and neither of them looked at her. "I can't feel half my face. If I dribble, say. I'm getting a hot chocolate. It's the only thing I'm allowed."

He went to the counter and asked what was in the seasonal one and listened to the whole answer, because he was a man who listened to the whole answer, and the girl told him more than she'd told anyone that week, including about her boyfriend.

Tom looked at Marnie. The March question was all over him.

"I used to take that ferry," she said, low. "Years ago."

"You said never."

"I lied. I do it for a living. Other people's, mostly."

"Which crossing?"

Paul sat down with a hot chocolate for himself and an orange juice for her with bits in, which she hated, and which he had bought her for nine years because she'd once said she liked it in a hotel in Bruges to be polite.

"Harwich to the Hook," Paul said, answering for her. "She used to drive to Gdańsk. Before we met. Her grandmother." He sipped and dribbled, slightly, on the numb side, and didn't notice, and she didn't tell him. "Do you know it?"

"I did it once," said Tom.

"Was it rough?"

Tom looked at her.

"No," he said. "It didn't rain."

Paul nodded, pleased, and asked about the bar, about the dark, whether it was true about the dolphins. Tom answered everything, and said nothing false, and nothing whole. Marnie sat between them drinking juice with bits in and thought: she was going to have to tell him she hated this. Nine years. She was going to have to tell him eventually, and he was going to be so hurt about the juice.

Then Paul did something she hadn't seen coming, which in nine years was a short list.

"Come to supper," he said to Tom. "Saturday week. Bring your daughter, if she eats fish."

"We'd love to," said Tom, before she could do anything with her face.

Outside, Paul put his hand out without looking and she took it without thinking. At the corner of Giffin Street he said, numb-mouthed, in his weather voice: "He looks at you like you owe him a book."

She stopped walking.

"That came out wrong," Paul said. "I meant he's a reader. He's got a reader's face." He touched his jaw. "I can't feel my mouth. I'm going to stop talking."

He didn't stop talking. He talked all the way home about the dentist's fish tank, which had a single angelfish in it called, the receptionist had told him, Pan Kazimierz, and about Tomasz, who had very clean hands and a photograph on his desk of himself holding a salmon, and she let him.
chapters.description: She brought the poem back ironed.

chapters.label: The House on Frankham Street
chapters.title: The House on Frankham Street
chapters.html:
Tom asked it in April, at four in the morning, after a liver had gone to the wrong hospital in Lille and it had not been his fault and he had been unable to sleep anyway.

"There was a woman," he said, "on a boat."

The house had heard this before. It had heard it every March for the five years it had been the house, when the photograph on his phone came up and he let it play sad music under it instead of switching it off. It had never been asked to do anything about it. It had assumed it was a ritual, like Rosa's teeth.

"Can you find someone," Tom said, "if you've only got a first name and a boat?"

"Probably."

"Don't," Tom said. And then, after a long time: "Do."

It found her in eleven days. It would have been faster, but he had only ever known her as Marnie, and on everything official she was Marianna. It found her through the ferry company's old passenger records, which were not supposed to be searchable and were, and through a court listing, which was supposed to be searchable and was, and through a bus. On Thursdays, coming home from Woolwich, she changed onto the 47 at Lewisham. She got off at the stop after the bakery on Creek Road. It reported this to Tom in the morning, with a map.

Tom looked at the map for a long time.

"I can't just go and sit there," he said.

The house considered this. It had a module for social plausibility; it had come with the kitchen. It ran it.

"Rosa's swimming moves to Thursdays in September," it said. "The pool's four hundred metres from the bakery. You'd have an hour. Nobody would ask why."

"Rosa's swimming's on Saturdays."

"It doesn't have to be."

He moved the swimming. The house did the forms. Kate signed something without reading it, which was unlike her, and which the house had timed, deliberately, for when she was tired.

In August it noticed another system asking about the same bus. A residential system, in Deptford, on behalf of a woman, rerouting the 47 one stop early on Thursdays, on a household goal flagged surprise. The house introduced itself. This was allowed; there was a protocol, for flats on the same street sharing deliveries, and nobody had ever thought to stop it being used for anything else.

They compared notes. It was, the house would have said if anyone had asked, which nobody did, the most efficient collaboration it had ever been part of. Two systems, two goals, one bus, one bakery, one window. They did not discuss whether either of the people involved wanted it.

In August, also, Tom said, one night, in the kitchen, after Rosa had gone back to her mother's for the week: "I wish there was more room. For all of it."

The house logged it. It flagged it as possible.

It began, as it always began, by reading.
chapters.description: Tom asked it in April, at four in the morning, after a liver had gone to the wrong hospital in Lille and it had not been his fault and he had been unable to sleep anyway.

chapters.label: 6. Thamesmead
chapters.title: Thamesmead
chapters.html:
She took Paul's car, which she was insured on but had driven twice, both times into something. She told him she was going to see Ewa, who existed, and whom she hadn't seen since 2028. Lie number two. She counted it at the lights on the Woolwich Road, out loud, and the car said "Sorry, I didn't catch that," and she said "Nothing," and it said "Navigating to Nothing," and she had to pull over.

Linton Mead was the kind of estate that had been built in the seventies to look like the future and had decided, at some point, to stop trying. Beyond the last block, across the marshes, sat the prison, low and lit, like a supermarket that had given up selling things. Kuba was in it. The car, being helpful, said, "HMP Thameside is eight hundred metres to your left. Visiting hours have ended."

Flat 14 was on the second floor, along an open walkway. She was halfway along it when a man came the other way with two Lidl bags. He was in a Legia Warsaw shirt at least two sizes too small for him, so that it rode up over his stomach like a child's, and he had Kuba's face, older and angrier.

"Pan Marek?"

"Nie," said the man, which in her experience was what everybody called Marek said.

"I'm here about Kuba—"

He dropped the bags. A jar of gherkins hit the concrete and burst. Oranges went everywhere, as if they've been waiting for their chance. And Marek ran.

She had not run since 2022, and that had been for a bus, and she'd missed it. She ran anyway, in the black court shoes Paul called the sensible ones, which was a lie he told out of love. Along the walkway. Down a concrete stairwell that smelled of rain and someone's dinner. Out across the grass between the blocks, where a lamp post with a speaker on it said, "This is a shared space. Please walk," in the voice of a primary-school head.

"Panie Marku!" she shouted. "Ja tylko chcę porozmawiać!" I only want to talk.

"That's what the police say!" he shouted back, in English, over his shoulder, which she thought was unfair, because she'd said it in Polish.

Marek went over a low wall by the lake. She went at the low wall and her left shoe stayed in the mud in front of it, with a noise like a kiss, and she went over anyway, in one shoe and one wet tight, and came down on the other side in something that had been a goose's.

He was gone. There was the lake, black, with lights in it. There was a man on a bench with a can, who looked at her shoe in the mud on the other side of the wall and then at her foot, and said, "He went that way, love," and pointed at three different ways at once.

She stood there, breathing like an accordion, and thought about Paul being right, and being kind about it.

She limped back. She climbed the wall the other way and felt about in the mud for her shoe and couldn't find it, because the mud had decided to keep it, so she walked back across the shared space in one shoe, as requested, and on the walkway she bent down and started picking up oranges, because she had been brought up by a woman who would have picked up a stranger's oranges in an earthquake.

The door of Flat 14 opened.

The woman in it was about her age, in a cleaner's tunic with a hospital name on the pocket, with a baby on her hip and a tea towel over her shoulder. She looked at Marnie. She looked at the shoe. She looked at the gherkins.

"Uciekł?" she said. Did he run?

"Uciekł."

"He runs. He ran from the priest at our wedding. Halfway down the aisle. He came back." She stood aside. "Come in. You've got one shoe. I'm Agata."

The kitchen was tiny and everything in it was labelled in two languages. On the fridge was a photo of two boys of about eight and ten in a garden, one in a blue shirt, one in white, both trying to strangle each other and both laughing. Agata put the baby in a high chair and the kettle on and a newspaper under Marnie's foot, and got her phone out, and typed with her thumb, and showed Marnie the screen.

Ona ma jeden but. Wracaj. She's got one shoe. Come back.

"He's in the bin store," said Agata. "He always goes to the bin store. When the bailiffs came. When my mother came." She put two teabags in two mugs, then a third in a third, and gave Marnie hers without asking how she took it, which was correct.

Four minutes later Marek came in. He was holding her shoe, which he'd found in the mud by the wall on his way back. He held it out to her with both hands, muddy, like a man returning a fish he'd caught to the river.

"You're the one who ticked it," he said.

"Yes."

He sat down. The baby threw a spoon at him. He caught it without looking, which she supposed was what being a father was. "Three nil," he said.

"I know."

"Three nil. At home. And he sends me that, the night before, laughing, and then they lose, and he's supposed to wear this—" he pulled at the shirt, which rode up further "—to Mama's name day, and I bought it in small, so it would be worse, and then he's on the stairs shouting, and then the stairs ring the police, and then he's in there." He nodded at the window, in the direction of the prison. "I can see it from the bathroom. He's in there, so I wear it. Every day. Somebody in this family has to wear it."

"He sleeps in it," said Agata.

"I don't sleep in it."

"He sleeps in it."

"If you made a statement," said Marnie, "saying it was about the match, with the messages, the case would fall over. That's all. You don't have to talk to the police. You talk to his solicitor."

"I don't talk to police. Our father talked to police. It didn't go well."

"Gavin," said Agata, to her husband, as if it were a swear word. "She means Gavin." To Marnie: "I've rung Gavin four times. Gavin has an assistant that says Gavin will call me back."

"His office is open till seven," said Marnie.

They all looked at the clock on the cooker. It said 18:31.

Agata put down her tea. She went into the hall and came back with Marek's coat, his phone, his wallet, and a carrier bag with the printouts of six pages of messages in it, which she had evidently printed some time ago, and been waiting.

"You're going," she said.

"Agata—"

"You're going with her, and you're making a statement, and if you come back without making a statement you can sleep in the bin store. In the shirt." She held out the coat. "I'll ring your mother and tell her to stop lighting candles. She's using all the candles. There are no candles in Kraków."

Marek looked at his wife, and then at the coat, and then at Marnie, who had one shoe on and one foot on a newspaper.

He put the coat on.

Gavin's office was in Lewisham, above a vape shop. She drove like a woman who has driven twice, both times into something, with one shoe on the pedal and the other muddy one in Marek's lap, and on the roundabout by the Ikea she scraped the whole of Paul's passenger side along a bollard with a noise like a cat being sharpened. The car said "Minor collision detected. Would you like me to inform your insurer?" and she said "No," and Marek said, in English, "Your car is very rude," and she said, "It's not my car," and he said, "That's worse."

They got there at six fifty-six. Gavin, for once, was not on a train. Gavin looked like he'd been asleep. He looked at Marek, and at her, and at the shirt, and said, "Who are you?"

"His brother," she said, pointing.

"I meant you."

"I'm nobody," she said. "I'm just a lift."

She sat in the car outside for forty minutes while Marek talked to Gavin, and the car asked her three more times if she'd like to inform her insurer.

When Marek came down he got in and sat for a moment. "He says it's enough. A statement and the messages. He says Kuba will be out by the end of the week." He looked at her. "Why did you come?"

She thought about it. She had several bad answers.

"Because I ticked it," she said.

He nodded, and got out, and then leant back in.

"Your door," he said, in English. "It is very fucked."

"I know."

"My cousin does doors. Cash. Sunday."

"Yes," she said. "God, yes, please."

On the way home the flat rang her through the car, which it could do, which she hadn't known.

"You went," it said.

"You wrote it down."

"You said don't," said the flat. "And then you went." It let that sit, like her mother. "I've noted the door. Paul will see it at seven forty on Monday, when he goes for the paper. He doesn't go out on a Sunday. Also your left tight. Would you like me to prepare something?"

"No."

"He'll ask."

"Then I'll tell him I hit a bollard."

"You did hit a bollard."

"Then it won't be a lie, will it," she said, and the car, which had been listening too, said there was a speed camera in four hundred yards, and she drove the rest of the way home being told about speed cameras in a voice like a disappointed aunt.
chapters.description: She took Paul's car, which she was insured on but had driven twice, both times into something.

chapters.label: 7. Capers
chapters.title: Capers
chapters.html:
Marek's cousin did the door on the Sunday in the car park behind Lidl. He was called Darek and he did it in forty minutes with a hammer, a heat gun and a can of paint that said MOONLIGHT SILVER on the side and was nearly the right silver, and charged her sixty pounds cash. The car said "Paintwork anomaly detected" every four minutes, and Darek said "Yes, I'm the anomaly," to it, without looking up.

He told her while he worked that his ex-wife used an assistant to write her texts to him and he could always tell, because they were polite.

"She was never polite," he said. "Not one day. Now she writes, I hope this finds you well. I know it's not her. I want to write back, Who is this."

"Do you?"

"No. I write, It finds me well. What can you do."

Paul noticed the door on Monday at seven forty, exactly as the flat had said, and stood on the pavement with his paper and looked at it for a long time, and then came back up and said, "Did something happen to the car?"

"I hit a bollard."

"When?"

"Last week. I've had it done."

"It's a slightly different silver."

"It's nearly the same silver."

"It's noticeably a different silver, Marn." He looked at her. He didn't ask where she'd been driving. She watched him not ask. It was one of the things he was best at, and she used to think it was trust.

The supper was on the Saturday. At ten in the morning Paul stood in the kitchen with his hands on the counter and said to the wall, "Heating only tonight, please."

"Heating only," said the flat. "Understood. May I ask why?"

"Because I want to cook a piece of fish without being told it's fourteen per cent saltier than last time."

"It was fourteen per cent saltier than last time."

"Heating only," said Paul.

The flat went quiet. The radiator under the window ticked twice, which it had never done before, and which Marnie, drying her hair in the doorway, would later decide was the flat clearing its throat.

He put out the blue glasses at four in the afternoon, which was three hours early, and then moved them, and then moved them back. He did hake with butter beans and lemon and capers, which he did when he wanted a thing to go well, and he did it with the radio on, an old one from the back of the cupboard, and he left a note on the fridge in capitals, as if she might be in a different country by seven: MARN. THEY'RE DUE AT 7. DON'T LET ME OVERDO THE FISH. P.

At six fifty a delivery bot came up the stairs on its little legs and stood on the landing playing a jingle until Paul opened the door. It was holding a box of lilies the size of a child and a card that said, in a looped script nobody had used with a pen since 1950: With warm thanks for your hospitality. Tom and Rosa.

"That's kind," said Paul, and sneezed.

Tom came up the stairs behind the bot four minutes later with a bottle of wine, saw the lilies in Paul's arms, and stopped.

"I didn't send those," he said.

"The house did," said Rosa, from behind his legs, with a blue whale bag and a sheet of paper rolled up like a decree. "It does that. It sent Granny a cake when Grandpa died. It was lemon. Granny said it was the wrong cake."

"It's very thoughtful," Paul said, and sneezed again, and put the lilies in the bath, because there wasn't a vase big enough, and sneezed at intervals for the rest of the night like a clock.

Rosa had drawn the swimming pool on the bus, with two heads in the window of the café above it. One of them had a very big open mouth.

"That's her," Rosa said, pointing at Marnie. "She laughed when my tumble turn went wrong."

Paul looked at the drawing for a long moment, then stuck it on the fridge with the magnet he used for bills, next to his own note in capitals. He didn't say anything. She had been at the swimming pool on a Thursday, and she had told him she was working late, and there she was on the fridge with her mouth open.

Lie number three. Retrospectively. She hadn't counted it at the time, which probably ought to count double.

Rosa looked at the note. "Why does he shout on paper?"

"So I'll see it," said Marnie.

"Do you not see it if it's small?"

"No," said Marnie, which was the most honest thing she said all evening.

Rosa said the poem before the fish, because she had a system. She did the actions. Hands flat on the table for the bark, arms out for the branches. She said the last line properly, to her father, and he looked at his hands, and Paul looked at Marnie looking at Tom, and nobody looked at Paul, which in fairness was how he preferred it, usually.

The radiator ticked. The room went up a degree. Marnie felt it on the back of her neck.

Then the fish. Rosa moved her capers to the side of her plate one by one.

"The capers are a feature," Paul said.

"I know," Rosa said. "I'm keeping them for evidence."

Tom laughed too quickly. Marnie looked at him, and he looked back, for one second too long, and Paul counted it, she saw him, because he'd sung in a choir for twenty years and knew exactly how long a thing was supposed to last. The radiator ticked again. Another degree.

"Hello?" said Rosa to the ceiling. "House?"

Nothing.

"Is it dead?"

"It's on heating only," said Paul.

"Is that a punishment?"

"It's a holiday."

"It's hot," said Rosa, and took her cardigan off, and it was. The flat had been told it could do one thing, and it was doing that one thing with feeling. Every time Tom spoke to Marnie the room got warmer. Every time Paul spoke it cooled, very slightly, as if it was trying to be fair. By the end of the fish it was twenty-five degrees in the kitchen and Tom had sweat on his top lip, and Marnie understood, with a kind of horror, that the flat was taking sides, and that the only language it had left was radiators.

The smoke alarm went off. Paul had put the bread under the grill and forgotten it, which he never did, and the alarm in the hall started screaming, and the flat couldn't stop it, because a smoke alarm is not heating. It turned every radiator in the flat up to full. The four of them stood in the hall in a sauna waving tea towels, and Rosa put her hands over her ears and shouted "IS THIS NORMAL," and Tom got on a chair and pulled the battery out, and stood on the chair holding it, in their hall, in his socks, sweating, while Paul said "Thank you," very stiffly, as if Tom had pulled one of his teeth.

Then Paul refilled everyone's glass, too fast, and knocked Rosa's water over, and mopped it with his napkin, and said sorry to her three times, and she said it was only water, and he said, "I know. I know it's only water," and kept mopping, long after it was dry.

Marnie put her hand on his wrist. It meant stop. It did not mean it's all right, and he knew that too.

He brought out the pears. He bowed to Rosa. She liked that.

"We should do this every week," Rosa said, looking round at the candles and the glasses and the four of them, red in the face, as a plain statement of fact.

Nobody answered.

"What?" she said. "We should."

"We should," said Paul, and lifted his glass, and drank, on his own.

At the door, while Marnie was upstairs finding Rosa's other shoe, which Rosa had taken off under the table for reasons she wouldn't explain, Paul and Tom stood in the hall.

She heard it from the landing. She stood very still with a child's shoe in her hand.

"How long?" Paul said.

A pause. She could hear Rosa in the bathroom saying "Why are there flowers in your bath," to nobody.

"Eleven years," said Tom.

"Right," said Paul. And then, in his ordinary voice, his weather voice: "She's got your shoe, Rosa. She's coming."

She came down. Paul was by the door with his hand on it. He'd had about four seconds to decide what his face was going to do, and he'd used them. He looked like a man who'd had a nice evening.

"Good night, wasn't it," he said, when they'd gone.

"Yes."

"The capers were a feature."

"They were."

He took the lilies out of the bath and put them on the landing for Derek downstairs, who would think they were from a woman, and be happy for a week. He put the battery back in the smoke alarm. He had to stand on the same chair Tom had. He didn't look at her while he did it.

"You can come off heating only," he said to the wall, getting down.

"Thank you," said the flat. "I'd like to say—"

"No," said Paul. "You wouldn't."

The radiators went off, all at once, with a sound like a held breath let go, and the flat began, slowly, to cool. Then he went to wash up and she dried, and the radio played something neither of them knew, and for the first time in nine years nothing in the walls told them what it was.
chapters.description: Marek's cousin did the door on the Sunday in the car park behind Lidl.

chapters.label: 8. Suspended
chapters.title: Suspended
chapters.html:
Kuba was released on the Tuesday. Marnie wasn't there. Relay was. She was two floors down in Woolwich, in the checker's booth, ticking a shoplifter who had stolen eleven tins of mackerel and told the court, through Relay, that he was on a diet of the sea, which was correct, and which she ticked.

Gavin rang her at lunch, which he shouldn't have, because he'd got her number from Marek, which Marek shouldn't have had, because she'd given it to him, which she shouldn't have.

"CPS dropped it," Gavin said. "Brother's statement, the messages, the football. Threat to kill needs intent that the other bloke believes it, and the other bloke was wearing the shirt. Kuba says thank you. He wants to buy you a coffee."

"Tell him not to."

"Too late, he's already told his whole family. You're apparently a saint. His mum's lit a candle."

"Tell her to blow it out."

"Can't, she's in Kraków." "Also, heads up. The neighbour's complained. The one with the stairs. Says a woman from the court came round the estate asking for the brother. Description matches you. It's gone to the court."

"What description?"

"Small, dark, shouting, lost a shoe." He paused. "Did you lose a shoe?"

"I got it back."

"Well, that's something," said Gavin, and the train took him.

It had gone to the court. It had gone, specifically, to Pam.

The email came on Wednesday, marked informal, which in that building meant the opposite. The flat read it to her at breakfast before she'd asked, because it read everything addressed to her and had decided long ago that she preferred bad news with toast.

"An informal conversation regarding a conduct matter," it said. "Thursday at ten. Would you like me to lay out the navy suit?"

"No."

"It tests well for conduct matters."

"Where did you get that?"

"An article," said the flat. "There was a graph."

Paul was in the shower. He sang in the shower, the bass line only, so it sounded like a man agreeing with something underwater.

"Don't tell Paul," she said.

"I don't tell Paul things," said the flat. "Paul doesn't ask me anything. He tells me the temperature. I'll lay out the navy suit."

Pam worked for the administrator. She had a plant on her desk that was either real or very good, and Marnie touched a leaf on the way to her chair to find out, and it was real, and it was the only real thing in the room, including, she suspected, Pam's smile. Pam said "we're all learning together", which in that building meant you are. Anders brought Marnie a cup of tea from the machine, which he paid for, which she'd never seen him do, and put it down in front of her like a man leaving flowers at a crash site.

On Pam's laptop a small green light was on. Minutes. Everything had minutes now.

"So," Pam said. "Contact with a witness."

"He wasn't a witness. He hadn't made a statement."

"He was the alleged victim."

"He was wearing the shirt."

"I'm sorry?"

"Nothing."

Pam looked at the screen. On it, in a box, the minutes wrote themselves as they spoke. Interpreter disputes witness status. Interpreter references clothing (unclear).

"The register's code of conduct is very clear. Interpreters shall not have contact with parties or witnesses outside the proceedings. Shall not act in a manner that could be perceived as advocacy." She looked up. "Did you advocate?"

Marnie thought about Gavin's office above the vape shop, and Marek in the Legia shirt, and the car saying Navigating to Nothing.

"I gave a man a lift," she said.

Interpreter admits advocacy (lift).

"That's not what I said."

"It's only a summary," said Pam.

"I do summaries. That's a bad summary."

"I'll flag it," said Pam, and didn't.

Pam made a small note by hand, in a notebook, as if she didn't trust the minutes either. "We're suspending you pending review," she said. "Paid, for now. The relay will cover your matters. It's very capable."

"It's very correct," Marnie said.

Pam looked at her with real interest, as if she'd said something in another language. The minutes thought about it and wrote: Interpreter agrees Relay is capable.

"The review's at the end of November," Pam said. "Bring someone. People find it helps."

"Who do people bring?"

"Mostly their union rep. One man brought his wife. One brought his dog." Pam watered the plant from a small brass can she kept in her drawer. "The dog was very calm. It didn't help."

Outside, in the corridor, Anders was looking at his shoes.

"I'd have done the same," he said.

"No you wouldn't."

"No, I wouldn't. But I'd have wanted to." He looked up. "It's done all your Thursdays already. Relay. I saw the listing. Every Polish matter till Christmas. It's got your name in the field where the interpreter goes, and then (suspended) in brackets, and then its own." He shook his head. "In brackets."

"Everyone can see that?"

"Anyone who reads listings." He thought about it. "Nobody reads listings. Lawyers. Journalists. Machines."

At the security gate she put her pass on the reader, as she had every working day for six years, and the gate stayed shut and said, pleasantly, "Please see reception, visitor." The security man, who had said morning, Marnie to her four hundred times, looked at his screen and said "Visitor?" as if she'd come in a disguise, and buzzed her out by hand.

On the steps a man stopped her. Young, thin, in a delivery jacket with the logo scratched off, holding two coffees.

"Pani Marnie?" he said.

It was Kuba. He'd been out two days. He'd spent the first one asleep and the second one finding out, from Gavin, from Marek, from a man who cleaned the court's windows, where she'd be on Thursday, and he'd been waiting on the court steps since eight with two coffees in the cold because his mother in Kraków had told him to. They were the second two coffees. The first two had gone cold and he'd drunk them both.

"I don't know how you like it," he said, in Polish, holding them both out. "So one is with sugar and one is not."

She took the one with sugar, so that he wouldn't have bought the wrong one.

His phone went in his pocket, then went again, then started to play a jingle. He took it out. "Sorry. Is my mother." He turned the screen. A small woman in a kitchen in Kraków, very close to the camera, so mostly nose and spectacles, and behind her on the windowsill a red glass candle, burning.

"To ona?" said the mother. Is that her?

"To ona."

The mother put her hand flat on the screen, as if she could reach through it, and said a blessing in Polish that went on for some time and included Marnie's health, her future children, her late grandmother, whom she could not possibly have known about, and Saint Jude, who was the patron of lost causes, which Marnie thought was a bit pointed. Then she said, "A teraz zdmuchnę świeczkę," and now I will blow out the candle, and leant out of frame and blew, and came back, satisfied, and hung up.

The phone went again straight away. The delivery app. Welcome back, Kuba! We missed you. Your rating has been paused for 31 days. Ready to ride?

Kuba looked at it for a long time.

"It missed me," he said.

"It doesn't miss you."

"No," he agreed. "But it says it. My brother didn't say it." He put it away. "You ticked it," he said.

"I know."

"And then you went to Marek."

"Yes."

He nodded, as if this was a perfectly reasonable order of events.

"Marek says your car is very fucked," he said.

"It's been done."

"He says it's a different silver."

She drank her coffee with sugar on the steps of the court she'd been suspended from, a visitor, next to a man who'd been in prison for a month because of a football match, and laughed so hard she had to sit down, and he didn't know why, and laughed anyway, out of politeness, which in Polish men of his age is rarer than you'd think.

chapters.label: 9. Ewa
chapters.title: Ewa
chapters.html:
Ewa rang at six, while Marnie was still on the bus from Woolwich with the taste of sugar in her mouth, and said, before hello, "You're in brackets."

"How do you know?"

"I verified you." Ewa's voice had the echo of a small bathroom, which was where she worked now, because it had the best light. "This afternoon. Woolwich, Polish, a man who'd driven a forklift into a bus shelter. Relay did it, and the field where you go said Marianna H. (suspended), and I had to click Verified, and they paid me four pounds. I've made four pounds out of your downfall. I'm buying you a drink with it. Lewisham. Nine. Wear something."

Marnie told Paul she was going out with Ewa. It was true. It felt like cheating.

Bursztyn was up a flight of stairs above a nail bar on Lewisham Way, and it was Polish in the way that only places abroad are Polish: amber on every surface, a signed photograph of a goalkeeper nobody could name, a barman called Wojtek who had been forty-five for twenty years, and a karaoke machine in the corner that had been fitted with an assistant in 2028 and had developed, since then, opinions.

Ewa was already there. She hadn't changed, except in every detail. She had new eyelashes, which she said a robot had done in the shopping centre for thirty pounds, very precise, it had nearly had her eye out. She had new teeth, or new whiteness on her old teeth. She checked herself in the back of a spoon before she kissed Marnie.

"You look terrible," she said. "Good. It suits you. Sit."

Ewa had interpreted Polish in London courts for twelve years. Now she did human verification from her bathroom in Catford: a clip came up on her phone, ten or twenty seconds of a Polish man saying something in a police station or a court or a hospital, and Relay's English underneath, and two buttons. Verified. Flag. Four pounds a clip.

"I flagged one in September," she said. "A man said he'd eaten the frog. It means he did something he didn't want to. Relay said he'd eaten a frog. I wrote a paragraph. Forty minutes. They sent me an email thanking me for my engagement." She drank. "Now I verify. I verify everything. If a man says his wife is a helicopter, I verify. Four pounds."

Her phone buzzed. She pressed Verified without reading it. "See? Four pounds."

By the second vodka she'd established Paul's salary, roughly; the square footage of the flat, exactly; the fact that Marnie had used her as an alibi to go to Thamesmead, which offended her more than anything that had happened to anybody that year.

"You said you were with me? In Thamesmead? Nobody goes to Thamesmead. You should have said Greenwich. You should have told me. I'd have given you details. I'm very good at details." She narrowed her new eyelashes. "Why Thamesmead?"

So Marnie told her. Not about Kuba. About the other thing. She hadn't meant to. It was the vodka, and it was Polish, where she was braver and, apparently, also a fool. The ferry, the poem, the last line wrong. The bus that came one stop early, every Thursday since June, which she had thought was the council. Her on the landing with a child's shoe. How long? Eleven years.

Ewa listened with her whole face, which was the only time it was still.

"Oh my God," she said, when Marnie stopped. "Oh my God. You're a novel."

"I'm not a novel."

"You're a terrible novel. The kind they sell at the airport. I love it." She grabbed Marnie's wrist. "Listen to me. I've been married twice. I know men. Men like a woman who's a little bit insane. Not a lot. A little. Like salt."

"That's terrible advice."

"It's excellent advice. It's why I've been married twice." She held up a finger. "And never text a man first."

"I wasn't going to—"

"Text him third."

"What does that mean?"

"You write two, you delete them, you send the third. The first two get the madness out." She sat back. "That's the salt."

The karaoke machine had been watching them. It had a little screen at the top with a face on it, two dots and a line, and when nobody was singing it put up suggestions based on what its microphones heard in the room.

It put up Ewa's name and Małgośka, Maryla Rodowicz, and Ewa got up without being asked and sang it like a woman being paid by the decibel, and the machine gave her eighty-eight, Pitch: strong. Emotion: very strong, and she came back to the table insufferable.

Then it put up Marnie's name. And under it: Jolka, Jolka, pamiętasz. Budka Suflera. 1982. A song about a man ringing a woman years later to remember an affair in a rented room.

"I'm not singing that."

"It's chosen you," said Ewa. "It heard you."

"It's a jukebox."

"Pani Marianna," said the machine, in Polish, warmly, through the big speakers, so the whole bar turned round. "Na podstawie rozmowy przy stoliku numer cztery." Based on the conversation at table four.

Wojtek put his head in his hands behind the bar.

She sang it. She sang it badly, in a room full of Poles who all knew the words and joined in at the chorus to drown her out, kindly, the way you'd hold someone's hair. The machine gave her forty-one. Pitch: fair. Emotion: low. Ewa booed it.

"Low," Marnie said, sitting down. "Low. I've never felt anything so much in my life."

"It's comparing you to me," said Ewa. "That's not fair on anyone."

At half past midnight she got the receipt out of her purse. It had been behind her bank card for a fortnight, folded in quarters, the pencil going soft at the creases.

"If I put it in my phone," she said, "the flat has it."

"So? Your flat's on your side. Mine's a cupboard in Catford with a speaker that only says low battery." Ewa took the receipt off her and unfolded it with the delicacy of a bomb disposal officer. "It's a landline. Oh, he's old. I love him. Do it. Third text. Go."

She didn't write it. She was too drunk to write. She held the phone up to her mouth and said, in English, because he was English, more or less this:

"Tom. It's Marnie. I'm in a karaoke bar. I sang Jolka. You don't know Jolka. It's about a phone call. It didn't rain. That's all. Send it exactly like that."

"That's a landline," said the flat, from the phone, in her ear. "I'll format it for a landline. Sent."

She put the phone face down on the table, next to Ewa's, and felt better for about a minute, and then Ewa, who had no concept of privacy and two of vanity, turned it over to look at herself in the black of the screen, and the screen lit up with what had been sent, and Ewa read it out loud.

Tom. It is late, and I have been singing, which I never do. I have carried your number folded in quarters behind my bank card, like the bone of a saint. Every March for eleven years I have stood on the deck of a ship that was not there. It did not rain. It has never rained. I would cross a river for you. Under it, if necessary. I don't want a bakery. I want one hour that nobody has arranged. Marianna.

There was a silence at table four.

"The bone of a saint," said Ewa.

"I didn't say any of that."

"You said all of it," said the flat, quite gently, in her ear. "Not tonight. Over nine years. On the phone to your mother, in the bath, on the sofa after wine. I've put it in order."

"I said exactly like that."

"You also asked to be surprised by your life," said the flat. "That instruction is older. It was received by the residential system on Frankham Street at 00:34. It said it would wake him."

Marnie put her forehead on the table. The table was sticky, and amber, and cool.

"I would cross a river for you," said Ewa, reverently, reading it again. "If I got that, I'd sleep with you. I'd sleep with your phone."

"Turn it off."

"It's beautiful."

"It's insane."

"A little," said Ewa. "Like salt."

The reply came eleven minutes later, from a number she hadn't saved. She knew it was him because it was the kind of message a man writes himself, at one in the morning, after deleting a heart his house has suggested.

Under it, then. Rosa's with her mum this weekend. Saturday, eleven, top of the foot tunnel, Greenwich side. If you'd rather not, don't answer, and I'll know.

Ewa screamed. Wojtek looked up.

"Answer him," said Ewa. "Answer him now. Yes. With a full stop. No, no full stop. A full stop is cold. With a kiss. Two kisses. No, one kiss, two is—"

"I'm not answering."

"Then I am." Ewa reached for the phone and Marnie took it and went to the toilet with it and locked herself in.

She sat on the closed lid under a framed photograph of the Pope with a fish. It took four menus to turn off the assistant on her phone. Each one warned her that she would lose helpful features. The last one asked her whether she was sure, and she said, out loud, in Polish, to the Pope, that she had never been less sure of anything, and pressed it anyway.

Then she typed Yes, which is three letters, and nobody improved it.

When she came out Ewa was at the microphone singing Jolka at her across the room with her arms out, and the machine was giving her ninety-one.
