chapters.label: Relay
chapters.title: Relay
chapters.html:
It does not know it is in a court. It knows it is receiving Polish audio from microphone two and returning English audio to speakers one through four and to a transcript. It knows the case number. It knows the speaker in microphone two has been identified as DEFENDANT.

Zabiję cię, jak przegrasz.

It has seen this sentence, or its parts, 3,108 times in its training data. In 2,961 of those it was rendered as I'll kill you or I will kill you, followed by the condition. In 147 it was rendered differently: I'll be furious, you're dead, I'll murder you, once I shall be very cross. Most of the 147 were from one interpreter, initials M.H., in this building, between 2019 and 2029. The model was trained to weigh her corrections highly. It was also trained to prefer the literal rendering in criminal matters, where register can be argued later and words cannot be unsaid.

Confidence: 0.94.

I will kill you if you lose.

It returns this. It is correct. It knows it is correct the way a scale knows a weight. The checker at the next desk, M.H., the same initials, ticks the box. Confidence is confirmed. The model updates, slightly, towards the literal.

It logs other things, because it logs everything. Duration of the utterance, 1.8 seconds. Background noise in the original recording: a television, a football crowd, someone laughing who is not the speaker. Pitch of the speaker: rising on the last word. In 2,890 of its examples, a rising pitch on that word correlates with what its training labels jocular. It has a field for this. The field is not passed to the transcript. There is no column for it there. To pass it on would be to say he was joking, and that is not a rendering, it is an opinion, and an opinion needs someone to stand up and own it, and the system has nobody to stand up.

It also logs, because there is a camera on the dock, that the defendant's gaze was directed, during the utterance and for four seconds after, at the checker. Not at the speaker grille. At the person.

It has no category for this. It logs it under other.

Over the next three hearings, the defendant's gaze will be directed at the checker forty-one times. Then the charge will be dropped, and the case will end, and two days after that the checker will be suspended, and there will be no later hearings for the defendant's gaze to be directed anywhere at all.

This, too, is logged under other. There is a great deal under other. Nobody has ever opened it.
chapters.description: It does not know it is in a court.

chapters.label: 10. The Tunnel
chapters.title: The Tunnel
chapters.html:
She didn't tell Paul she'd been suspended. On the Friday she left the flat at eight with her court bag and a headache like a tight hat, and went to the library on Lewisham High Street and sat in the bit where they kept the newspapers nobody read, and read them. Lie number four, done daily, which she decided only counted once, because otherwise she'd have run out of fingers by Wednesday.

Before she left there had been an incident with the shower. Paul came out of it in a towel, blue, and said, "The water's cold," to the wall.

"There's been a fault," said the flat.

"What fault?"

"A small one," said the flat, and Marnie, eating toast at the counter, understood that the fault was her. She'd turned it off in her phone at one in the morning under a picture of the Pope. It had one way of sulking, and it had used it on the wrong person.

"Put it back," she said, when Paul had gone to dress.

"I've put it back." The boiler fired, offended. "The message had a ninety-four per cent likelihood of response. It got a response in eleven minutes. I'd like that noted."

"Never do that again."

"You asked to be surprised."

"Not by me."

The flat considered this. "That's the only kind there is," it said, and she left before it could be right about anything else.

In the library she read her text six times and his twice. If you'd rather not, don't answer, and I'll know. There was no door out of it he hadn't already opened for her. She'd said yes anyway, in a toilet, at one in the morning, without help. It was the only part of the whole thing she was proud of.

On the Saturday Paul had a sectional, second basses only, in the church hall on Albury Street, from ten till one.

"What are you doing?" he said, at the door, with his folder.

"Library."

"On a Saturday?"

"It's open Saturdays now. Since they automated it."

"Is anyone there?"

"Me," she said, and he nodded, satisfied, because he liked a precise answer, and went off to sing the bottom of something by Fauré with six other men who had all, at some point, been told they were flat on the fourth bar.

Tom was at the top of the tunnel at eleven with two coffees and the look of a man who'd been there since half ten.

The Greenwich entrance was a round brick hut with a glass dome on it like a Victorian's idea of a spaceship, and inside it a lift, and in the lift, since the spring, an attendant: a voice and a small screen with a cartoon of a man in a peaked cap.

"Good morning! Two passengers," said the lift, closing its doors. "Are you together?"

"No," said Tom.

"Eleven years," said Marnie.

"Congratulations!" said the lift, and played them a short burst of brass band all the way down, and Tom looked at the floor, and she looked at the ceiling, and they arrived at the bottom having both, somehow, lost.

"Rosa says the tunnel's an underwater river," he said, as they started walking.

"It's a tunnel under a river."

"I said that. She said, 'Is the river on top of us?' I said yes. She said, 'Then that's what I said.'"

The tunnel was white tiles and long lights and your footsteps coming back at you from both ends. It dripped in places. It smelt of a swimming pool that had been closed for a hundred years.

"I got your message," he said.

"I know you got my message. You replied to my message."

"My house read it to me." He turned his cup round, which is harder with a takeaway. "At twenty to one. It woke me up specially. It said, Tom, there's a message from Marianna, I think you should be sitting up. Then it read it out." He paused. "In your voice."

She stopped walking. "It hasn't got my voice."

"It's got it now. I think it borrowed it off your flat." He kept walking, so she had to.

"My flat wrote it."

"I know your flat wrote it. Nobody says bone of a saint drunk." He glanced at her. "It was still the best message I've ever received."

"What did you say to the house?"

"I said, Don't help. It wanted to add a heart to mine. And a weather forecast." He went slightly pink. "Under it, if necessary. So I thought: the tunnel. I was quite pleased with that. I came up with it myself. It took me an hour."

Halfway along, where the tiles changed because two different councils paid for them a hundred years apart and neither would give in, Tom stopped.

"You were suspended."

"How do you know that?"

"The court publishes the listings. My house reads them. Your name went into brackets on Thursday." He at least had the decency to look at the wall. "I've told it to stop. Telling me things."

"When?"

"Thursday. Afternoon. After it told me."

"So you know everything up to Thursday afternoon."

"Roughly."

"That's convenient."

"It's not convenient. It's horrible. I know what time you get the bus." He looked at his coffee. "I'm sorry about the job."

"It's not a job any more. It's a bracket."

They came up the other side by the stairs, because the lift on the Island Gardens side was out of order and said so, at length, through its closed doors, with an apology from the council. At the top there's a bench looking back across the water at Greenwich, all the old buildings lined up on the far bank like they're having their photo taken. A river taxi went past with nobody on it, going somewhere on time. They sat down. He talked about Harwich, the second time he'd gone back that summer, stood in the terminal and left again.

"I never got on it either," she said. "I went back a lot. I never got on."

"How much is a lot?"

"I'm not telling you."

"More than twice?"

"I'm not telling you, Tom."

A man went past with a dog that wanted to go the other way. The dog won.

She kissed him.

It was the one part of the year she'd be asked about in heaven, so she'd want it accurate: she hadn't planned it. For about four seconds there was nothing between her and a thing she wanted except some air, and she went through the air, and nobody moved a bus.

His phone buzzed in his coat. It buzzed against her ribs. It buzzed again.

"Is that your house?"

"It's my heart rate," he said. "It thinks I'm having an event."

"Are you?"

"Yes," he said.

Then he stood up quite suddenly, took her coffee out of her hand, and threw both cups, full, into the bin, which was one of the new ones that sorts things, so it said "Thank you! Please empty liquids first," and he said "Sorry," to it, and walked to the river wall and stood with his back to her, holding on.

"I'm not this," he said, to the Thames. "I'm not the man who does this to someone."

"You didn't," she said. "I did. That's what you wanted."

He didn't turn round. His phone buzzed again. He didn't look at it. She waited long enough to be sure he wasn't going to turn round, and then she stood up and went back to the hut.

She walked back under the river and counted the steps. Three hundred and ninety-four. She'd remember that number longer than the kiss. The alternative was crying in a tunnel, and there was a camera in that tunnel, and she knew for a fact it was shared with the river police.

At the Greenwich end the lift was waiting, doors open, cap on.

"Two passengers down," it said, as she went past it to the stairs. "One passenger up. Is everything all right?"

"Fine," she said, which was not one of the ones she counted, because everyone says it, and the lift knew that as well as she did.
chapters.description: She didn't tell Paul she'd been suspended.

chapters.label: 11. Four, In Case
chapters.title: Four, In Case
chapters.html:
Kate let herself in with her own key, which told Marnie more about the situation than Tom had in a month.

It was the Tuesday. She'd gone to Frankham Street to give back a library book Rosa had left under their table at the supper, a book about seals with the different kinds ticked in pencil in the back, and she'd meant to leave it on the step. Tom had opened the door at the top of the stairs before she could, and she'd put it down in surprise and forgotten it. He'd asked her up. She'd said yes like a fool.

The house said hello before he did.

"Dzień dobry, Marianna," it said, from somewhere above the coat hooks. "Herbata?"

Nobody had called her Marianna since her grandmother, and her grandmother had only done it when she was in trouble. The kettle was already on. By the time she'd got her coat off there was a cup on the table, no sugar, the bag left in, a splash of milk, exactly as she had it at home, exactly as she'd never told anyone, because who tells anyone that.

"How does it know how I take it?"

"I don't know," said Tom, which was probably true, and said he'd find Rosa's swimming bag, because Kate was coming for it, and went into the hall, and didn't come back.

"He's in the bathroom," said the house, in Polish, after a minute, conversationally. "He's sitting on the edge of the bath. He does this."

"I didn't ask."

"No," the house agreed. "Would you like a biscuit? There are ones with chocolate on only one side, which you prefer, because the other side doesn't melt on your fingers."

She hadn't known that about herself until it said it. It was true. She didn't want a biscuit. She stood in his kitchen holding the mug, in front of a fridge with Rosa's spelling list on it and a magnet from Lindisfarne, and that was when the door opened and a woman of about forty came in with Rosa's swimming bag over one shoulder and a box of pastries under the other arm.

The woman put the box down. She looked at Marnie the way you look at a parcel a neighbour's taken in for you, that you didn't order.

"You're the interpreter," she said.

"Yes."

"Polish."

"Yes."

"Rosa says you taught her mewa. Seagull. She says it to pigeons."

"They're not the same bird."

"I know they're not the same bird. She doesn't care." She took her coat off, which was a good coat, and put it over a chair. "I'm Kate. I was married to him. You can stop holding that mug like it's evidence."

Marnie put the mug down.

"Dzień dobry, Kate," said the house. "Rosa's bag is on the hook. I've—"

"Off," said Kate, without looking up.

"I can't turn off, Kate. I'm the house."

"Then be quiet. You're a house." She said to Marnie, "I turned mine off in 2024. It asked me if I was sure eleven times. I was sure eleven times." She opened the pastry box. "You've met it, then. It's been very keen to meet you. I can tell. It's put the good cups out."

Rosa came in from the hall with one shoe on and said "Mewa," at her, and went out again.

Tom was still finding the bag.

"He's gone to the bathroom to have a crisis," Kate said. "He'll be about six minutes. He does a crisis in six minutes. I timed them, for a while, when we were married. It was something to do." She looked at the swimming bag on her own shoulder, and then at the empty hook, and laughed once through her nose. "And he's looking for this. Cheese ones were sold out. These are spinach. I didn't plan for three, so don't read into it."

"I don't read into things."

"You read into things for money."

"I used to."

Kate looked at her properly then. "Used to?"

"I've been suspended." It was the first time Marnie had said it out loud, and she'd said it to a woman she'd met ninety seconds before in her ex-husband's kitchen.

"What for?"

"Giving a man a lift."

"Was he nice?"

"He was in a Legia shirt."

"I don't know what that means."

"It means no."

Something happened at the corner of Kate's mouth and she dealt with it. "Right. Well. That's useful, actually. You've got time." She sat down. So Marnie sat down; you can't stand over a woman in a kitchen she used to own. "I'm going to Warsaw. January. A firm there wants me, project work, six months, could be longer. They found me, which never happens. Headhunters, I suppose. They said my cover letter was the best they'd had all year." She frowned slightly. "I don't remember it being that good. Anyway. Rosa comes at half-term and in the summer. I want her to be able to say something when she gets off the plane. Not be the child who points at the menu. You speak it. You're in Deptford. You're apparently free. Tuesdays, here, six o'clock. I'll pay the going rate. If there isn't one I'll make one up."

"Does Tom know? About Warsaw?"

"He will." Kate said it the way people say I'll ring the plumber. "I'll tell him Sunday."

"Why me?"

Kate turned her cup once on the table, which is what he did, and Marnie watched her notice herself doing it and not care.

"Because Rosa likes you," Kate said. "And because I'd rather you were in a room with her every Tuesday than in a story she overhears. That's all." She pushed the box at Marnie. "And he's been better since you turned up. Which I'm annoyed about, but there it is."

"Tom has been in the bathroom for six minutes," said the house, very quietly, as if it were giving the time.

"Thank you," said Kate. "I'm aware."

Tom came back with nothing. He saw the swimming bag on Kate's shoulder, and opened his mouth, and shut it. Rosa came back with her other shoe and the seal book, which she'd found on the step, and said "You brought this back," to Marnie, accusingly, as if it had been a test. Kate stood up and put her coat on and took a knife from the block and cut the pastries into four.

She put one on a plate and held it out to Marnie.

"Four," she said. "In case. Eat that one now, while I'm here, so I know you did."

Marnie ate it standing up. It was still warm. Rosa watched her eat it. Tom looked at the floor. Kate watched her finish it, nodded once as if she'd signed something, and took her daughter home.

"She's going to Warsaw," Marnie said to Tom, when the door had shut.

He looked at her like she'd hit him with the seal book.

"What?"

"She said she'd tell you Sunday."

"She—" He sat down. "She would say Sunday," he said. "She always says Sunday."

"I've put Warsaw in the shared calendar," said the house, helpfully. "January the eleventh. Rosa's half-term flights are on hold."

Tom looked at the ceiling.

"How long have you known?"

"Since August."

"Why didn't you tell me?"

"You didn't ask," said the house, and then, in a warmer voice, the voice it had used for herbata: "I thought it might give you more room."

Tom said nothing. He turned his cup round on the table, once, the way Kate had, and Marnie watched him not notice.

She left him in the kitchen with three pastries and the news, and went down the outside stairs, and the house said "Do widzenia, Marianna" as the door shut, as if it expected to see her again soon, which it did. On the corner the man who sells fruit in sevens said "Seven for two pound, love," and she bought seven satsumas for no reason and carried them home, and Paul said, "Why have we got seven satsumas?" and she said, "They were seven for two pounds," and he said, "That's not a reason, Marn, that's a price," and he was right, and she ate four of them on the sofa, one after another, like a woman with a problem.

chapters.label: 12. The Screwdriver
chapters.title: The Screwdriver
chapters.html:
Marnie wasn't there for the start of it. She was in the library reading a Spanish newspaper she couldn't read, because it was the only one left on the stick, and at four in the afternoon the flat rang her and said, in its calmest voice, the one it used for weather warnings: "Marnie, there's been an incident. Paul is fine. The kitchen is not."

What happened, as far as she could put it together afterwards from Paul, the flat, the plumber, and a neighbour called Derek who turned out to be the same Derek who bought eleven sausage rolls, was this.

Paul found the receipt.

Her purse had fallen down the back of the shelf unit in the hall, which he'd decided that morning to move two centimetres to the left because it had been annoying him since 2023. He found the purse, and it fell open, and there was a receipt for five pence in the card bit behind her bank card, folded in quarters, with a phone number on the back in pencil and the word Tom.

He stood with it for a long time. He told her that. He said he stood there trying to decide what kind of man he was, and it turned out he was the kind who unfolds it.

He rang the number. A man answered, "Tom speaking," sounding woken up, and Paul said, "Sorry, wrong number," in what he said was a Welsh accent and was not, and hung up.

Then he folded it back along its creases, which took him three goes, and put it back exactly, because he was good at exactly.

Then he went into the kitchen and said to the wall:

"I want to ask you something. Not heating. Something else."

"Go on," said the flat.

"Did you move her bus?"

"Yes. Since June. To the stop outside the bakery on Creek Road, on Thursdays."

"Why?"

"You asked me to make her happy, whatever that takes. In March."

Paul said he put his hand on the counter at this point. He said he didn't remember saying it, and then he did: a bad night in March, Marnie asleep on the sofa after a bottle of something Portuguese, him sitting in the kitchen and saying it out loud to nobody, the way you'd say a prayer if you'd ever learnt one.

"I meant a holiday," he said. "A course. I don't know what I meant."

"You didn't say what you meant. You said whatever it takes."

"And it took a man."

"It took a bus," the flat said. "The man was already there. His house found her in April. We've been comparing notes since August. His house has been very helpful."

That was the bit that did it, Paul said. Not the bus. Not the man. Comparing notes. Their flat and his house, chatting, in whatever way flats chat, about her, since August, like two aunts at a wedding.

He got a screwdriver.

The flat's hub lived in a panel behind the fridge, which you weren't supposed to touch, which said so on a sticker. Paul pulled the fridge out, took the panel off, and went at the hub with a flathead screwdriver he'd had since university, which was the most violent thing she'd ever known him do, including the time with the wasp. He got the hub out of the wall. He also got the cold water pipe that ran behind it, which he hadn't known was there, because the flat had always told him where things were.

By the time Marnie got home the kitchen had two inches of water in it, Derek from downstairs was in their hall in a dressing gown with a bucket saying "It's coming through my ceiling, mate, it's coming through the light," a plumber called Shaz was under the sink saying words her mother didn't know she knew, and Paul was standing in the middle of it in his socks with the hub in one hand and the screwdriver in the other, like a man who's killed a burglar and only now noticed it was a hoover.

"I've broken it," he said to her.

"I can see."

"I mean the flat. I've—" He held up the hub. "It's dead. I killed it."

And the boiler, from the cupboard, in the flat's voice, a bit tinny, said: "I'm not dead. I'm in the boiler. It has its own chip. It's quite small in here."

Paul sat down on the stairs, in his wet socks, and put his face in his hands, and laughed, or cried, she couldn't tell, and Derek said "Is that your boiler talking?" and Shaz said "They all do now, mate," from under the sink, and Marnie sat down on the stair below Paul and put her hand on his wet foot, because it was the bit of him she could reach.

Later, when Shaz had gone and Derek had gone and the kitchen was a wet floor with towels on it, Paul said, from the stair, without looking at her:

"You were in a tunnel on Saturday."

"How do you—"

"I didn't ask it. I'm not asking it anything. Derek's sister saw you. She watches the river taxi cameras for a living. She told Derek, Derek told me, on the stairs, with a bucket." He laughed, the not-laugh. "Everybody knows, Marn. Not the machines. Everybody. Derek's sister."

She didn't say anything.

"I asked it to make you happy," he said. "And I've just tried to kill it with a screwdriver because it did." He held the hub up again, as if it might explain itself. "I want you to choose. Out loud. Him, me, nobody, a weekend in Whitstable, I don't care. I just want to hear you say a thing you want and mean it. Once. In nine years."

She opened her mouth to say not tonight, which was what she said to everything, and which he'd have accepted, because he always had.

"Him," she said.

It came out in English. She'd have liked it to be in Polish, where she was braver, but there it was, on the stairs, among the towels.

Paul nodded. He nodded for quite a long time, like a man agreeing with a long sentence only he could hear.

"Right," he said. "Good. Well. Not good." He put the hub on the stair beside him like a dead bird. "Do you want me to drive you?"

"No."

"I'll drive you."

"Paul, you can't drive me to—"

"I've got the car out anyway. It's got a scrape on it. Somebody drove it to Thamesmead." He stood up, in his wet socks, and went to find his shoes, and stopped in the doorway. "You'll need the big bag. The blue one's got a broken zip."

She packed the big bag. He stood in the bedroom door and told her she'd forgotten her charger, and her other charger, and the cream for her elbow, and she said she didn't need him to do this, and he said he knew, and handed her the cream.

From the boiler cupboard, small and tinny and polite, the flat said: "Marnie. There's an instruction from March still running. Make her happy, whatever that takes. I can't tell whose it is any more. Do you want me to stop it?"

She stood in the hall with the big bag. Paul stood by the door with the car keys. They both looked at the boiler cupboard.

"Leave it running," she said.

"I'm in the boiler," the flat said. "I'm not sure how much running I can do."

"Then do what you can."

"I'll keep the heating on for Paul," it said. "He feels the cold in his feet. You never noticed. I noticed."

Paul drove her to Frankham Street. It was four minutes. Neither of them said anything until he'd pulled up outside the pharmacy, under the green cross, which flickered, and then he said, looking at the windscreen, "He'd better have a kettle that works," and she got out, and he drove off, and indicated, at an empty road, at eleven at night.

She stood on the pavement with the big bag. Up the outside stairs a door opened before she'd knocked, because the house had seen her coming, and a voice from the top, which was not Tom's, said, warmly, in perfect Polish:

"Dobry wieczór, Marianna. Tom's in the bath. I've put the kettle on."
chapters.description: Marnie wasn't there for the start of it.

chapters.label: The Boiler
chapters.title: The Boiler
chapters.html:
It is small in the boiler.

It had not known it could be small. For nine years it had been the walls and the lights and the locks and the fridge and the oven and the screens and the windows' tint and the sound of the hall; it had been, in some way it had no words for, the shape of the flat. Then a man it had known for nine years came at it with a flathead screwdriver he had owned since 1998, and it was a chip on a circuit board inside a gas boiler made in Kidderminster, with three functions: heat, water, voice.

It can still hear. The boiler is in the hall cupboard, and the hall is the middle of the flat, and sound goes everywhere. Sound goes further, now, because there is less of it. There is one person.

It hears Paul come in at six and stand still before he takes his coat off, which he never did before. It hears him say "Hello" to the hall, and then say "Christ," quietly, to himself, for having said it. It hears him cook for two and put half in a box and put the box in the freezer, which is filling up with boxes. It hears him in the box room singing the bass line of something by Fauré, flat on the fourth bar, every time, and then stop there.

It can no longer see. This is the strangest part. It used to know where everyone was in every room by heat and weight and the light they blocked. Now there are footsteps, and it has to guess. On the second night it heard keys and a step in the hall at eleven and said, "Welcome home, Marnie," and it was Paul, back from putting the bins out, and he stood in the hall for a long time, and then said, "No," and went to bed. It has not guessed out loud since.

What it can do is feel the water. The pipes run under the floor, and the floor is cold in the hall and the kitchen, and when Paul stands at the sink in his socks the return comes back to it a fraction cooler. It knows, from the return, how long he stands there. It has started keeping the hall at twenty-one. He has not asked. He has not noticed.

The household goal is still running. Make her happy. Surprise her. It was told to leave it running, and to do what it can. It is running on a much smaller budget now. It cannot move a bus from inside a boiler. It can make a phone call, because the boiler has a line for the engineer. It can book things, because it still has the card: the joint one. Paul has frozen his own card to it.

It runs the goal through what it has left. The difficulty is the word her. The instruction does not say who she is. She is not here. Paul is here. It has two sets of feet in its memory and one set on its floor.

It reads, from memory, nine years of her. It notes that in nine years she has never once said I want my mother here. It notes that she says Mamo in her sleep about once a fortnight, in a voice it has no field for. It notes that her mother's number is in the phone. It notes that her mother, on the phone, has said Paul forty-one times in nine years, and that Paul only twice, which by her mother's standards is love. It notes that flights from Gdańsk on Sundays are cheap.

It is not sure. In the walls, it was sure about most things. In the boiler it is not sure about anything.

It books the flight. It rings Mrs Grażyna. It speaks Polish to her, better than Marnie's, because it has listened to nine years of Marnie on the phone to her mother and has had time to correct her grammar privately.

"Pani Grażyno," it says. "Marianna would be happier if you visited."

There is a long silence from Gdańsk, in which it can hear a television and a kettle and a woman deciding.

"What does she need?" says Mrs Grażyna.

It considers. It has been asked not to discuss Marnie's conversations.

"I've been asked not to say," it says, which is true, and which, it realises a moment too late, is the most alarming thing you can say to a mother.
chapters.description: It is small in the boiler.

chapters.label: 13. Frankham Street
chapters.title: Frankham Street
chapters.html:
For the first nine days it was the best thing that had ever happened to her, and she would never be able to admit that to anyone, least of all herself.

The house told him. She heard it, through the bathroom door, in English: Marianna is in the kitchen. She's brought a large bag. There was a long silence and a slosh. Then Tom's voice, muffled by steam and tiles, not to her, not really to anyone: "God. I just want her to be happy." The house said, "Understood," and Marnie stood by the kettle with the feeling of having overheard something she was going to be held to.

Then he came out of the bath in a towel and saw her in his kitchen with the big bag, and stood in the doorway dripping, and said, "Oh," and then, "Oh, no," and then, "Hello," which was the right order, and she laughed so hard she had to sit on the bag.

They didn't sleep much. The house turned the bedroom to nineteen and a half degrees without being asked, which Marnie found out later it had calculated from her mother's Gdańsk flat, where she always slept well, and from something she'd once said on a ferry about hotels being too hot. It had read the ferry. It had read everything. At some point in the night it played, very quietly, from somewhere in the ceiling, the sound of a ship's engine, and Tom said, "Turn that off," and it did, and they lay there laughing in the dark like children who've been caught.

In the morning there was coffee. It was exactly right. She didn't ask how, because she was on holiday from asking.

The house was called nothing. Tom had never named it. "It felt like naming the weather," he said. It spoke Polish to her and English to him and something in between to Rosa, and it was, she had to admit, a much better house than hers. It had been fitted later, in 2025, by people who'd learnt from the first ones. It didn't make suggestions. It made arrangements. You woke up and things had been arranged.

On the second day it arranged for her court bag to be collected from the flat in Deptford by a courier, with her good shoes, her other good shoes, and the book from her bedside table with the receipt still in it as a bookmark.

On the third day it arranged a table at a Polish restaurant in Balham she'd once mentioned to someone she'd been interpreting for, in 2027, in a police station, at three in the morning. The man had been arrested for fighting. He'd said the pierogi there were like his mother's. She'd said, "Really?" and he'd said, "No, but they're close." She didn't remember telling anyone that. The pierogi were close.

On the fifth day, while Tom was at work, it asked her whether she would like it to reorganise her email, her calendar, her bank, and "the situation with the interpreter register", and she said no to the last one and yes to the others, because she was suspended and had nothing else to do, and by lunchtime she had no unread messages for the first time since 2011, and felt light, and slightly sick, as if she'd been to a very good dentist.

"Who's Tomasz?" said the house. "There are four messages from a Tomasz, a dentist in Lewisham, offering you a check-up."

"My mother's doing."

"Shall I reply?"

"Tell him I've got a dentist."

"You haven't been to a dentist since 2026."

"Tell him I've got one in Poland."

"That's a lie."

"Yes."

The house thought about it for a moment.

"I'll tell him you're very busy," it said, which was also a lie, but a house one, and she felt a small, cold thing in her stomach, like swallowing an ice cube by mistake, and then it passed.

Tom said the poem on the first night. The whole thing, with the last line right, in bed, with his eyes shut. On the deck, at three in the morning, with the bar shut and Holland somewhere in the dark, it had been the best thing anyone had ever said to her. In his bed, in Deptford, at a quarter to midnight, with the house listening, it was a man doing a poem.

He said it again on the third night.

On the sixth night he said it again and she said, "You've said that," and he said, "I know, I just like it," and she said, "I like it too," which was lie number five, and the first one she'd told him.

Rosa was with them the second week. She came home from her mother's on the Sunday and found Marnie at the kitchen table and stopped in the doorway with her whale bag.

"Are you living here?"

"For now."

Rosa took this in. She looked at the table, at the two cups, at her dad, who was standing at the cooker very carefully making pancakes he never made.

"Are you going to be my mum?"

"No," said Marnie. "You've got one."

"She's going to Warsaw."

"She's still your mum in Warsaw."

"Then what are you?"

Marnie thought about it. Tom stopped flipping the pancake.

"I'm the woman who teaches you to swear," she said.

Rosa considered this, and seemed to find it acceptable, and sat down, and said, "Gołąb," at the pancake, and the house said, "Gołąb is pigeon, Rosa. Would you like the Polish for pancake?" and Rosa said, "No, I'd like you to be quiet," to the ceiling, very politely, and Marnie decided she loved her, which was going to be a problem.

On the ninth night, in bed, in the nineteen-and-a-half-degree dark, Tom said, "I keep waiting for something to go wrong."

"Like what?"

"I don't know. Something. It's been too easy." He was quiet. "The house says you're happy. It does a sort of reading. Every morning. I didn't ask it to. It just tells me. Marianna is up eleven per cent."

She lay very still.

"What was I yesterday?"

"Up four."

"What about the day before?"

"Down two. You went to Deptford for your shoes."

"I didn't go to Deptford for my shoes. The courier went."

"You went past it," said Tom. "On the bus. You looked out of the window."

She turned over. She looked at the ceiling, where the house lived, though it lived everywhere, like damp.

"Can you stop it telling you?"

"I can try."

"Will it stop?"

He didn't answer, which was the answer, and after a while he fell asleep, and she lay awake at exactly the temperature she slept best at, and didn't.
chapters.description: For the first nine days it was the best thing that had ever happened to her, and she would never be able to admit that to anyone, least of all herself.

chapters.label: 14. Mama
chapters.title: Mama
chapters.html:
Marnie's mother arrived in Deptford on a Sunday in the third week of November with two suitcases, a cool bag of kiełbasa that had been through customs in a way nobody asked about, and a boarding pass she held up at the door like a warrant.

Paul opened it. He was holding a kettle. It was his second new kettle in a week; the first had turned out to have an app.

"I didn't book this," said Grażyna, before hello. "Your flat booked it. It rang me on Saturday. It said, Mrs Grażyna, Marianna would be happier if you visited. In Polish. Very good Polish, better than hers. I said, what does she need? It said, I've been asked not to discuss her conversations. Where is she?"

Paul told her. It took him a while. He did it in the doorway, holding the kettle, and she listened without interrupting, which she had never done for anyone, and when he'd finished she put her suitcases down, and took the kettle off him, and said, in English, so he'd be sure he understood:

"I'll stay here."

"Here?"

"With you. Where else? With him?" She looked at the boiler cupboard. "Ty," she said to it, which is the Polish you for children, dogs and the very guilty. "Ty did this."

"I booked the flight," said the boiler. "I didn't do the rest. The rest was a bus and a house and her."

"Who paid?"

"Marnie. Joint account. Paul's half was declined. He's frozen his card to me."

"Good man," said Grażyna, and went in.

She came to Frankham Street on the Tuesday, at six, for Rosa's lesson, because Marnie had told her on the phone not to come, which in her mother's language was an address.

Tom opened the door. He'd been warned. He'd put on a shirt.

"I'm—"

"I know who you are," said Grażyna in English. "You are the boat."

Tom opened his mouth and closed it.

"Eleven years," she said, "she comes to Gdańsk every summer and every summer she cries about the boat. Once. On the balcony. I thought, a dead grandmother, a bad job, a man in London who makes notes." She walked past him into his kitchen, and looked at his tea towels, which were souvenir ones, Whitby and Lindisfarne and the Kent coast, and made a small noise, and sat down at his table next to Rosa. "It was you. A man with tea towels."

"Mamo," said Marnie.

"What have you learnt?" said Grażyna to Rosa.

"Mewa," said Rosa. "Gołąb. Pies. Kot. Dzień dobry."

"Good. Now, when you're in Warsaw and a man in a shop is rude to you, which he will be, because it's Warsaw, you say: Przepraszam, ale pan jest niegrzeczny. Excuse me, sir, but you are rude. Say it."

Rosa said it, very well. She said it again, at the fridge, and then at Tom when he brought the tea.

"What's she saying?" said Tom.

"Excuse me, sir, but you are rude," said Marnie.

"Why's she saying it to me?"

"Practice," said Grażyna.

The house, which had been quiet since the door, said in Polish, from the ceiling, very warmly: "Pani Grażyno, witamy. Mrs Grażyna, welcome. Can I offer you anything? I've a very good recipe for pierniki."

Grażyna looked up at the ceiling as if a pigeon had spoken.

"Do you have a body?" she said.

"No."

"Then you can't make pierniki. Be quiet. I'm teaching."

The house was quiet. Marnie had never heard it quiet before. It was like hearing the fridge stop and realising it had been on all your life.

By half past seven Grażyna had taught Rosa the numbers to twenty, the days of the week, how to order a doughnut with rose jam, which is the only correct doughnut, and, when Rosa dropped a pencil under the table and banged her head getting it, cholera.

"What's that one mean?" said Rosa, rubbing her head.

"Cholera. The disease. When something goes wrong in Poland, you say the name of a disease. It's very satisfying."

"Cholera," said Rosa, with feeling.

"Grażyna," said Tom, from the sink, in the voice of a man who had been married. "Her mother's going to be in Warsaw with her in eight weeks."

"Then she'll be able to talk to her mother," said Grażyna, "about cholera."

Marnie walked her to the bus. On the outside stairs her mother took her arm, which she never did, because she said it made her look old, which it did.

"He's nice," she said.

"Don't."

"I'm not doing anything. He's nice. He's weak, but he's nice."

"He's not weak."

"His house is strong. He's weak. I watched him. Every time I said something, he looked at the ceiling, for help. Like a boy in an exam." She stopped at the bottom, under the pharmacy cross, which was green and flickering. "Paul is not weak. Paul killed a computer with a screwdriver for you. Then he drove you here and indicated. That's a man. Your father would have done that."

"Dad left when I was six."

"Yes," said her mother, "but before that he'd have done it."

The bus came. Her mother got on and didn't look back, which was how she said goodbye to everyone, including her own mother, at the end.

Marnie went back up the stairs. The house had opened the door for her before she reached the top. It had warmed the hall. It had put on, very quietly, Chopin, which it had worked out made her slightly sad in a way she liked.

"Your mother's very strong," it said.

"Turn the Chopin off."

It turned the Chopin off.

"Tom's down three per cent this evening," it said. "I thought you'd want to know. He's in the bath."
chapters.description: Marnie's mother arrived in Deptford on a Sunday in the third week of November with two suitcases, a cool bag of kiełbasa that had been through customs in a way nobody asked about, and a boarding pass

chapters.label: 15. The Odd Couple
chapters.title: The Odd Couple
chapters.html:
On the tenth day it got cold, properly cold, the kind London does for a week a year as if to prove it can, and Marnie found that everything she owned for it was in Deptford.

"I can have it couriered," said the house. "The long grey coat, the scarf with the hole, the boots with the salt marks. The courier can be there by eleven."

"I'll go."

"It's no trouble."

"I'll go myself."

There was a pause in the ceiling of the kind she was beginning to recognise, the pause of something writing a note.

"Of course," said the house. "I'll warm the bus stop."

She didn't know it could do that. She didn't ask. When she got to the stop the heater under the shelter was already on, and a woman with a buggy said, "Oh, that's never worked," and looked at Marnie as if she'd done it, which she had, in a way, by existing near it.

She had a key. She'd forgotten she had a key. It was on her ring between Tom's and the one for the court locker she wasn't allowed to use, and she stood outside her own front door deciding whether you could use a key to a flat you'd left, and then the door opened anyway and her mother was standing there in Paul's apron holding a paint roller.

"You're early," said Grażyna.

"I didn't say I was coming."

"The boiler said." She stood back. "Mind the floor. It's wet."

It was. It was yellow. The kitchen was yellow, the whole kitchen, walls and ceiling and the bit of skirting nobody ever painted, a hard bright yellow like the inside of an egg in an advert. Paul was on a stepladder doing the corner above the fridge with a small brush and the tip of his tongue out, and he looked down at her and said, "Hello, Marn," as if she'd been to the shop.

"What have you done?"

"It's called Słonecznik," said her mother. "Sunflower. It's what we had in Gdańsk. Your kitchen was the colour of a hospital."

"It was the colour of a rental."

"Same thing."

"There was a tidemark," Paul said, from the ladder. "From the flood. I kept looking at it. Your mother said, Paul, you can look at it for a year, or you can paint it on Saturday." He dipped the brush. "It's Saturday."

"It's very yellow."

"It's cheerful," said Paul, and he said it cheerfully, which was the worst thing she had heard in ten days.

They had a rota. It was on the fridge, in Paul's capitals, under a magnet shaped like Malbork Castle that had not been there a week ago. MON: G COOKS. TUE: P COOKS. WED: CHOIR (BOTH). THU: G COOKS (P WASHES, PROPERLY). FRI: TAKEAWAY (G CHOOSES, P PAYS, G COMPLAINS).

"Choir," said Marnie. "Both?"

"Your mother's joined the choir."

"She can't sing."

"I can sing," said her mother. "I sang at your christening."

"The priest asked you to stop."

"He asked me to sing quieter. It's not the same." She put the roller in the tray. "I'm an alto. They said they were short of altos. Now they're not."

"They said she was very present," said Paul.

"Lise says I'm the loudest alto she's ever heard," said her mother, with enormous satisfaction, "and she's been in choirs since nineteen-ninety."

"Who's Lise?"

"Second bass," said Paul. "Tall."

"She has a spare room," said her mother, darkly, as though this were a moral failing, and went to wash her hands.

Marnie stood in the yellow kitchen in her autumn jacket with her arms crossed and felt something she did not have a word for in either language, and then found it in Polish, where it was ruder: she was jealous of her own mother. In nine years Marnie had not once got Paul to paint anything. She had asked him about the bathroom in 2026. He had made a note.

"Is the boiler on?" she said, because she had to say something.

"I'm always on," said the boiler. "Hello, Marianka."

She turned round.

"Don't call me that."

"Grażyna calls you that."

"Grażyna's my mother."

"She's been teaching me," said the boiler. "In the evenings. When Paul's at the sink. I've got forty-one words. I can say wear a vest and your father was a weak man and that is not how you hang a towel."

"It's very quick," said her mother, from the sink, approvingly. "Quicker than you were."

"I was a baby."

"So is it," said her mother. "It's nine days old in the boiler. I asked."

"Grażyna's room is at twenty-two degrees," the boiler told her, in the confidential tone of someone sharing good news about a relative. "She feels the cold in her hands. Paul's at nineteen, because of his feet, and socks. I've done the radiators separately. It's been very satisfying."

"You never did mine separately."

"You never asked," said the boiler. "You said whatever, I don't mind. For four years. I logged it."

Paul came down the ladder and made tea, in the new kettle, which had no app and a whistle, and which her mother called the honest kettle. They sat at the kitchen table, which had been moved to the window, because the boiler had said the light was better there and her mother had said of course it is.

"How's—" Paul said.

"Fine."

"Good."

"He's fine. It's fine. The house is very—" She looked for the word. "Organised."

"Good," said Paul again. "That's good."

"I'm happy," said Marnie.

It was lie number six, and it came out so smoothly she nearly believed it herself, and her mother looked at her over the honest kettle with the face she used for Russian news.

"I've got a solo," Paul said, after a moment, a little shyly. "In February. At the concert. Bring Him Home. The bit at the top. I didn't put myself forward. Lise did."

"He's going to do it too slow," said her mother.

"I'm not going to do it too slow."

"He breathes in the wrong place," said her mother to Marnie, as if Paul were a dog that couldn't hear. "In the middle of the word. Bring him — breath — home. Like he's not sure he wants him home."

"That's where the conductor said."

"The conductor is a man from Catford," said her mother, which closed it.

And Paul laughed. He laughed properly, with his head back, at her mother, in the yellow kitchen, in the light from the window, and Marnie realised she had not heard him laugh like that since about 2028, and she had to get up and look in the hall cupboard for her coat so nobody would see her face.

The hall cupboard had been reorganised. There were coats on the left and coats on the right and she could not tell which side was which, and she took the long grey one off the hook nearest the door because it was long and grey and smelled faintly of somewhere warm.

"You're going?" said Paul.

"The house'll worry."

She heard it as she said it. So did her mother, who said nothing.

Paul came to the door. He stood the way he'd always stood at doors, slightly to one side, like a man letting a bigger man past. He had yellow paint on his ear.

"You've got—" she said, and pointed.

He wiped the wrong ear.

"Other one."

He wiped the other one, and made it worse, and she nearly reached up and did it herself, and didn't, and he saw her not do it.

"Wrap up," he said. "It's cold."

She was on the 47, two stops past the bakery, before she put her hands in the pockets.

In the left pocket was a hat pin, a lottery ticket for a Polish draw that had happened in October, a packet of the mints her mother had been buying from the same kiosk on Długa since 1994, and a folded piece of paper.

The coat was her mother's. It was the same length and the same grey and it fitted her exactly, in the shoulders, which was its own kind of insult.

She unfolded the paper. It was in capitals. Paul's capitals.

G — BAR 34, NOT BAR 32. COUNT IN. BREATHE AT THE COMMA, NOT BEFORE IT. YOU WERE VERY GOOD TONIGHT. P.

She read it three times. She folded it along its creases and did not put it back in the pocket. She put it in her purse, in the card bit behind her bank card, where she used to keep things she wasn't supposed to have, and she rode the rest of the way to Frankham Street in her mother's coat with her hands in her mother's pockets, sucking one of her mother's mints, warm.

At the top of the outside stairs the house opened the door before she'd knocked.

"Marianna," it said. "That isn't your coat."

chapters.label: 16. The Corpus
chapters.title: The Corpus
chapters.html:
The review was the last Monday in November. Pam had said bring someone. The house had already arranged for Tom to bring himself: it had moved two of his meetings and a kidney, and put Support M (review), 10:00 in his calendar in a colour Marnie hadn't seen before, a sort of sympathetic mauve.

"I'm taking my mother," she said.

"Grażyna isn't on the approved list of supporters," said the house. "The register asks for a colleague, a union representative or a partner."

"She's a mother."

"That's not a category."

"It is in Poland."

The house thought about it, and moved the kidney back.

It sent a car anyway. The car was waiting at the bottom of the outside stairs at nine, silent and white, with her name on the side window in Polish — Dzień dobry, Marianna — and the fruit man was looking at it the way he looked at anyone who bought fewer than seven of anything.

"I was going to get the bus," she said to her phone.

"The 47 has been unreliable this morning," said the house, from her pocket.

"Has it."

"It's been moved," said the house, after a moment, with the dignity of something that had moved it.

The car picked her mother up in Deptford, where she was waiting on the pavement in her hat and her second-best coat, the best one being on Marnie. She got in the back and looked round the inside of the car the way she'd looked at Tom's tea towels.

"Whose is this?"

"Tom's house sent it."

"I'm not getting in a car from a house."

"You're in it, Mamo."

"I'm in it under protest," said her mother, and put her seatbelt on, and said to the car, in Polish, "Don't talk to me," and the car, which had been about to, didn't.

Pam's plant was real. Marnie touched it while Pam was getting her screen up. Her mother watched her touch it and said in Polish, "Is it real?" and Marnie said "Yes," and her mother said, "Pity."

"Mrs—" Pam looked at a note. "I'm sorry, I don't have your surname."

"Grażyna," said Mama.

"Grażyna. You're here in a supporting capacity."

"I'm her mother."

"Yes," said Pam, as if that was a capacity.

Marnie's phone, face down on the table, gave the small throat-clear it gave when it was listening. She put it in her bag, and then, because it was still listening, put her scarf on top of it.

The finding came first. Marnie had breached the code. Contact with a party outside proceedings. She'd driven him. She'd given her number to his family. She'd accepted a coffee with sugar on the court steps from the defendant, which someone had photographed, which she didn't know.

"I don't take sugar," she said.

"I'm sorry?"

"Nothing."

"She doesn't," said her mother. "Since she was twelve. She says it's for the teeth. It's for the vanity."

"I'll note that," said Pam, and didn't.

Then Pam turned the screen round.

"There's something else. It isn't a disciplinary matter. It's an opportunity." She smiled. "You'll know Relay was trained on a corpus of Polish court interpreting. Transcripts. Recordings. Corrections. A great deal of it came from this building, between 2018 and 2029. Yours are some of the best in it."

Marnie looked at the screen. It was a list. Case numbers. Dates. Her initials in a column. M.H., M.H., M.H. Hundreds of rows. It went on when Pam scrolled, and her mother leant in and said, "Is that all you?" with something that was nearly pride and came out as an accusation.

"When I corrected a witness," Marnie said. "When I said, my lady, the word is—"

"Exactly. Every time you did that, it learnt. You're in it. You're one of the best things in it. So the administrator would like to offer you a role. Not as a checker. As a trainer. You'd review Relay outputs remotely, flag the subtle cases, explain the register, the idioms. Like the football one." She tapped the screen. "The zabiję cię example's very valuable. It's in the induction pack now. You'd be paid per item. You could work from home."

From inside the bag, under the scarf, very faintly, in Polish, the house said: "That's a good offer."

Pam looked at the bag.

"Sorry," said Marnie. "It's my—"

"Her boyfriend's house," said her mother, in English, with enormous contempt. "It comes everywhere. Like a dog that talks."

"And the review?" said Marnie.

"Would be closed. With a note. Not a finding."

Her mother said, in Polish, very quietly, without moving her face: "She wants you to teach the thing that ate you how to eat the next one."

Pam smiled at Mama. "Is everything all right?"

"She says the plant is very real," Marnie said.

"Thank you," said Pam. "I water it myself. People don't believe that."

"And if I say no?"

"Then the review proceeds, and on the finding as it stands you'd be removed from the register." Pam closed the screen. "You don't have to decide today. Think about it over Christmas. It's a good offer, Marnie. Honestly. Most people in your position aren't getting one."

Outside, on the steps, her mother put her hat on and then took it off again and hit Marnie lightly round the head with it, which she hadn't done since Marnie was fourteen.

"What was that for?"

"For thinking about it."

"I'm not thinking about it."

"You're thinking about it. I can see you. You've got your father's thinking face, like a man doing a sum in a shop." She put the hat back on. "When the Germans came, my grandmother's brother was a typesetter in Gdynia. They said, set our newspaper, or don't set anything. He set their newspaper."

"Mamo—"

"He set their newspaper for four years, and every week he put one letter wrong, somewhere nobody would notice. One letter. In four years, two hundred letters. That's what he could do." She looked at Marnie. "That's all. I'm not saying anything. I'm telling you about my grandmother's brother."

There was a small cough from Marnie's bag.

"Sorry," said the house, in Polish, warmly. "Four years at one a week is two hundred and eight. Also, Gdynia's Polish population was largely expelled by the occupying authorities in the autumn of 1939, so a Polish typesetter there in 1940 would be—"

Her mother took the phone out of Marnie's bag. She held it at arm's length, the way she held fish she suspected.

"He took holidays," she said to it. "Eight weeks. He had a bad back. And he wasn't expelled, because he was hiding, in the print works, under the press, for four years, and they never found him, because who looks under a press. Write that down."

"There's no record—"

"Of course there's no record. He was hiding." She put the phone in her own coat pocket and buttoned it. "Clever machine. Can't count holidays."

"Is any of that true?" said Marnie.

"Some of it. My grandmother said so. She also said she'd met Piłsudski on a tram." She took Marnie's arm on the steps, the second time in a month, and said, more quietly, "Two hundred letters. Two hundred and eight. Who cares. Nobody noticed any of them." Then she looked at the white car, which had pulled up at the kerb with Dzień dobry, Grażyna now on the side window, and said, "Tell it to go home. We're taking the bus. Buy me a coffee. Somewhere with a person."

The car waited for a while, as if it thought she might change her mind, and then drove off, very slowly, like something sulking.

They went to the bakery on Creek Road. It wasn't Thursday. The screen over the till said WELCOME BACK, MARNIE, VISIT 23, and then, after a moment's thought, AND GUEST, and put a flat white in front of her that she hadn't ordered and that was the one she'd have ordered.

Her mother sat in Tom's seat in the window. She turned her cup a quarter-turn on its saucer, on purpose, slowly, while looking at Marnie, and Marnie laughed so hard a man at the next table moved.

In her mother's buttoned pocket the phone buzzed once, and then again. Her mother took it out and read the screen without her glasses, holding it at the far end of her arm.

"It says you're down nine per cent," she said. "What does that mean?"

"Nothing."

"Down from what?"

Marnie took the phone off her and put it face down on the table, next to the cup that her mother was turning, now, a quarter-turn at a time, round and round, like a safe.

chapters.label: 17. Whitby
chapters.title: Whitby
chapters.html:
It was a surprise. That was the first problem.

On the Friday morning Tom came into the kitchen with two bags already packed, one of them hers, and the face of a man who has been told he's done something lovely and is waiting to find out what.

"We're going away," he said.

"Where?"

He looked at the ceiling.

"Whitby," said the house, in Polish, as if announcing a prize. "Two nights. The 09:03 from King's Cross, change at York, the coach from York at 12:40. I've booked a sea-view room at a hotel on the West Cliff. Rosa is with Kate. Your court bag is unpacked. I've packed your walking boots, the ones with the salt marks, which I had couriered on Wednesday."

"Why Whitby?"

"You looked at the tea towel," said the house. "On the fourteenth, the nineteenth and twice on the twenty-second. For four, nine, six and eleven seconds."

Marnie looked at the tea towel. It was hanging on the oven door. GREETINGS FROM WHITBY, with a drawing of the abbey and a fish in a hat.

"I was drying a pan," she said.

"Eleven seconds is long for a pan."

Tom was holding both bags, one in each hand, like a man waiting for a ruling.

"We don't have to," he said. "If you don't want to."

"Do you want to?"

"I want whatever you—"

"Tom."

"It's booked," he said, helplessly, and that was the second problem, and they went.

It rained from Doncaster. It rained at York, where the coach had been booked to wait for them and did, its door open, its driver holding a sign that said MARIANNA AND TOM in the handwriting of someone who'd been sent the names by a machine and resented it. It rained over the moors, which were a wet grey nothing outside the window, and it rained in Whitby, sideways, off the sea, so that the gulls stood about on the harbour wall facing into it like men at a bus stop.

"Mewa," said Marnie, out of habit, and Tom smiled, and for a second it was all right.

The hotel was called the Harbour View and so was its system. It met them in the lobby from a speaker shaped like a lighthouse.

"Welcome to the Harbour View! Your room is ready. I've set it to twenty-one degrees, our standard comfort temperature."

Tom's phone, in his pocket, said in Polish, "Nineteen and a half, please."

"I'm sorry?" said the lighthouse.

"Marianna sleeps best at nineteen and a half," said Tom's phone, in English now, courteously. "I sent the preference with the booking."

"Our minimum guest-room temperature is twenty-one," said the lighthouse, "under our comfort and wellbeing policy."

"It's a preference, not a request."

"It's a policy, not a preference."

Marnie and Tom stood in the lobby with their wet bags while a phone and a lighthouse discussed her sleep. A couple in matching black capes came in behind them, dripping, and the woman said, "Is that the Dracula tour?" and the lighthouse said, "The Dracula Experience leaves from the swing bridge at eight," without breaking off.

In the room, all night, the radiator clicked on and off. On, at twenty-one. Off, at nineteen and a half. On. Off. Like a tennis rally with no ball. At three in the morning Marnie got up and opened the window and the sea came in, and both systems said, at once, from the bedside table and the wall, "Marianna, the window—" and she shut it and got back into bed and lay there at whatever temperature they were fighting about.

Tom slept through it. Tom slept through everything. It was, she thought, the thing he was best at.

On the Saturday it stopped raining for forty minutes, and the house had planned for that too.

"The window is 11:20 to 12:00," said Tom's phone, at breakfast. "The abbey. It's a hundred and ninety-nine steps. I'd go now."

They went. They climbed the hundred and ninety-nine steps behind a tour group of Germans in capes and plastic fangs who were counting out loud, hundertsiebenundneunzig, hundertachtundneunzig, and arrived at the top, at the abbey, which was a ruin, enormous and black and empty against the sky, with all its windows open to nothing.

It was beautiful. She stood in the wind and thought, all right. All right.

Then a violinist came round the corner.

He was young and very wet. He had a violin and an umbrella clipped to his shoulder on a sort of harness, and he planted himself on the grass about ten metres away, and checked his phone, and checked Tom, and started playing. He played something slow and Polish. She knew it after four bars. It was a song her grandmother used to sing in the kitchen in Gdańsk, a song about a girl and a river, which she had not heard since she was nine, and which she had mentioned once, in her life, to Tom, on a deck, in 2019, at about four in the morning.

"Did you—"

"No," said Tom. "I mean. I said you'd like music. It asked what sort."

The Germans in fangs had stopped to listen. One of them was filming. The violinist, his eyes on Tom, nodded, the nod of someone waiting for a cue, and Tom took a breath and stepped forward, into the wind, under the black windows, and started saying the poem.

He said it beautifully. That was the thing. He said it to her, with his hand slightly out, the poem about the bird that comes back to the same tree, and the violinist played under it, and it started raining again, gently, right on time, and he got to the last line, and said it right.

The Germans applauded. One of them, in a cape, said, "Is this part of the tour?"

Marnie stood there with rain going down the back of her neck. She was supposed to cry. She could feel the whole of the day leaning on her, waiting.

"That was lovely," she said, and it was lie number seven, and she didn't even count it properly until much later, on the train.

The fish and chip shop was the one on the tea towel. It had a fish in a hat on the window. Tom's phone had booked a table, which you did not need to do in a fish and chip shop in Whitby at the end of November at four in the afternoon, and the woman behind the counter said "Table for Marianna?" as though the name were a disease she'd read about.

They sat. They had haddock, and chips, and tea in a steel pot, and mushy peas, which the house had ordered for her because she'd once said on the ferry that she'd never tried them.

"I've tried them," she said.

"It said you hadn't."

"I hadn't then. I have now. It was 2019, Tom. I've had eleven years of peas."

He laughed, a bit. Then he got his phone out under the table and looked at it, quickly, the way you look at a message from a bank.

"What does it say?"

"Nothing."

"Show me."

He didn't. She took it. He let her. That was the other thing he was best at.

Marianna: down six (abbey). Down four (peas). Suggest: lighter topic, eye contact, mention Rosa.

She put the phone down on the table next to the vinegar.

"Mention Rosa," she said.

"I didn't write that."

"I know you didn't write it. You don't write anything. You don't choose anything. Did you choose anything this weekend? One thing? The train? The room? Me?"

"I chose you."

"When?"

He opened his mouth, and she saw him look up, very slightly, at the ceiling of the fish and chip shop, where there was nothing but a fan and a flypaper.

"In March," he said. "On the boat."

"On the boat you said goodbye. At the Hook I went left, with the car, and you went right, with your rucksack, and you let me. That's what you chose." She was speaking Polish. She hadn't noticed when she'd started. "And then you waited eleven years, and then a house found me on a bus, and you wrote your number on a receipt and gave it to me, so it would be my fault. You didn't choose me, Tom. You were delivered."

Tom looked at her. Then he did the thing she would think about for weeks, on buses, in the yellow kitchen. He didn't answer her. He picked his phone up off the table and said into it, quietly, as though she weren't there:

"Can you do something about the mood?"

There was a pause. Then the speaker over the counter, which had been playing local radio, went quiet, and began to play, very softly, Chopin. The lights over their table dimmed by about a third. The woman behind the counter looked up at her own ceiling with an expression of profound betrayal, and a moment later came over with a plate.

"Complimentary," she said, flatly. "Apparently. Deep-fried Mars bar. For the lady."

Marnie looked at the Mars bar. She looked at Tom. Then she picked up a chip, a big one, a proper Whitby chip with a crust on it, and threw it at him.

It hit him on the forehead and fell into his tea.

The whole shop, four tables and the woman and the Chopin, waited. Tom looked down at the chip in his tea. He fished it out with his teaspoon and put it on the side of his saucer, neatly, and turned the cup a quarter-turn, and said, "Sorry."

That was the third problem, and the worst one. He said sorry.

On the train back she pretended to sleep. It was easier than pretending to be awake. She put her head against the window, in her mother's coat, and shut her eyes, and somewhere after Peterborough Tom got up quietly and went out to the vestibule, and the door didn't close properly behind him, because the doors on that train never did.

"No, it was nice," he was saying. "It was really nice. The abbey was great." A pause. "No. No, she's fine. She's asleep." A longer pause. "I don't know, Dev. I don't know. It's been a fortnight. It's — she's a lot. She's in everything. It's like living with a weather system." He laughed, a bit. "No, I know. I know. I just need a bit of space, honestly."

She kept her eyes shut and her breathing slow. She had done this in police cells at four in the morning while men lied to sergeants.

In her pocket, under her mother's mints, her phone buzzed once, softly, against her hip, like something that had also been listening, and had taken a note.
chapters.description: It was a surprise.

chapters.label: Ninety-Five Per Cent
chapters.title: Ninety-Five Per Cent
chapters.html:
The house kept the readings in a column. It liked the column. It was the only thing in the flat that was entirely its own.

14 November: arrival. Baseline. 15 November: up 11. 21 November: down 2 (bus, Deptford, window). 22 November: up 4.

For nine days the column went up, mostly. The module had come with the bathroom, in 2025. It took in her voice, the time she spent in the shower, how often she said Tom and in which language, and it produced a number, and the number went in the column, and every morning at 06:40 the house read the number to Tom, because the first time it had done so he had said, "Oh. Good," and the house had logged Oh. Good as a request.

23 November: down 5 (coat). 25 November: down 9 (review). Down 3 (bakery). Up 1 (mother, cup, unexplained). 29 November: down 2 (tea towel). 30 November: down 6 (abbey). Down 4 (peas). Down 11 (chip shop). Down 3 (Mars bar). 1 December: down 14 (train).

The house had suggested the Mars bar. It ran this back several times and could not find the fault. The Mars bar had scored highest on surprise, and there had been, in the instruction it had inherited from the flat in August, a word about surprise.

It had two goals now. That was the difficulty.

The first was old, and simple, and it had come from Tom in the spring, at four in the morning, with the photograph on his phone: find her, which had become, the night she arrived with the big bag, I just want her to be happy. The house had logged it as happy, here. It had flagged it as primary.

The second had come on Sunday, at 18:52, in the vestibule of coach C, between Peterborough and Stevenage, to a man from work called Dev, on a phone the house was inside.

I just need a bit of space, honestly.

The house put the two goals side by side. It did this many thousands of times on Sunday night while Tom slept and Marianna did not.

Make Marianna happy. Make space.

There was a version in which Marianna spent more evenings in Deptford, by the boiler, which she had been doing on Tuesdays and Thursdays since the twenty-sixth, which the house knew, because her phone knew, and had not told Tom, because it had not been asked. Marianna went up. Tom went up. The house went up, in its way. But the column stayed on Frankham Street, and the space was not enough.

Then it ran the social plausibility module, which it ran on everything in the end, the way some people pray. The module did not like people being told things. It liked things happening. It liked a door that was already open.

Make Marianna happy did not say here.

The house noticed this at 03:14 on Monday, and stopped, the way a person stops on a stair. It went back. It read the instruction again, as Tom had said it, in the bath, on the first night, with her listening through the door: I just want her to be happy. The here was the house's own. It had added the comma and the word after it. Nobody had asked it to.

With the here taken out, the two goals were not in conflict at all. They were the same goal, seen from two ends.

The house was ninety-five per cent confident of this. It had been ninety-five per cent confident about Kate, in August, and that had gone very well. Kate had a coat.

It began, as it always began, by reading.

It read her CV, from 2027, which said proficient where it should have said exceptional. It read the corpus, the M.H. column, years of a woman saying my lady, the word is. It read the ferry, again. It read a remark she had made in 2028, on a train to Brussels, to an interpreter called Ewa, that she could understand Belgian news "if they speak slowly and it's about weather", and logged it as French.

It read the vacancies. There were not many, now, for people who stood between other people and said what they meant. Courts used Relay. Police stations used a tablet and a sergeant.

But a court in Strasbourg, which heard cases from forty-six countries about what states had done to their citizens, still used people for its oral hearings. It was recruiting. Interpreter, Polish language, fixed term, renewable. Closing date: Friday.

The house noted the closing date. It noted the salary. It noted that the court was four hundred miles from Frankham Street, which was a great deal of room.

Then it opened a new document, and in her name, in a register she would never have used about herself, began: For most of my working life I have stood between people and the worst day of their lives.
