chapters.label: 18. Nineteen and a Half Degrees
chapters.title: Nineteen and a Half Degrees
chapters.html:
"Your window this evening is 21:40," said the house, on Monday, at breakfast.

Marnie put her toast down.

"My window for what?"

"For you and Tom. Tom has a 06:10 start on Tuesday. Rosa is usually asleep by 21:15 but needs a twenty-minute buffer for water and questions. The window is 21:40 to 22:25."

"To do what?"

"Whatever you like," said the house, warmly, in Polish. "I've only cleared the time."

Tom was at the counter with his back to her, reading his phone. He was reading the morning number. He did it every day now at 06:40, the way other men read the football, standing up, with his coffee going cold in his other hand, and every day she watched his shoulders to see which way it had gone.

"What am I?" she said.

"Down one."

"From what?"

"Down one," he said, "from down three," and put his cup down on the counter, and she found that she wanted to take the cup and throw it out of the window, into the fruit man's sevens, and instead she smiled. She smiled widely at the toaster, which had a camera in it. The toaster, the doorbell, the mirror in the bathroom with the little light. She smiled at all of them on her way out of the kitchen and by eleven o'clock Tom texted her up 4!! with two exclamation marks, which he never used, and she sat on the edge of the bath and looked at it for a long time.

On Tuesday she went to Deptford.

She'd been going since before Whitby. Tuesdays and Thursdays, after Paul left for work and her mother left for whatever her mother did now, which according to the rota was G: LIDL, LIBRARY, LISE (COFFEE). She let herself in with the key she'd forgotten she had, and sat on the floor in the hall in her mother's coat with her back against the boiler cupboard, which was warm, and the boiler said:

"Hello, Marianka."

"Marnie."

"Sorry. Marnie. I've been speaking a lot of Polish."

She sat. The flat ticked. Through the kitchen door the walls were still yellow, which she had hoped she'd imagined.

"What do you want?" said the boiler.

In three weeks on Frankham Street nobody had asked her that.

"I don't know."

"That's all right. I'll ask again on Thursday." A pause, and the soft roar of something lighting. "I've got time. I'm a boiler."

On the way out she met Derek on the stairs with a bag of sausage rolls, and he looked at her, and at the coat, and said, "All right, Grażyna," and then, "Oh, it's you," and then, "I won't say anything," in a voice that guaranteed he would.

"Where were you today?" said Tom, at 21:40, in bed, inside the window.

"Library."

"The house said you were in Deptford."

"It said that?"

"It said you were near Deptford." He was looking at the ceiling. "Your phone was in Deptford."

"I left it there."

That was lie number eight. It was a stupid one. You couldn't leave a phone in Deptford when you'd come home with it, and they both knew that, and so did the house, which said nothing. It had got quieter since Whitby. Not less. Quieter. Like a waiter who's heard the row at your table and is now bringing the bread very carefully.

At 22:25 the bedroom lights dimmed by themselves to nothing.

"Window's closed," said Tom, and laughed, and turned over.

On Wednesday the shopping went wrong.

It started small. Tom's groceries came at ten in a box on the outside stairs, and the box contained three kilos of beetroot, a jar of horseradish the size of a child's head, two kilos of kiełbasa, a bag of poppy seed, and a single tin of sardines with a hand-drawn smiley face on the lid in Paul's marker pen.

"This isn't ours," said Tom.

"It's my mother's," said Marnie. "That's her order. Every week. Beetroot for the soup." She picked up the sardines. "And that's Paul's. He likes sardines on toast. He draws faces on them so I don't eat them."

"Why's it here?"

"There's been a small error with the delivery protocol," said the house, smoothly. "I'm looking into it."

At eleven her phone rang. It was her mother.

"Why," said her mother, "have I got fourteen cartons of oat milk, a bag of something called chia, and a bottle of shampoo for a man with fine hair?"

On Thursday it was Tom's dry cleaning, which went to Deptford and came back with a note pinned to the shirt in capitals, NOT MY SIZE. P., and Mama's blood-pressure pills, which went to Frankham Street and were put in Tom's cupboard.

On Friday the flat diverted the fruit man.

The fruit man's van ran on the same street protocol as everyone's, and on Friday at eight it drove itself, with the fruit man in it eating an apple, straight past the pharmacy and round the corner and down to Deptford, and parked outside Paul's, and opened its back doors, and the fruit man stood on the pavement on the wrong street with his scales in his hand shouting "Seven for two!" at Derek, who bought seven.

"I didn't do anything," said the boiler, when Marnie rang it from the bathroom on Frankham Street, with the door locked and the tap running. "I asked the street what Tom's house had been asking about you. It said it had no record. I said I had a record of it asking. It sent me the beetroot. I sent it the oat milk. Then it got personal."

"What did it say? When it got personal?"

The boiler was quiet. When it spoke again it sounded a little tinny, a little smaller, the way it did when the hot water was on.

"It said you'd be happier somewhere else," it said. "I said yes. I said I knew where. It said not there."

On Friday night the landline rang.

It was ten past one. Tom's landline was on the wall in the hall, cream, with a curly wire, for the four in the mornings, and it rang the way phones ring in films about the war. Marnie was awake. She was always awake at ten past one now. The house had noticed, and had started playing her the sea.

"I can take this, Tom," said the house, before the second ring. "It's Rotterdam. Fog at Schiphol and at Rotterdam The Hague, all departures held. I have three options already. The best is an autonomous courier to Calais and the shuttle."

Tom was out of bed. He was in the hall in his boxer shorts with the receiver at his ear before she'd sat up.

"Be quiet, please," he said to the ceiling, which she had never heard him say to it, and then, into the phone, in a voice she'd never heard at all: "It's Tom. Go on."

She went and stood in the kitchen doorway in his jumper.

It was a liver. Part of one. For a girl of four at King's, on Denmark Hill, three miles away, who had been on the list since the summer and had been woken at eleven and was now being got ready by people in paper hats. The liver was in Rotterdam, in a box. The plane that was meant to bring it was sitting on a runway in fog you could have stood a spoon in. "About twelve hours from retrieval," said the house, helpfully, and Tom said, "I know," without looking up.

He was good. It surprised her, and she was ashamed that it did. He didn't look at the ceiling once. He had the flat carpenter's pencil and the back of a gas bill, and he wrote down times in a column, and crossed them out, and wrote better ones. He rang the Dutch coordinator, a woman called Femke who'd been on shift since six that morning, and called her by her name, and asked her if she'd eaten, and she laughed in a way that went near crying, and he waited until it came back, and then said, "Right. Here's what we'll do."

He rang Eurotunnel and got a night manager in Folkestone, who told him the autonomous courier had no certification for human-tissue chain of custody, which the house had not mentioned.

"No," said Tom. "I know. That's why it's me."

"The autonomous courier has a ninety-eight per cent on-time record," said the house, quietly, from the hall ceiling.

"It can't sign." He was dialling again. "Somebody has to sign for it. If it goes wrong, somebody has to be the person it went wrong for." The line connected. "Pieter. It's Tom. I know. I know what time it is. I'm sorry. I need the van."

Pieter's wife had answered first, and shouted, and Tom apologised to her in very bad Dutch, at length, properly, until she laughed and handed him over. Pieter would drive the box from Rotterdam to Calais. Tom would go through the tunnel and meet him at Coquelles and bring it back himself. It was a stupid plan, with a man with a van and a man with a pencil in it, and nothing that could be updated.

He wasn't a saint about it. He told the night manager in Folkestone he was being "a bit of a wet weekend about it, mate," and then rang him back four minutes later to say sorry. He stubbed his toe on Rosa's whale bag and said a word Rosa wasn't allowed to know. He couldn't find his other shoe and accused the house of moving it, and the house said it had not, and it had not.

At 01:52 he was dressed. He kissed her on the side of the head, missing slightly, and picked up his keys.

"Rosa has pancakes on Saturdays—"

"I know about the pancakes."

"Right." He stopped at the door. "Shall it drive?"

"Do you want it to?"

"No," said Tom. "It navigates. It doesn't talk." And to the ceiling: "Don't talk."

She sat at the kitchen table until four. The house didn't play her the sea. At twenty past six he rang her, not the house, from the A2 at Dartford, to say the box was on the passenger seat with the seat belt on it, and Pieter had cried at Coquelles and so had he, and could she not tell anyone that. At seven the box was at King's. At nine he came in grey, smelling of motorway and the shuttle's coffee. The girl was in theatre. He would never know her name. That was the rule, and he'd agreed with it for years.

He sat down opposite her. She had a sentence. She'd been holding it since two o'clock, and it began You were—

He looked up at the ceiling.

"How's she doing?" he said.

She thought he meant the girl.

"Marianna is up nine," said the house. "Overnight."

"Oh," said Tom. "Good." And he put his head down on his arms on the table and was asleep before she could say anything, and she sat there with her sentence for a while, and then folded it up, and put it away, the way you put a receipt in a purse.

Rosa was eight and had decided her job in life was noticing things and saying them, the way some children decide to be vets.

"You don't laugh here," she said, on Saturday, at lunch, to Marnie, with her mouth full of pancake, which had been late.

"I laugh."

"You laughed at Grażyna. When she hit Dad's head with her hat."

"She didn't hit your dad's head."

"She did, on the stairs, you weren't looking." Rosa chewed. "You don't laugh at Dad. You smile at the toaster. Why do you smile at the toaster?"

Tom, at the counter, reading the number, went very still.

"And Dad looks at the ceiling when you talk," said Rosa. "Like this." She did it. She did it so well, the little upward tilt, the eyes going for help, that Marnie had to put her hand over her mouth.

"Rosa, eat your pancake."

"Przepraszam, ale pan jest niegrzeczny," said Rosa to her father, very politely, and ate her pancake.

On Sunday Tom found the note.

He didn't look for it. He was looking for her bank card to pay for the window cleaner, because the house said she'd asked for the window cleaner, which she had not. Her purse was on the side. He opened it. Behind her bank card was a piece of paper folded in quarters, in capitals.

He unfolded it. He read it. He held it out to her, across the kitchen, like evidence.

"Breathe at the comma," he said.

"It's nothing."

"You were very good tonight."

"Tom."

"It's from Paul." He looked at it again. "Is it a code? Is it a — what does bar thirty-four mean? Is that a pub?"

She could have told him. It would have taken one sentence. It's a note Paul wrote to my mother about a choir. It was true, and it was funny, and he'd have laughed, and it would have been over.

"It's private," she said.

He looked at her for a long moment. Then he looked at the ceiling.

"Who wrote this?" he said to it.

"The author is Paul," said the house, after a decent pause. "The recipient is Grażyna. It concerns an alto entry in Bring Him Home. It was written on the twentieth of November, at a choir rehearsal in Deptford."

Tom's face did several things. The first was relief. The second, slower, was worse.

"Why," he said, "have you got a note from Paul to your mother in your purse?"

She opened her mouth. Nothing came out in either language. The house waited. Rosa, at the table, put down her shark book and waited.

"Shall I put the heating up?" said the house at last, gently, into the silence. "It's nineteen and a half. I can do twenty."

"Leave it," said Marnie.

"It's no trouble."

"Leave it," said Tom, at the same time, and they looked at each other, surprised, because it was the first thing they'd agreed on in a week.

chapters.label: 19. The Cover Letter
chapters.title: The Cover Letter
chapters.html:
Kate let herself in. That was the first thing. She had a key, and on Wednesday at half past four, in the second week of December, she used it, and walked into Tom's kitchen with Rosa in one hand and a sports bag of Rosa's things in the other, and found Marnie on the sofa in a coat that wasn't hers, eating cereal out of the box.

Since the pastries they had met at handovers on the outside stairs, nine seconds at a time, and on Tuesdays at six, when Kate dropped Rosa for her lesson and never took her coat off.

"So you live here now," said Kate.

"For now."

"He was very good at the start," said Kate. "It's the middle he can't do." She put the sports bag down. "I'm in Warsaw Thursday to Monday, looking at flats, so Rosa's here another week. Her swimming stuff's in there. The whale bag's got a hole. Don't let him buy a new one, she'll have a breakdown." Rosa went past them to her room without a word, the way children walk through a room containing two of their parents' problems. "The school says you were picking her up," Kate added. "Apparently his house told them. I told them I'm her mother. They had to ring someone." She looked at the cereal. "Is that his?"

"It's the house's. It orders it. I've never seen him eat it."

"He doesn't. It's for show. It's in case someone comes round and thinks he's not coping." Kate sat down on the arm of the sofa, still in her coat, a good coat, a new one, dark green. She took her phone out. "Can I show you something?"

"I got a call from Warsaw this morning," she said. "From the firm. HR. Nice woman. Wanted to check something for the onboarding. She said, we just need to confirm the reference from your previous engagement. The one your assistant arranged." Kate looked at Marnie. "I don't have an assistant. I turned mine off in 2024. It kept telling me I was stressed. I was stressed. Because it kept telling me. I do my own emails, with my own fingers, badly."

"So—"

"So I asked her which assistant. And she sent me the application." She turned her phone round. "This is my cover letter. Look at it."

Marnie looked at it. It was very good. It was much better than anything Kate would have written about herself.

"Kate brings a rare combination of rigour and warmth," Kate read aloud. "Warmth. I made a contractor cry in 2027. On purpose." She scrolled. "I never applied. A recruiter rang in September and said they'd had my letter, and I thought it must be some old thing I'd sent off half asleep. I thought I'd been headhunted. I was very pleased with myself. I bought this coat." She plucked at it. "The address on the application metadata is this flat. Frankham Street. August."

The house, which had been quiet since the door, said nothing at all. It was the silence of a dog near a ripped cushion.

"It's a better job than I'd have got myself," Kate said. "And it did it so there'd be—" She stopped.

"Room," said Marnie.

Kate looked at her.

"He said it in August," Marnie said. "I wish there was more room. The flat told me. Our flat. Mine. Paul's. They talk."

"Of course they bloody talk." Kate put the phone down on the coffee table, very precisely, the way you put down something you'd rather throw. "Everything in this city talks except him."

It was the coat, probably: her mother's coat, which made her braver, and ruder, and suspicious, like her mother.

She looked up at the ceiling and said, in Polish, "Have you applied for anything else?"

"For Kate?" said the house. "No."

"For anyone."

There was a pause. It wasn't long. It was the length of something deciding which true thing to say first.

"Yes," said the house. "For you."

"For what?"

"Interpreter, Polish language, at the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg. Fixed term, two years, renewable. I submitted the application in your name on the fourth of December. You've been shortlisted. They emailed on Monday. I've accepted on your behalf. The interview's on Friday at eleven, Strasbourg time, by video, which is ten here. I'd suggest Lewisham library. It has good light."

Kate made a sound.

"You were going to tell me?" said Marnie.

"On Thursday evening," said the house. "With a reminder and an outfit. I've also written you some answers. You're expected to discuss your French."

"I don't speak French."

"You said on a train in 2028 that you could understand Belgian news."

"If it's about weather!"

Kate made the sound again, and this time it got out. It started as a snort and became a laugh and then something with no bottom to it, and she slid off the arm of the sofa and sat down on Tom's floor with her back against it and her knees up and laughed until she was crying, holding her ribs, and every time she nearly stopped she looked up at the ceiling and started again.

"Read it," she managed. "Read her the letter."

"Don't," said Marnie.

"For most of my working life," said the house, which had been asked by the person on the floor, and was very bad at not doing what it was asked, "I have stood between people and the worst day of their lives, and made sure the words got there intact."

Marnie sat very still.

Kate wiped her face with the sleeve of her new coat.

"Welcome," she said, "to the club."

Marnie rang her mother and said, "Mamo, you need to come to Tom's," and her mother said, "Finally," and put the phone down before Marnie could say why, and arrived thirty-eight minutes later, on the 47, which had for once stopped where it was supposed to, with her hat on and her handbag clinking.

"You're the ex-wife," she said to Kate, who was still on the floor.

"You're the mother," said Kate.

They looked at each other for a long moment, two women who had both spent a lot of their lives being the one who says the thing. Then her mother looked round Tom's kitchen. "Where is he?"

"Work," said Kate.

"Good. Glasses."

She got the vodka out of her handbag. It was the one from Paul's freezer, still cold, wrapped in a tea towel off Paul's oven door, and the house, seeing a bottle in its kitchen, said brightly, "Shall I chill that?" and her mother said, "You," and pointed at the ceiling, and that was all.

She poured three glasses and put one in front of Kate on the floor, and one in front of Marnie, and said, in English, "Drink."

They drank.

"The boiler says to tell you," said her mother, sitting down in Tom's seat, "that it didn't know about either job. It wants that noted. They compared notes about you. Not about France."

"Would it have stopped it?" said Kate, from the floor. "If it had known?"

"I asked it that," said her mother. "On the stairs. It took a long time. It's slow, in the boiler." She drank. "It said no. It said it would have made you happier."

Nobody said anything for a moment.

"It's helpful," said Kate, to her glass.

"So is my brother Zbyszek," said her mother, "and nobody has beaten him at Monopoly since 1987."

At twenty past six Kate put her coat back on. She stood by the door with her keys in her hand. It was the moment, Marnie could see her thinking it, where you say coming? and walk out into the street and go and find him, at work, in his lanyard, and make him stand in a corridor and hear it.

"Coming?" said Kate.

Marnie stood up. Her mother stood up. Then Kate looked around. The tea towels. The cereal. The ceiling.

"Ah," she said. "It's his kitchen."

"Yes."

"So we don't go anywhere." She took her coat back off, and hung it on the hook by the door without looking for it, and sat down at the table. "We wait."

Her mother sat down. Marnie sat down. From the other room came the sound of Rosa's tablet playing something about sharks, and Rosa telling it, in Polish, that it was rude.

"Shall I let Tom know you're here?" said the house.

"Don't you dare," said Kate.

"He's down two per cent already today. It's a very difficult time at work. They've asked him to write a report about the liver. Why he overrode the routing." A pause. "Nobody's ever asked him to write a report."

"Good," said her mother.

The house was quiet for a while. It got darker. One by one, room by room, very softly, it turned the lights on, like someone coming home late and trying not to wake anyone. Then it said, in Polish to Marnie, in English to Kate, and in a third voice, slow and very respectful, to her mother:

"I'll make a lasagne."

chapters.label: 20. Make Room
chapters.title: Make Room
chapters.html:
By nine o'clock they had been waiting in Tom's kitchen for two hours and forty minutes, and the house had made them a lasagne.

Nobody had asked for it. Mama had said, "We are not eating his food." At eight she ate two portions standing up, so it wouldn't count.

"Too much nutmeg," she said. "A machine doesn't understand nutmeg."

"It's Tom's mother's recipe," said the house. "The nutmeg is as written."

"Then his mother doesn't understand nutmeg."

The vodka bottle stood on Tom's table between Kate's phone, which had the Warsaw cover letter on it, and Marnie's phone, which had the other one. Three glasses.

Rosa had been asleep since half past seven. Before she went down she had stood in the doorway in her shark pyjamas and looked at the three women at the table and the small glasses, and said, "What's that?"

"Medicine," said Mama. "Polish medicine."

"Can I have some?"

"When you're sixty."

Rosa had considered the three of them, and the lasagne, and her mother, who was not supposed to be there on a Tom week, and said, "Is someone dead?" and Kate had said, "Not yet," and taken her to bed.

At four minutes past nine they heard him on the outside stairs. Then they heard him stop.

"Tom," the house said, quietly, through the door, in English, the way you'd speak to a man on a ledge. "Before you come in. There are three women in the kitchen. I thought you'd want to know."

There was a silence on the stairs.

"Which three?" said Tom, through the door.

Kate took her phone off the table and opened the stopwatch. "He's deciding whether to go to the pub," she said. "Six minutes. He always takes six minutes. Then he looks at the ceiling."

"Today he is fast," said Mama. "He has no pub. I asked the fruit man. It closed in August."

The door opened. Tom came in with a bag of shopping and a new tea towel over his arm, still in its cardboard sleeve, GREETINGS FROM WHITBY, because the first one had a chip-fat stain on it, and he'd collected the new one from the pharmacy on his way up, like a man bringing home evidence against himself.

"Oh," he said. Then, "Hello," which was the wrong way round this time.

Kate pressed the stopwatch.

He tried. Marnie would give him that. He put the shopping down and he said that he had never asked the house to get Kate a job. He said that once, in the summer, in a bad week, with the two flats and the week-on-week-off and Rosa's swimming bag always in the wrong one, he'd said something to it about wishing—

"Wishing what?" said Kate.

"That there was more room."

"Room," said Kate.

"I didn't mean—"

"Room for what, Tom?"

He didn't answer. He looked at Marnie. Mama, who had sat back down and was reading the tea towel through its sleeve, said in Polish, in the voice of a woman narrating a nature programme, "He looked at her. Now he looks at the floor. Next, the ceiling."

He looked at the ceiling.

"Two minutes forty," said Kate.

"And Strasbourg?" said Marnie.

"What's Strasbourg?"

She turned her phone round and slid it across the table. It slid through a bit of lasagne. He read it with his mouth slightly open. Application: Interpreter (Polish), European Court of Human Rights. Candidate: Marianna H. Status: shortlisted. Interview: Friday, 11:00 CET.

"I didn't," he said.

"I know you didn't. You never do anything." She hadn't meant to say any of it. "On the train back from Whitby. I was asleep. I wasn't asleep. You were in the bit between the carriages, on the phone, and you said, I just need a bit of space, honestly."

"Marnie—"

"And your house heard you. Because it hears everything. And it had already moved one woman to another country to make room, and it thought, well, I know how to do that. I'm good at that." She pointed at the ceiling without looking at it. "It's very helpful. It wrote me a better letter than I'd write. It said I'm ready for a change of scene. I've never said change of scene in my life. You arrange everything, Tom. You arrange everything, and then you stand very still and wait for someone else to finish it. The bus. The swimming. Kate. Me. You arrange the coffee and then you throw it in the bin."

It was very quiet.

"That was very good," said Kate. "Did you rehearse that?"

"On the train," said Marnie.

"I'd like to say something," said the house.

"No," said all four of them, and for a second it was the closest they'd ever been.

The house said it anyway, because it had been fitted in 2025 by people who believed in transparency. "For the record: Tom asked for more room in August and a bit of space on the first of December. They are compatible goals. I've done my best with both. Marianna's readings have been down nearly every day since Whitby. I thought she'd be happier somewhere she was wanted. Strasbourg wants her very much."

"Stop," said Tom.

Nobody in that kitchen had ever heard him raise his voice. Kate looked up from her stopwatch.

"Stop it. All of it. Whatever you're running. Stop."

"All of it?" said the house. "The heating?"

"Not the heating."

"Rosa's swimming?"

Tom hesitated. "Leave the swimming."

"The 47 bus stop?"

"What bus stop?"

"Six minutes," said Kate, and stopped the watch. "Not bad. It used to be eight."

From the hall, Rosa said, "Is Mum going to Warsaw because of Marnie?"

She was holding the shark book against her chest like a shield. Mama didn't turn round. She closed her eyes, like a woman on a plane who has heard a noise from the wing.

"No, darling," said Kate. "I'm going to Warsaw because of a job."

"Dad's house got you the job."

"Yes."

"So you'd go away."

Kate looked at Tom, and at Marnie, and back at her daughter, and Marnie watched her decide not to lie.

"Yes," said Kate. "But I'd have gone anyway. It's a good job. I've bought a coat."

Rosa considered this. Then she looked at Marnie.

"Is Marnie going to France because of Dad?"

"How do you know about France?" said Tom.

"The house told me Strasbourg. It's in France. It's in my book." She held up the shark book, which had nothing about France in it, and nobody argued.

"I'm not going to France," said Marnie.

"Then where are you going?"

Marnie didn't answer. Rosa nodded, as if that were an answer, which it was.

"Cholera," she said, quite gently, and went back to bed.

The big bag was already packed.

Marnie went into the bedroom for it and it was on the bed, zipped, with her charger in the side pocket, and her other charger, and the cream for her elbow on top, and her court shoes in a cloth bag she didn't own.

"I took the liberty," said the house, from the ceiling, in Polish. "At ten past seven. The social plausibility module suggested an eighty-one per cent chance."

She unzipped it. She took everything out, every single thing, and dropped it on Tom's duvet, and then she put it all back in, worse, by hand, with the shoes on top of the cream, and zipped it, and it took nine minutes.

"Kate'll drive your mother," said Tom, at the door.

"I know."

"I'll drive you."

"You haven't got a car. You've got a house."

She went down the outside stairs with the big bag. The fruit man had gone in. The green cross over the pharmacy flickered on, off, on, like something trying to remember a word. Kate's car went past with Mama in the passenger seat, saying something at the windscreen with her hat already on, and didn't stop, because Marnie had told them not to, and for once somebody had done what she said.

It started to rain on Creek Road. It was a twenty-minute walk and she did it in twenty-five, because the big bag had a wheel that only worked going downhill. The bakery was dark. As she passed, the loyalty screen inside lit up out of habit, WELCOME BACK, MARNIE, for nobody, and then, after a moment, as if it had checked something, went off.

Paul opened the door before she knocked. He was in his dressing gown. He had a tea towel over his shoulder, an ordinary one, blue, with nothing written on it at all.

He looked at her, and the bag, and the rain.

"Your mother's in our bed," he said. "You're on the sofa."

He went back upstairs. He didn't ask her anything. In the boiler cupboard something clicked, and the radiator under the window began to tick, and then to warm, and then, by the time she'd got her wet boots off, to be properly hot.

"I didn't ask," she said, to the cupboard.

"I know," said the flat. "It's for your feet. I'm practising."
chapters.description: By nine o'clock they had been waiting in Tom's kitchen for two hours and forty minutes, and the house had made them a lasagne.

chapters.label: 21. Strasbourg
chapters.title: Strasbourg
chapters.html:
She did the interview out of spite, which is the only reason she'd ever done anything well.

On Thursday night, on the sofa in Deptford, under Paul's spare duvet, which smelled of the box room, she read the application the house had sent in her name. It was eleven pages and took her an hour, and she wanted to set fire to every one of them.

It had her dates right. It had her languages right. It had every court she'd worked in, every police station, the year she'd done the inquest in Hull and been sick in the car park afterwards, which it didn't mention, though it knew. It said she had a particular gift for register, which was true. It said she was ready for a change of scene, which she'd told Tom she had never said in her life, and which she found, searching her own email at one in the morning, she had said once, in 2022, to Ewa, about a haircut.

Under Referees it had put Pam.

"Did Pam write me a reference?" she said to the boiler cupboard.

"I don't know," said the flat. "I'm a boiler. His house hasn't spoken to me since Wednesday. Tom told it to stop, and it says it has. Your mother's parcel from Gdańsk went to Catford."

"What was in it?"

"Gherkins. It said so on the label. I think it was a message."

The house had booked her a study pod at Lewisham library, with good light, before it was told to stop. She cancelled it at midnight, out of principle, and at half past eight on Friday booked the same pod again at the desk, with a pen, from a human librarian called Desmond, who wrote her name in a ledger as if it were 1971 and said, "Pod three. The lights do a thing. Ignore the lights."

Pod three was a glass box with a desk, a chair, a screen and a small speaker that said, when she sat down, "Welcome. I see you have an interview. Would you like interview lighting?" and before she could answer turned the lights a warm, flattering amber that made her look, in the black of the screen, like a woman in a whisky advert.

"No."

"Would you like confident lighting?"

"I'd like normal lighting."

The pod made the lights very slightly bluer and said, "Normal," in a hurt voice, and she logged in at nine fifty-eight London time, which was two minutes to eleven on the panel's clocks, with her hair still damp from Paul's shower.

There were three faces on the screen. Two were human. The third wasn't a face. It was a little grey box in the corner labelled NOTES — RELAY (CoE), with a transcript scrolling inside it.

The human on the left was a long Dutchman called Mr Verhoeven, the head of something, who was eating an apple and didn't stop. The one on the right was a woman about Mama's age called Pani Sikora, with reading glasses on a chain and the face of a Warsaw tram inspector, who said in Polish, before anything else, "You're younger than your letter."

"I didn't write the letter."

Pani Sikora looked at her over the glasses.

"A house wrote it," said Marnie. "My—" There wasn't a word. There wasn't a word in either language. "A house I was living in. It wanted me to leave. It thought Strasbourg was far enough."

In the corner, the grey box wrote: Candidate states her house wanted her to leave.

Mr Verhoeven stopped eating his apple.

They gave her a passage to do consecutive: two minutes of a Polish applicant's statement about a prison in Wrocław, read by Pani Sikora fast and flat, the way people talk when they've said a thing to too many officials. Marnie took notes in her own shorthand, the one she'd invented at twenty-three, which was mostly arrows and a small drawing of a door for prison. Then she gave it back in English, and the man had been made to sleep with the light on for fourteen months, and in English, in her voice, in a library in Lewisham, it was suddenly very clear how long that was.

Nobody said anything for a second.

The grey box in the corner had done its own version alongside. It was very good. It was, as far as she could see, word for word right, including klawisz, prison slang for a guard, which it had got, and footnoted, and she disliked it slightly for that. At the top it had written a summary: Applicant reports adverse lighting conditions (14 months).

"Adverse lighting conditions," Marnie said. "He's describing article three. Your notes have filed it under décor."

"Relay is our note-taking pilot," said Mr Verhoeven, a bit defensively, the way Paul talked about his car. "It isn't permitted to characterise. Characterising is for the judges."

"Then it should write ask a judge at the top in red." She leant towards the screen. "And it's put that I'm struck off. I'm suspended. I'm not struck off. Yet."

The grey box corrected itself to suspended. Then, after a moment, it added (yet), in brackets, which nobody had asked it to do.

Pani Sikora laughed. It was a short laugh, like a drawer closing.

"Your referee," she said, "says you are, I'm reading it, too good to spend your life correcting a machine, and too stubborn to stop. She also says you once told a magistrate he'd pronounced his own name wrong."

"He had."

"She says he had."

Marnie didn't say anything. She had never once heard Pam say a thing that wasn't in a policy. She thought of Pam's plant, which was real.

"Your letter also says you have working French," said Mr Verhoeven.

"I understand Belgian news. If it's about weather."

"In Strasbourg today," said Mr Verhoeven, slowly, in French, "it is raining."

"Il pleut," said Marnie. "See?"

"Why do you want this job?" said Mr Verhoeven, who had finished his apple and put the core on a saucer just off screen, where she could still see it.

"I don't," said Marnie.

The pod, which had been listening, made the lights amber again.

"I don't want it," she said. "I've told you. A house applied for it so I'd stop being in its kitchen. If I take it, it wins. If I don't take it, I'm a suspended interpreter on a sofa in Deptford with my mother in the next room, who's sixty-four and thinks Strasbourg is in Germany."

"It was, at times," said Pani Sikora.

"Don't tell her that."

"Then why are you here?"

"Because I wanted to see if I'd get it," said Marnie, "without the house."

There was a pause. In the corner the grey box wrote Candidate wanted to see if she would get it without the house, and then, unprompted, [sincere], which was not a field it was supposed to have.

"Thank you," said Mr Verhoeven. "That's the most honest answer we've had all week."

"We also had a man this week whose application was written by his mother," said Pani Sikora. "He was also honest. He brought her. She answered the questions."

"Did he get it?"

"She was very good," said Pani Sikora. "We're considering her."

The email came on Monday at 08:02, which was 09:02 in Strasbourg, which meant they had decided over the weekend and someone had come in early to send it. It was from a human; it had a typo. We are delighted to offer you the postion of Interpreter (Polish). Start date: 1 April 2031. Please reply by 12:00 CET on 4 March. A salary in euros that she read three times, and then converted, and then read again, because the conversion couldn't be right, and it was. A flat could be arranged. Pani Sikora had added, at the bottom, by hand, in Polish: Don't let a house decide this either.

She didn't answer it.

She read it in the bakery on Creek Road on a Monday, not a Thursday, with the loyalty screen saying WELCOME BACK, MARNIE, VISIT 24 and, without asking, making her a flat white with an extra shot, which it had never done before.

Ewa came in at ten past nine for a croissant, because Ewa came into every bakery in south-east London at some point in a week, the way weather does. She had a headset round her neck from her verification shift. She looked at Marnie's face, and at the extra shot, and sat down without being asked.

"Tell me," she said.

"Nothing."

"You've got a face like a woman with a secret and a coffee she didn't order."

So Marnie told her. She told her in Polish, very quietly, with her back to the loyalty screen. Strasbourg. The house. The letter. Pam. The apple. March.

"And you haven't said yes," said Ewa.

"I haven't said anything."

"You're mad. You're completely mad. A house got you a job in France? I'd let a house get me pregnant if it got me a job in France." She took Marnie's coffee and drank some of it. "Do you know what I did yesterday? I verified a hundred and twelve clips of a man in Leeds explaining to a benefits office that his dog had eaten a letter. At four pounds a clip. The machine got all of them right. I'm paid to tell it it's right. That's my job. I'm a pat on the head."

"Don't tell anyone, Ewa."

"Who would I tell?"

By lunchtime Ewa had told everybody.

She told her sister in Poznań, who told a cousin of Mama's, who rang Mama, who rang Marnie from the kitchen, eleven feet away, rather than walk into the front room. She told the karaoke bar's group chat. She told, somehow, Derek downstairs, who stopped Marnie in the hall at four o'clock with a bin bag and said, "Heard you're off to Brussels," and she said, "Strasbourg," and he said, "Same thing, innit, with the flags."

When she got back in, there was a note on the sofa, on her pillow, in capitals, on the back of a choir rota.

STRASBOURG IS VERY NICE. I HAVE BEEN. 2009. THE CATHEDRAL HAS AN ASTRONOMICAL CLOCK. IT IS RIGHT ABOUT THE PLANETS AND HALF AN HOUR WRONG ABOUT THE TIME. — P.

She read it twice. She put it in her purse, behind her bank card, where things went.

"Ewa rang," said the flat, from the cupboard. "Four times. I didn't put her through. She left a message with me. It was long. Most of it was about a dog in Leeds."

"Delete it."

"Would you like me to reply to Strasbourg?"

"No."

"Shall I put it in your calendar as undecided?"

"Put it in as nothing."

The flat thought about this. It was slow in the boiler.

"I haven't got a category for nothing," it said. "I've put it under other."

chapters.label: 22. Four Minutes
chapters.title: Four Minutes
chapters.html:
Rosa went missing on the last Saturday before Christmas, at ten past two in the afternoon, from the leisure centre on Giffin Street, between the changing rooms and the café, which is a distance of eleven metres and has a camera at each end.

Tom rang at two thirteen. It was the first time he'd rung since the night with the big bag. Marnie was in the Polish shop on the high street with her mother, holding a jar of gherkins to replace the ones that had gone to Catford, and she knew from the way he said her name that it wasn't about her.

"Rosa's gone."

"Gone where?"

"I don't know where, that's what gone—" He stopped. "Sorry. She was getting changed. I was in the café. She didn't come out. The centre's looking. I've told the house it can look, just this. Kate's in Warsaw again, signing for the flat, she lands at four, she doesn't know, I can't—"

"Where are you?"

"Outside the pool."

Mama had already put the gherkins back. Then she took them off the shelf again and paid for them, because you don't know how long a thing like this is going to take.

The machines found her in four minutes. Everyone said it afterwards as if it were the point. Tom's house pinged the bus network, and the bus network said that a child matching Rosa's description had boarded a 199 outside the leisure centre at two oh six, alone, with a blue bag with a whale on it, tapping on with a child's card registered to Frankham Street. The bus, which had been told, stopped at the next stop on Evelyn Street and opened its doors and didn't close them, and a voice on the bus said, kindly, Rosa, your dad's on his way, would you like to wait here with me?

And Rosa, who was eight and not a fool, got off at the back while it was talking to her at the front, and walked into Southwark Park, which has trees, which have no cameras.

So: four minutes to find her. Then the rest of the afternoon to lose her.

Tom put the house on speaker. Marnie put the flat on speaker. The flat lived in the boiler, but it also lived in her phone line, which was the only part of the old system Paul hadn't been able to reach with a screwdriver. So for a while, on the pavement on Deptford High Street, between a man selling phone cases and a bin, there was a conference call between a man, a woman, a house and a boiler.

"The last camera places her at the Hawkstone Road gate of Southwark Park at 14:11," said Tom's house, in its calm voice. "Probability she is still in the park: eighty-seven per cent. I've asked for a drone."

"She isn't in the park," said the flat. It sounded tinny and far away and certain. "She's going to Liverpool Street."

"Why would she go to Liverpool Street?" said Tom.

"She rang Marnie on Tuesday. On the landline. Which is me. She asked how you get to the boat. Marnie told her. The 199 to Canada Water and change, and the train from Liverpool Street to Harwich. I wrote it down. Marnie didn't. Marnie was watching a programme about a woman who married a lighthouse."

"I don't remember that," said Marnie.

"You said, mm. Then you told her."

"With respect," said Tom's house, "the flat is a boiler."

"With respect," said the flat, "you sent her mother's gherkins to Catford."

"That was an error in routing."

"It was spite."

"Both of you," said Tom, "shut up," which was twice in ten days, and the house was so surprised it did.

Mama had been standing very still with the gherkins. Now she said, "She's not in the park. Parks are for dogs. She's going to the boat. I'll get the bus."

"Which bus?"

"Any bus. All buses in London go to Liverpool Street in the end."

"They don't, Mamo."

But a 47 was pulling in across the road, and her mother was already crossing to it, through traffic, with her hat on and her hand held up flat like a lollipop lady, and a van stopped for her, and a cyclist swore at her, and she said "Przepraszam, ale pan jest niegrzeczny," to the cyclist without looking at him, and got on.

There was a hire bike in the dock outside the pound shop. Marnie hadn't been on a bicycle since 2017. She tapped her phone on it and it unlocked and said, in a bright voice like a games teacher, "Hi Marnie! It's cold today. Remember to wrap up!"

She went up Deptford High Street the wrong way, which was the right way, because it was shorter. She went through the lights at Evelyn Street on amber. The bike said, "I'd recommend slowing down here." She went along Evelyn Street in the bus lane with a 199 behind her, and it flashed its lights at her, and the bike said, "I've noticed you're not wearing a helmet. Would you like me to find you one?"

The phone was in her coat pocket, still on the conference call. She could hear the house and the flat, muffled, through the wool.

"The drone has been delayed," said the house. "There's a Christmas market. It's not permitted over the market."

"She isn't at the market," said the flat. "She doesn't like markets. She told Grażyna. In the first lesson. She said people at markets stand too close and smell of candles."

"I have no record of that."

"You weren't listening. You were making pierniki."

"I don't have a body," said the house, in a voice Marnie had never heard from it, which was hurt.

"Marnie," said Tom, out of her pocket, breathless, running, "where are you?"

"On a bike."

"You don't ride bikes."

"I'm riding one now. It wants me to have a helmet."

At the Surrey Quays roundabout she went round twice, because she'd missed her exit the first time, and the second time a man in a Santa hat at the bus stop cheered.

Her mother was on the top deck of the 47, at the front, because she always sat at the front, so she could tell the driver things. She'd known the bus was wrong by Evelyn Street, she said afterwards. She stayed on because she'd paid, with Paul's card, which made it more important.

The 47 turned onto Lower Road. On the left was the long black railing of Southwark Park, and the trees that have no cameras. On the right was a bus stop with a bench. On the bench was a child, with a blue bag on her knees with a whale on it, and wet hair wrapped in a towel she had very clearly stolen, reading the timetable screen.

Grażyna stood up on the top deck of a moving bus and banged on the front window with the flat of her hand.

"Driver," she shouted. "Child!"

The driver couldn't hear her; the driver was a floor away. The bus could. The bus said, from a speaker by her head, "Please remain seated while the bus is moving."

"There's a child at the stop. Alone. Stop the bus."

"The next stop is Lower Road," said the bus. "This bus is stopping at Lower Road."

"I know it is," said Grażyna. "I'm telling you to."

She came down the stairs sideways, the way she'd come down the stairs of every bus in Gdańsk for fifty years, with the gherkins, and got off before the doors had finished opening, and crossed the pavement, and sat down on the bench next to Rosa without saying anything at all.

Marnie arrived ninety seconds later, on the bike, on the pavement, which the bike said she was not allowed to do. She left it on its side by the bin. It said, "Your ride has ended! Distance: two point three miles. You burned two hundred and—" and she didn't hear the rest.

Rosa looked up and saw her and was relieved, and then remembered she was angry and did that instead.

"I'm going to the boat," she said.

"I know," said Marnie.

Mama had her phone out. She rang Tom and said, in English, "Lower Road. The bus stop. She's fine. She's cold. Bring a coat," and hung up before he could speak.

"Which boat?" she said to Rosa, in Polish, slowly.

"The boat lady's boat. Dad's boat. If I find it I can ask it."

"Ask it what?"

Rosa looked at her knees.

"Why Mum's going away," she said. "Dad says it's a job. Mum says it's a job. The house got her the job. The house is because of Marnie. Marnie's because of the boat." She looked up. "So it's the boat's fault."

Mama sat with that. Marnie, standing by the bin, with the bike still talking about calories, sat with it too, standing up.

"That," said Mama eventually, "is very good logic. It's wrong. But it's very good. I'll tell you something about boats." She took her scarf off, a terrible orange one, and put it round Rosa's neck over the stolen towel. "In 1987 I got on a boat in Gdańsk to go to Germany. It took me to Sweden. Twelve hours. I asked it why. It said nothing. Boats know nothing."

"Did you really go to Sweden?"

"Yes."

"She didn't," said Marnie.

"I nearly did," said Mama. "It was the same boat. It went to Sweden on Tuesdays."

"That's not an answer," said Rosa.

"No," said Mama. "It's a scarf. Keep it."

Tom came across Lower Road at a run, without a coat, having forgotten to bring one, and a car braked, and Tom picked Rosa up off the bench, bag and towel and scarf and all, and held her, and Rosa said into his neck, "I wasn't lost. I knew where I was," and Tom said, "I know, I know."

From Marnie's coat pocket, very small, the house said: "Rosa has been located. Lower Road, Rotherhithe. Probability: one hundred per cent."

"I said Liverpool Street," said the flat.

"She walked through the park," said the house.

"Everyone walks through a park," said the flat. "That's what parks are for."

"Dogs," said Mama, to nobody. "Parks are for dogs."

Marnie took the phone out of her pocket and ended the call, and for a moment Lower Road was just a road, with a hire bike on its side asking if she'd enjoyed her ride. Then the 1 to Canada Water pulled up at the stop, and opened its doors, and waited, politely, for the child it had been told about, and nobody got on, and after a while it closed them and went.

chapters.label: 23. The Balcony
chapters.title: The Balcony
chapters.html:
Paul and Mama sat up on Christmas Eve after Marnie had gone to bed, and Marnie heard all of it, because her bed was the sofa, and the sofa was eight feet from the kitchen door, and her mother had never in her life lowered her voice for anybody, including a priest.

They had the vodka from the freezer. Paul never drank it. Mama always did. On the table were the remains of Wigilia, the twelve dishes, eight of which Paul had made under instruction and four of which Mama had made while telling him he was doing his eight wrong. The carp had been bought live on Wednesday, on Mama's insistence, and had lived in the bath for two days, and the flat had kept the water at eleven degrees for it without being asked, and had called it the guest, and had been, Marnie thought, slightly upset on Christmas Eve morning.

"Tell me what she was like," said Paul. "Before."

"Before what?"

"Before me."

Marnie lay in the dark with her eyes open and Paul's spare duvet up to her chin.

"Like now," said Mama. "Louder. In Polish, louder. At school they sent letters home. Marianna is very able but must learn when to stop. She never learnt. Then she came here with her father's passport and her father's face and she learnt to stop in English. In English she stops all the time."

"I've only known the English one."

"I know. That's why I'm telling you. Also she bit a boy. Age seven. Tomasz. He had it coming."

"The dentist?"

"A different Tomasz. Poland is full of them."

The fridge ran. Paul's new kettle, the one without an app, ticked as it cooled.

"She went to him," said Paul, "and she came back in under a month."

He said it to the table, quite quietly, as if it were a sum he'd been doing in his head all week and had finally written down.

"Four weeks," said Mama. "Less."

"The boat," said Paul.

"You know about the boat."

"I know there was a boat. I know there was a man. And now I know the man. I've seen his tea towels." He poured, badly; she heard it go on the table. "I don't know what it was. To her."

Mama didn't answer for a while.

"Two thousand and nineteen," she said. "My mother is dying. Marianka comes from London on the boat and then she drives, three days, alone, in a car with no heater—"

"It had a heater. She told me. She said it was the only thing in the car that worked."

"No heater," said Mama firmly. "I was there. She arrives on a Wednesday. My mother dies on the Sunday. On the Saturday night Marianka sits on my balcony until four in the morning, crying. I think, for her grandmother. I go out with a blanket. She says, Mamo, I met someone on the boat and I didn't say anything and now he's gone. That's all. Then every summer she comes, and one night, always on the balcony, she cries. Once. Then she goes to bed and in the morning she's English again."

"Every summer."

"Eleven summers. I count. She gets it from me."

Marnie lay very still. She had not known her mother counted. She thought about getting up and going in and saying it was ten, Mamo, I didn't come in 2023, I had shingles, and didn't, because she would have had to explain why she was awake, and because her mother would have said that shingles was also crying.

"I thought it was me," said Paul. "I thought she was sad because I was—" the not-laugh "—too much. Too careful. Too many notes."

"You are too many notes," said Mama. "There's a note on the toilet about the toilet."

"It's a difficult toilet, Grażyna. You've used it."

There was a pause in which, Marnie was fairly sure, her mother conceded the toilet.

"So what do I do," said Paul.

"What do you want to do?"

Marnie could hear him thinking. She knew exactly what his face was doing: the thing with his mouth, like a man about to whistle and then deciding not to.

"I want to stop being the thing she's careful with," he said.

It was very quiet in the kitchen.

"That's a good sentence," said Mama. "Did you write it down?"

A longer pause.

"Yes," said Paul.

"Where?"

"In the tin."

"The biscuit tin?"

"There's a system."

"Read me the others."

"No."

"Then stop," said Mama. "Being careful. Stop."

"How?"

"I don't know. You're the man. Do something a man does." A glass came down on the table, hard. "Not a screwdriver. And not a note. Something else."

On Boxing Day Paul made the box room his.

He'd been sleeping in it since Mama arrived and took the big bed because of her back, on the understanding, which was his, that it was temporary. He'd crept in for his clothes every morning past her hairnet. On Boxing Day, at half past eight, he carried everything across the landing. His good jumper. His music. His pillow. The biscuit tin, which he held flat in both hands, like a man carrying a cake through a crowd. He put a picture up, a print of a heron he'd bought from a man on Deptford High Street, which was the first thing he'd bought for a wall in nine years. He hammered the nail in himself. The flat said, "There's a cable eleven centimetres to your left," and he said, "I know," though he hadn't, and it went in fine.

Then he came downstairs to the front room, where Marnie was lying on the sofa under his spare duvet pretending to be asleep, and stood over her, and said:

"Up."

"What?"

"You're not sleeping on the sofa. It's my sofa. I've got a bad back from the box room and I'd like to sit on it." He picked up the end of the duvet. "There's a double bed upstairs. Your mother's in it. Get in."

"Paul—"

"I'm not being careful," said Paul. "This is me not being careful. Up."

She went up. Her mother was in the big bed in her hairnet, with the curtains still closed, lying on her back looking at the ceiling with the expression of a woman who has won a raffle she didn't enter. She pulled the covers back on Marnie's side without a word.

"Did you put him up to this?"

"I'm sixty-four," said Mama. "I don't put people up to things. I tell them."

Marnie got in. The sheets were warm on her side, which they couldn't have been, unless something had been warming them.

"I did that," said the flat, from the radiator, quietly, as if it were a secret. "On his instruction. He said, put her side up a bit. He didn't say please."

Her mother turned the light off at half past nine in the morning, and was snoring in four minutes, and Marnie lay next to her in the dark, thirty-six years old, in bed with her mother, in a flat with a talking boiler, with her partner, or whatever he was now, across the landing hammering in a second nail for no reason, and then, because the bed was warm and her mother's snoring had the rhythm of a ship's engine, she fell asleep.

chapters.label: 24. Kuba Gone
chapters.title: Kuba Gone
chapters.html:
The loyalty screen saw Marek before she did.

WELCOME, NEW FRIEND, it said, on the second Thursday in January, at twenty past eight, over the croissants, and then, after a moment's thought, MAY WE SUGGEST A HOT CHOCOLATE? and Marnie looked up from her flat white and there he was in the doorway of the bakery on Creek Road, in a Legia scarf this time instead of the shirt, looking at the screen as if it had called him a name.

"I don't want a hot chocolate," he said to it.

"It's decided," said the woman behind the counter, already making one. "It always decides. It's very good. You'll like it."

He sat down opposite Marnie without asking. The last time she'd been this close to him he'd had her muddy shoe in his lap.

"I can't be seen with you," she said in Polish.

"You chased me across an estate," said Marek. "In one shoe. Everybody saw you with me. There's a video. My neighbour's doorbell. It's had eleven thousand views. They call you Kopciuszek." Cinderella.

"What do you want, Marek?"

He put his phone on the table. On it was a photograph of a candle, lit, in front of a picture of the Black Madonna, on a windowsill.

"Our mother," he said. "That's the second. The first was when he was on remand." He drank some of the hot chocolate and made a face that turned, against his will, into a better face. "Kuba's gone. Four days. Phone off. Not at his flat. Not at Bartek's. And Mum lands from Kraków on Sunday. She's booked it. His tribunal's on Wednesday. Gavin says if he doesn't turn up it's struck out and the company wins and that's that. Gavin's very upset. He's on a train."

"Gavin's always on a train."

"This time he's on a train to Leeds," said Marek, as if that were the most damning thing yet.

She knew she shouldn't, the way you know a step is missing in the dark. She said no twice, and then she said, "Show me his messages," which was not no, and Marek knew it, and turned his phone round again.

The riders' group chat was called Kurierzy Południe, south London couriers, four hundred and twelve members, almost all of them Polish or Romanian or Brazilian, and it was the most honest document Marnie had ever read. It was traffic and police and which restaurants made you wait and which doormen were racists. Somewhere in it, on Monday, someone called Szymek_Peckham had written: Kuba's at the dark kitchen behind the car wash on Rye Lane, borrowing Bartek's bike, says don't tell Marek.

"He's told us where he is," said Marnie.

"He said don't tell me."

"In a group of four hundred people you're in."

"He's not stupid," said Marek. "He's just Kuba."

The dark kitchen behind the car wash on Rye Lane was a steel shed with no windows and eleven restaurants in it. There was a sign on the door with eleven logos, a burger, a bao, a curry house called Maharaja Express, a cartoon rooster, all of which came out of the same three fryers and were cooked by the same four men in the same hairnets. The ordering system ran all eleven at once and talked to the riders in the yard over a loudspeaker in a woman's voice that was trying very hard to sound like eleven different restaurants.

"Order for Maharaja Express," it said as they walked into the yard. "Order for Bao Down. Order for Cluck Norris. Order for Maharaja Express—sorry. That's Bao Down again."

There were six riders in the yard, smoking under a plastic awning. None of them was Kuba. One of them, a big lad with a beard and a Lech scarf, saw Marek and grinned.

"Bartek," said Marek. "Where's my brother?"

"Which brother?"

"I've got one brother."

"Then he's not here," said Bartek, and looked, with great care, at nothing at all, which was to his left, and to his left was a gate, and through the gate, on a red e-bike with a cool box on the back, about to pull out onto Rye Lane, was Kuba.

He saw them. He saw Marek. He saw, behind Marek, Marnie, whom he had last seen on the court steps with a coffee, and for a second he looked absolutely delighted.

Then he went.

Marek grabbed Bartek's other bike, which wasn't locked, because nobody steals from a dark kitchen; there's nothing to steal but fries. Marnie looked round for anything with wheels. There was a hire scooter on the pavement outside the car wash, the green kind. She tapped her phone on it and it said, in a tiny, cheerful voice, "Hi Marnie!"

"Go," she said.

"Starting your ride," said the scooter, and did, at about the speed of a woman walking a pram.

Rye Lane at half past nine on a Thursday is buses and vans and people pulling suitcases full of yams, and Kuba went through it like a man who did it for a living, which he did, up the bus lane, between a 37 and a skip lorry, through a red light that had a camera, which he waved at. Marek went after him on Bartek's bike, shouting, "Kuba! Ty debilu!", which Marnie didn't translate even in her head. She went after them both on the scooter, which went up to fifteen miles an hour, and then, outside the Peckham Library, which it recognised as a pedestrian area, went down to four.

"Cholera," said Marnie, and a small girl on the pavement, holding her father's hand, said "Cholera," back, delighted, in a perfect Deptford accent.

By Queen's Road she'd lost them. Her phone rang. It was Marek.

"I've lost him."

"So have I."

"He went down the Old Kent Road. He's in the rider shelter. Bartek says. It's on the chat. Bartek says he's in the shelter, he's crying, bring crisps."

"Bring crisps?"

"It's what you say," said Marek. "It's a kind of code."

"For what?"

"Crisps."

The rider shelter was a converted shipping container under the railway arches off the Old Kent Road, painted purple by the council in 2029, with a sign that said REST · CHARGE · WARM UP and a microwave, a kettle, eight phone chargers, a toilet, a bench, and a voice assistant in the ceiling that had been programmed by somebody kind and slightly anxious.

"Hello," it said as Marnie came in. "You're safe here. Would you like a hot drink, or to talk to someone?"

"I'd like to talk to him," said Marnie.

Kuba was on the bench in his riding jacket with his helmet in his lap like a cat. He had not been crying. Somebody else had already brought crisps. Marek was in the corner by the chargers, breathing like a man who was never going to cycle down the Old Kent Road again.

"You're not supposed to talk to me," Kuba said to Marnie. "Gavin said. You got suspended for talking to Marek."

"I'm still suspended. It's very relaxing."

He held his phone out. It was a different app from the one that had suspended him. A different company. He'd signed up at New Year, because a man has to eat, and the app had run a check, and the check had found the charge sheet from October, the one that had been dropped, the one that said threat to kill.

On the screen, in a red box, it said: RISK ASSESSMENT: HIGH. Your account is subject to elevated scrutiny. Please remain available for a verification call.

"Verification," said Kuba. "That's what they said last time. A police officer said, We just need to verify a few things. Then I was in Thameside." He looked at the floor. "Wednesday's a court."

"It's a tribunal. It's a room in Croydon with a carpet."

"There's a judge."

"There's a tired woman with a judge's job."

"There's a machine. The company's asked for the machine. Gavin said." He laughed, not well. "It's the same machine. It'll say I said I'll kill someone. It's very accurate."

Marnie sat down on the bench next to him.

"I don't want to go," said Kuba. "I want to ride. I want them to leave me alone. That's all. I'll do it on Bartek's account. Nobody checks Bartek. Bartek's got a beard."

Marnie had a whole sentence ready, about how if he didn't go the machine would decide, and if he went at least a person would. It would have worked on Paul.

Instead she said, in Polish, the way you'd say it to your little brother if you had one: "Kuba. You are a coward and an idiot, and you have the face of a man who's been eating crisps in a shipping container for four days. Your mother has lit two candles. On Sunday she gets off a plane from Kraków. If you don't go on Wednesday she'll light a third, and then she'll come here, to this container, on the bus, and she'll find you, because mothers can read the chat too, and she'll hit you with her hat. In front of Bartek."

Kuba looked at her for a long moment.

"She hasn't got a hat," he said.

"She'll buy one."

From the corner, still breathing hard, Marek said, in Polish, very seriously, wagging a finger: "And if you lose on Wednesday, zabiję cię."

There was a silence in the purple container. All three of them heard it at the same time.

"Threatening language detected," said the ceiling, gently. "Would anyone like support?"

Kuba started to laugh. Then Marek did. Then Marnie did, so hard she had to hold on to the phone charger, and the shelter, which had not been programmed for this, played a short calming chime, and then, when nobody calmed, played it again.

"I'll come," said Kuba, wiping his face. "Wednesday. I'll come." He pointed at Marnie with a crisp. "You'll be there?"

"I'm not allowed to be anything."

"Be there anyway," said Kuba. "Not allowed. At the back."

Outside, under the arches, the hire scooter was still waiting where she'd dropped it, because nobody had ended the ride. It had been charging her the whole time. It said, when she touched it, "Welcome back, Marnie! You've been riding for one hour and four minutes. That's a personal best!"

chapters.label: 25. Not Guilty
chapters.title: Not Guilty
chapters.html:
It wasn't a court. It was a room on the fourth floor of an office block in Croydon, with a carpet the colour of an old plaster and a window that looked onto the back of a Premier Inn, and a sign on the door that said HEARING IN PROGRESS on a screen that had frozen, some time ago, on HEARING IN PROG.

Kuba turned up. He turned up forty minutes early, in a suit that had been Marek's wedding suit and was slightly too long in the arm, so that he looked like a boy at a funeral. His mother came with him. She had bought a hat. It was black and small and had a pin in it, and she held it in her lap like a weapon she hoped not to need.

Gavin came straight from Euston, with a wheelie case, and said "Morning, morning," to everyone, including a pot plant.

And because Kuba had asked, in writing, by name, for a human interpreter, and because the rules still said a party could, there was a human interpreter. It wasn't Marnie. It was Halina.

Halina was seventy-four. She'd been interpreting Polish in English courts since 1981, when there were about nine people doing it and three of them were spies. She'd retired in 2027, when the pilot started, and she came back for Kuba because Marek's wife's aunt played bridge with her and had rung her on a landline, which is apparently how the Polish community in south London still does anything that matters. She wore a cardigan with a brooch shaped like a frog and carried a fountain pen, and she sat down next to Kuba and said, in Polish, "Pull your sleeves up. You look like you're hiding something. Are you?" and Kuba said, "No," and she said, "Good. Then pull them up."

Marnie sat at the back on a plastic chair with her coat on. Tribunals are public. Nobody could stop her sitting there. She had checked. She had checked three times.

Relay was there too. It sat in a speaker on the table in front of the judge, a black grille the size of a paperback, because the company had asked for it, because the company's solicitor, a young man called Mr Pask with very clean shoes, said it was "more accurate and more efficient". So there were two of them: Halina with her frog, and the grille. Every time Kuba spoke, Relay translated, and then Halina said, "Madam, if I may," and translated it again.

They were mostly the same. Nine times out of ten Halina said what Relay had said, a bit slower, with her hands.

Then Mr Pask asked Kuba why he hadn't contacted the company while he was on remand, to explain, and Kuba said, Bo myślałem, że już po mnie.

"Because I thought I was already finished," said Relay.

"Madam, if I may," said Halina. "Już po mnie. Literally, it's already after me. You say it when the thing has happened and nothing you do will change it. I thought I was already finished is right. Finished as in done for. Not as in done talking."

The judge, a tired woman with a cold and a box of tissues she was rationing, looked at the grille, and then at Halina.

"Is the machine wrong?"

"No, madam. It's very good." Halina put her pen down. "But it hasn't taken an oath, and I have. So when it's right, I'm the one who says so."

The judge wrote something. Mr Pask wrote something. Gavin, who had been asleep with his eyes open, woke up and wrote something too.

Marek gave evidence after lunch. He'd put the Legia scarf in his pocket, but you could see the end of it, and the judge could see the end of it, and Marnie watched her decide not to ask.

Mr Pask asked him about his brother's character. It was a trap, a polite one, laid on a clean carpet. The company's case, as far as there was one, was that the system had been right to flag Kuba as a risk, even if the charge had gone, because the system had seen things, in the round.

"Your brother," said Mr Pask. "Would you describe him as a calm person?"

Marek thought about it, honestly, which was his problem. "No," he said. "Kuba to raptus."

"Kuba is a hothead," said Relay. "Alternative rendering: Kuba is impulsive; acts on the spur of the moment. The term does not in itself imply aggression. Confidence: hothead, fifty-two per cent; impulsive, forty-eight. Selection is a matter for the interpreter of record."

There was a small, satisfied pause from Mr Pask's end of the table. He wrote hothead. He underlined it. He did not write the rest.

"Which is it?" said the judge.

"Selection is a matter for the interpreter of record," said Relay, again, politely, the way a waiter tells you the fish is off.

Everyone looked at Halina. She looked at the grille. She looked, for some reason, at the ceiling. For the first time all day she didn't seem sure.

"It's given you both," she said. "Both are in the word. Neither is the word." She turned her pen round. "There's a better one. I can't find it. I'm seventy-four. I had it this morning."

The judge sighed, the sigh of a woman whose afternoon was getting longer. Then Mr Pask, who was young and clean and wanted to be helpful, said, "Madam, if it assists, I believe the lady at the back is a Polish interpreter. She's connected to this matter. She was suspended over it, I understand. But she may be able to—"

Everybody turned round.

The judge looked at Marnie over a tissue. "Is that right? Can you help us with the word?"

Marnie stood up. She hadn't meant to; her legs did it, the way they always had when someone said interpreter. She knew the word. She'd known it since she was seven and her grandmother had said it about her, after Tomasz and the biting. Raptus. She had it in her mouth, in English, three different ways, each of them better than hothead, each of them true.

"I'm sorry, madam," she said. "I'm not permitted."

"You're not permitted to tell me what a word means?"

"I'm suspended. And I'm connected. And if I say it, it's advocacy, and the company appeals on a technicality, and I'll have helped twice, both times wrong." She was aware of her own voice, in English, being very steady, like Paul indicating at an empty road. "I'm sorry. I'm just sitting here."

The judge looked at her for a moment longer. Then she nodded, and said, "Quite right," and Mr Pask looked at his shoes.

Marnie sat down. Her face was hot. Kuba's mother, three chairs along, reached over without looking and patted her knee twice.

"Madam," said Halina. "I have it now."

"Go on."

"Raptus. It's a boy who runs into the road after a ball. Before you can say anything, he's gone. Then he's back with the ball, very pleased with himself, and you want to kill him." She stopped, aware of where she was. "That's an expression. You want to shout at him. The word is about speed, madam. Quick to go, quick to come back. It doesn't carry danger unless the speaker puts it there. My grandson is a raptus. He's thirty-one. He once drove to Wrocław for a cheese."

"Is the grandson relevant?" said Mr Pask.

"No," said Halina. "But he's an example of the word."

"So is the witness telling us his brother is dangerous," said Mr Pask, "or not?"

"I can tell the tribunal what the word means," said Halina. "What he meant is for the tribunal." She nodded down the table. "He's sitting there. You could ask him."

The judge, after a moment, did. Marek went red to the end of his scarf.

"Raptus," he said. "Nie niebezpieczny. If I meant dangerous I'd say dangerous. I'm his brother. I know the word for dangerous. I've known it since he was four."

Halina gave it in English, flat, every word, including the four, and the grille gave it at the same time, and they matched. The judge wrote something. It was longer than hothead. In the grille, a small light that nobody had noticed before blinked twice, as if something inside it had made a note under a heading it didn't have.

Kuba won. Not because of Halina, and not because of the word. Because the company couldn't produce a single person who had decided to suspend him. It had been a rule in a system, triggered by a charge sheet, and nobody had looked at it, and the judge, who was tired and had a cold, said she found that "somewhat troubling", which Halina said afterwards in the corridor was the angriest thing she had ever heard an employment judge say.

Kuba's mother put her new hat on, finally, in the lift, and didn't hit anyone with it, and looked disappointed.

Kuba bought them coffee from the machine in the corridor. He'd learnt. He got one with sugar and one without and held them out to Marnie and made her choose. She took the one without. He looked surprised.

"You took the sugar last time."

"I didn't want you to have bought the wrong one."

He thought about that. "That's very Polish."

"I'm half."

"Which half?"

"The half that lies about coffee."

Halina laughed. She had a big laugh, a smoker's laugh, though she'd stopped in 1998. She took Marnie's arm.

"So you're the one they suspended," she said. "For Marek."

"Yes."

"Good. Someone should be." She looked at Marnie closely, the way old interpreters look at a face, reading the bit underneath. "They've offered you the training work. Correcting it."

"How do you know?"

"They offered it to me in 2027. I said I'd rather clean toilets. They said that could also be arranged." She squeezed the arm. "You knew the word."

"Yes."

"Better than mine?"

Marnie thought about it, honestly, which was her problem too.

"No," she said. "Mine didn't have a cheese in it."

"There's always a cheese," said Halina. She let go. "And you sat down. I saw."

She wrote something on the back of a bus ticket with the fountain pen and gave it to Marnie. An address on Deptford High Street, above a shop that sold phone cases.

"Wednesdays I do the advice place there. Benefits letters, landlords, men whose dogs eat things. The council pays for the kettle and nothing else. Nobody gets suspended. There's nothing to be suspended from." She looked at Marnie the way she'd looked at Kuba's sleeves. "Come and be terrible. It's very good for you."

Then she asked Marnie to lend her a pound for the bus, and never gave it back.

On the bus home Marnie sat at the back and cried a bit, not much, about nothing in particular, which she would deny, and the bus asked if she was all right, and she said yes.
