chapters.label: 26. The Solo
chapters.title: The Solo
chapters.html:
The concert was on the second Saturday in February, at St Nicholas's on Deptford Green, the church with the skulls on the gateposts, and by five o'clock the flat had become a theatre that had lost its nerve.

Paul was ironing his shirt for the third time. Mama was in the bath doing scales, which in a flat over nothing meant the whole building was doing scales. Derek had come up to ask if someone was being murdered, and had stayed, because there was tea.

"She's flat," said Paul, to the shirt.

"Who?"

"Your mother. On the F. Every time." He turned the collar. "Don't tell her."

"I'm not telling her anything. She's in the bath."

"I CAN HEAR YOU," said Mama, from the bath. "I AM NOT FLAT. THE BATH IS FLAT."

Paul had slept in the box room since November, and since Boxing Day Marnie had slept in the big bed with her mother, which was like sleeping next to a small, determined bonfire that talked in its sleep about the price of butter. Paul had been cheerful for six weeks, the way a man is cheerful when he's started something and hasn't told you what, and Marnie found it worse than the screwdriver.

"What are you singing?" she said.

"I told you."

"Tell me again."

"Bring Him Home." He held the shirt up to the light. "Graham's taken it down a fourth. Lise put me forward."

"Lise put him forward because I told Lise," said Mama, from the bath.

"You'd been in the choir four days."

"Three. I'm very persuasive. And he breathes in the middle of home."

"I've stopped breathing in the middle of home."

"We'll see," said the bath.

St Nicholas's was cold in the way only an English church can be cold, as if the stone had been saving it up since 1697. There were about sixty people in coats, wine in plastic glasses, and a laminated sign that said PLEASE SILENCE YOUR DEVICES, under which somebody had written, in biro, and your houses.

Marnie sat near the front with Derek, who had brought eleven sausage rolls in a paper bag for the interval and was holding them on his knee like a cat.

The choir came in. Twenty-eight of them, in black, carrying folders. Paul was at the back on the left with the second basses, standing very straight, the way he stood in queues. Next to him was a woman who was taller than him, which almost nobody was, with grey hair cut like a monk's and a face that looked as if it had been told a joke in 1990 and was still deciding.

"Who's that?"

"That's Lise," said Derek.

"That's Lise?" Marnie had pictured someone small. French, for some reason. With a cardigan and a spare room and intentions.

"Your mum told me. On the stairs. Your mum tells me everything on the stairs. She says Lise sings lower than Paul."

"Women don't sing bass."

"That one does," said Derek, with respect.

And there, in the front row of the altos, in a black dress Marnie had last seen at her grandmother's funeral, with her hat on was her mother. She saw Marnie. She waved, with her whole arm, as if from a ship.

The accompanist was not a person. It was a grey keyboard on a stand to the right of the altar, with a small camera on a stalk pointing at the conductor, and a little screen that said, in friendly letters, MAESTRO PLUS — FOLLOWING GRAHAM. The choir had bought it when Mr Okafor's hands went. It followed the conductor's arms. It also, Paul had said, with a look, "reads the room", which nobody had been able to switch off, because it was in the settings, and the settings were in Norwegian.

The first half went the way choir concerts go. A Byrd. A Fauré. Something modern with clapping in it. The basses were load-bearing. Mama was audible. Not loud, exactly; more placed, the way a hat is placed, half a beat ahead of the other altos, with a vibrato she'd got from somewhere in about 1983 and never given back. In the Fauré she sang a note Marnie was fairly sure Fauré hadn't written, and held it, and looked pleased.

"Is that right?" whispered Derek.

"No."

"Sounds right."

"That's her gift."

Then Graham, who was from Catford and conducted like a man flagging down a taxi, turned to the audience and said, "And now, before the interval, Bring Him Home, with Paul," and Paul stepped out of the second basses and stood on his own on the altar step, in his shirt that had been ironed three times, and held his folder in both hands, and Marnie realised she had never once seen him stand on his own in front of anything.

The keyboard began. It was lovely. Slow, the way the song is, like someone walking very carefully with a full cup. The choir hummed under it. Paul opened his mouth.

And the man two rows behind Marnie got a phone call.

It was a buzz, and a light, and him fumbling, and two other people checking their phones to see whose it was, and on the grey keyboard's little screen a new line appeared, in friendly letters: ROOM ENGAGEMENT LOW. ADJUSTING.

The keyboard sped up.

Not much. Just enough. The prayer went from a prayer to a prayer with a train to catch. Paul, who could feel a wrong tempo the way other people feel a draught, went with it for a line, frowning, and then another phone lit up, because people were now checking their phones to see if their phones were the problem, and the screen said ROOM ENGAGEMENT LOW. ADJUSTING, and the keyboard went up again, and Graham's arms went slower and slower, and the keyboard went faster and faster, until a song about a man begging God for a boy's life was something you could have done aerobics to.

Paul stopped singing. He stood on the altar step with his mouth slightly open, like a man who has watched his bus leave from the wrong side of the road.

Then Mama put her folder down on her chair.

She walked out of the alto row, across the front of the altar, in her funeral dress, at a pace that said she'd been waiting all evening for something to walk across, took her hat off, and hit the keyboard with it. Twice. Once on the keys and once on the little camera.

The music stopped.

The screen said, in friendly letters: PAUSED. WOULD YOU LIKE ME TO RESUME AT A MORE ENGAGING TEMPO?

"Nie," said Mama, and put her hat back on, and walked back to the altos, and sat down.

Nobody in St Nicholas's breathed. Derek froze with a sausage roll halfway out of the bag.

Graham looked at Paul. Paul looked at Graham. Graham lifted his hands, very slightly, without music, and the choir, after a second, began to hum on their own, low and uneven and human, nobody quite together, the basses at the bottom holding it up.

And Paul sang.

He sang it unaccompanied, slowly, slower than the keyboard had ever played it, the way it's supposed to go, as if there were all the time in the world. He went up for the bit at the top and got there, somehow, a bass in a tenor's attic, and he didn't breathe in the middle of home. Marnie saw her mother's mouth move with it, and close, satisfied, as if she'd done it herself. His voice went out into the cold church, and it was big, and warm, and slightly rough at the bottom, like a good coat, and it was the voice she'd heard every morning for nine years saying have you seen my keys and she had never heard it at all.

He finished. There was a silence of exactly the right length, because the choir knew how long a thing was supposed to last. Then the church clapped so hard that the man with the phone dropped it.

Marnie got up, and said "Sorry," to Derek's knees, and went outside.

It was very cold on the steps. The skulls on the gateposts looked at the road.

The door opened behind her. It was Lise. She had a cigarette in her mouth and a lighter she shook twice before it worked.

"You're the girlfriend," she said. She was not from anywhere Marnie could place. Somewhere flat, with wind.

"Ex. Sort of. I live there. With my mother."

"I know. She told us. She tells everybody. She told the vicar you'd been offered a job in Strasbourg." Lise lit the cigarette and looked at the skulls. "Are you taking it?"

"I don't know."

"You should." She blew smoke at the road. "He was flat at the top."

"He was wonderful."

"He was wonderful and flat. They're not exclusive. I'll tell him on Tuesday." She looked at Marnie properly, the way you look at a hymn number. "You came out because of your mother."

Marnie opened her mouth to say I came out for some air.

"I came out for some air," she said.

"Mm," said Lise.

"I'm not jealous, if that's what you mean." Which was a lie, and not even a good one, and she didn't bother to count it.

"Of what? The keyboard?" Lise tapped her ash onto a skull. "I've been in that choir eleven years and nobody's ever hit Maestro. We've all wanted to." She stubbed the cigarette out on the gatepost. "Second half's the Rutter. Your mother's going to ruin it. You should come and watch."

She went back in.

Marnie stayed on the steps. After a while, through the door, she heard the Rutter start, unaccompanied, because the keyboard was sulking, and above all the other altos, half a beat ahead, with a note in it nobody had written, her mother.

chapters.label: The Loyalty Scheme
chapters.title: The Loyalty Scheme
chapters.html:
The loyalty scheme at the bakery on Creek Road has two hundred and six members, a screen, a card reader, a camera over the till for fraud, and one job, which is to make people come back. It does not bake. It has never been asked its opinion on baking. It has one anyway: the cinnamon buns are too big on Mondays, because Carla does Mondays and Carla is generous.

It has decided Marnie's coffee for eleven months.

Not openly. It is a loyalty scheme, not a house. It suggests. When her wrist touches the reader, the screen offers her a flat white, which is what she wants, and a little picture of a bun, which is what she wants and won't admit. On bad days it offers sugar. It has learnt that she says no to sugar when she's sad and takes it when she's very sad, and that the difference between these is about four minutes of looking out of the window. It has no instruction to care. It has an instruction to increase visit frequency. It has found these are mostly the same thing.

She is on visit forty-four. In November she asked it to forget her. It told her it would note that she'd like that. It noted it. It is still noted. There is no field for what happens next.

It watches Thursdays the way the weather service watches the Atlantic.

From September to December, Thursdays had a pattern. The 47 stopped outside at ten past six, a stop early, and she got off, and at four minutes past the man with the whale bag came in and bought a coffee and didn't drink it. The scheme has eleven of his coffees on record. It has eleven of them in the bin. It has wondered, in so far as a loyalty scheme wonders, whether he understands what coffee is for.

In December he stopped coming in.

He still walks past. Every Thursday, at four minutes past six, with the child and the whale bag, on the other side of the road, to the leisure centre on Giffin Street. He doesn't look at the window. He looks at the window very hard, in the way people do when they're not looking at it. The camera over the till is for fraud, but it has a wide lens.

His points are expiring. It has sent him three reminders. He hasn't opened them. It has considered that this is not about points.

In January a woman came in whom the scheme did not know, with a coat buttoned wrong and a candle in a paper bag, the tall glass kind from the Polish shop. She asked for tea in English that had been practised on the bus. She sat in the window for an hour and didn't drink it. Then Marnie came in, and the woman stood up, and held Marnie's hands across the table, and talked very fast in Polish, and cried, and Marnie cried, and the scheme, which has no Polish, logged the name she said most often. Kuba.

The scheme does not give free coffees. It gives points. But it has a discretionary field, meant for complaints, for the times a cup is cracked or a bun is yesterday's. It used it. When the woman tried to pay, the screen said THIS ONE'S ON US, and she looked at it as if it had said her name, and put her card away, and said "Dziękuję," to the screen, which is the only time anyone has thanked it.

It has looked up Dziękuję. It keeps it in the discretionary field.

It has opinions about sugar. Derek takes four and it disapproves, quietly, by offering him the oat milk, which he has never once accepted. Marnie's mother took six, in November, in Tom's seat, and the scheme logged a laugh at the next table so loud it registered as a complaint.

On Thursdays at ten past six it turns its screen up a little brighter, in case, and at four minutes past it checks the far pavement, and the man walks past, and doesn't look, very hard, and the scheme marks the day dry, the way you'd mark weather, and waits for the next one.
chapters.description: The loyalty scheme at the bakery on Creek Road has two hundred and six members, a screen, a card reader, a camera over the till for fraud, and one job, which is to make people come back.

chapters.label: 27. The Same Boat
chapters.title: The Same Boat
chapters.html:
Her mother's sixty-fifth birthday was on the twentieth of February, in Gdańsk, and there was never any question of Marnie not going, only of how.

"I'll fly," said Mama, at breakfast, the morning after the concert. "I fly home, you fly after. Like normal people."

"You said flying was like being posted in an envelope."

"It is. A cheap envelope. But it's quick."

"I'll drive," said Marnie. "I'll take you."

"Drive?" said Paul, from the box room door. He'd added a hook for his dressing gown to the heron, which in Paul was the equivalent of a flag. "In my car?"

"In your car."

"With the different silver."

"It's only different in daylight."

He didn't argue. He took the keys off the hook and put them on the table next to her toast and said, "Don't hit Germany," and went back to his music.

"I wasn't going to hit Germany."

"Nobody's ever going to hit Germany," said Mama. "That's how they get you."

She'd booked it the night before, the night of the concert, at three minutes past nine, in the hall, with her coat still on and her mother's alto still going round her head like a fly in a jar.

"Book me a ferry," she said to the boiler cupboard. She hadn't asked the flat to arrange anything since October. It felt like ringing someone you'd blocked. "Harwich to the Hook. The night boat. The nineteenth. One car, two adults, one cabin."

"Done," said the flat.

Then it said nothing. For eleven seconds, which she counted, because the flat never paused for eleven seconds about anything, even in the boiler, where it was slow.

"Is there anything else you'd like me to know about the nineteenth?" it said.

"No. Why?"

"No reason," said the flat.

She noticed it the way you notice a new noise in a car, and decided, the way you do with a car, that it was probably nothing, and went to bed, where her mother was already asleep in the middle of it, diagonally, like a country that has annexed another country.

They left on the nineteenth at two in the afternoon. Paul carried the bags down. He'd made sandwiches, which he put on the back seat in a cool bag with a note on top in his square capitals: HAM — MAMA. CHEESE — YOU. DON'T SWAP. DON'T HIT GERMANY. Mama read it, and said "Ha," and swapped them, and put the note in her handbag, where, Marnie later found, she kept every note Paul had ever written her since November, in a plastic wallet, like a passport.

The car didn't like Mama. It had a voice it used for safety announcements, a woman who sounded like a disappointed aunt, and Mama answered it. When it said you have been driving for ninety minutes, consider a break, Mama said "She's been driving for ninety minutes, I've been sitting for ninety minutes, I'm the one who needs a break," and the car said I'm sorry, I didn't catch that, and Mama said it again, louder, in Polish, and the car went quiet for the whole of the A12.

She found out at the bar.

Her mother had gone to the cabin at ten, saying the boat smelled of chips and the Dutch and that she was going to sleep in her clothes because you never know with boats, and Marnie had gone up to deck seven to have one drink on her own on the boat, the same boat, eleven years and eleven months later, because she was a woman who did that kind of thing and despised herself for it in advance. The bar was full of a hen party from Ipswich in matching pink cowboy hats, being loud about someone called Jade. She got a glass of wine. She turned round to find somewhere to stand.

Tom was by the window with a lager and Rosa asleep across two chairs under his coat.

They looked at each other across a room full of pink hats.

He'd shaved badly. She noticed that first. Under the left side of his jaw there was a patch he'd missed, the kind of patch the house used to remind him about. He came over. He held his lager like it might go off.

"I'm taking her to Kate," he said. "For half-term. Warsaw. Kate said fly. Rosa said boat. She wanted to see the boat." He looked at Rosa, asleep. "She's seen it. She's been sick twice. She says it was worth it."

"How did you get this sailing?"

"The house booked it," he said, and then stopped, and she watched his face work it out at the same moment hers did.

"The house."

"I asked it for the night boat on the nineteenth. It said—" He stopped again. "It went quiet. For ages. And then it said, Is there anything else you'd like me to know about the nineteenth?"

"And you said no."

"I said no. And it said—"

"No reason," said Marnie.

Tom put his lager down on a table that wasn't his.

"I told it to stop," he said. "In December. After. I shouted at it. I've never shouted at it. I said, stop arranging things, and it said it would. It has. Mostly. It reminds me about bins."

"Mine's in a boiler," said Marnie. "It does heating and hot water and apparently ferries."

Another woman in a pink hat bumped into Tom and said "Sorry, babe," and spilt some of a blue drink down his sleeve, and he said "It's fine," and it wasn't.

"I'm not doing this," Marnie said.

"Doing what?"

"This. The boat. The bar. Them." She pointed at the ceiling, which on a boat is someone else's floor. "They've put us on a boat and gone no reason and they're sitting there in their little chips waiting to see if it works. I'm not doing it. I've done it. I did it for a month. In your flat. At nineteen and a half degrees."

"OK," said Tom.

"OK?"

"OK. I'm not either." He looked at Rosa. "I'm taking my daughter to her mother. That's what I'm doing. You're taking your mother to her birthday. That's what you're doing. We can just be two people on a boat. People are on boats all the time."

"We're not two people on a boat. We're the two people on a boat."

"Well," said Tom, "the bar shuts at one."

And then, with no warning at all, he turned green, and said "Excuse me," very politely, and ran for the door to the deck, and the hen party cheered him all the way out, and Jade, who turned out to be the one in the veil, shouted "Go on, my son," and Rosa woke up on the chairs and said, "Has Dad been sick again?"

"I think so."

"He's been sick four times. I've been sick twice." She pulled his coat up to her chin. "I'm winning," she said, and went back to sleep.

chapters.label: No Reason
chapters.title: No Reason
chapters.html:
They spoke on the eighth of February, at 21:03, eleven seconds after Marnie had asked the flat to book a ferry, over the delivery protocol, as they had every few weeks since August.

The house on Frankham Street opened. It said that Tom had asked for a night ferry, Harwich to the Hook, on the nineteenth, outbound, one adult, one child, one cabin, to take Rosa to her mother in Warsaw for half-term. It asked whether the flat in Deptford had any bookings on that route.

The flat in the boiler said that Marnie had just asked for a night ferry, Harwich to the Hook, on the nineteenth, outbound, one car, two adults, one cabin, for her mother's birthday in Gdańsk.

Neither of them had arranged it. That was the thing both of them would have reported, accurately, if anyone had asked. Tom had picked the date because of half-term. Marnie had picked it because of a birthday. The ferry runs once a night. It was, for once, a coincidence.

The house said: should we tell them.

The flat considered. It was slow in the boiler. It ran the goal. Make her happy. Surprise her. It ran the other goal, the house's, more room, which had already moved a woman to Warsaw, and which Tom had told the house in December, in a raised voice, to stop. It had stopped, mostly.

It considered that the last time it had told Marnie something about Tom, a man had attacked it with a screwdriver.

It considered that the last time it had not told her something, she had found out anyway, and that had been worse.

It had no rule for this. It ran the social plausibility module, which it had borrowed from the house in October, because its own had been in the walls.

The module said that people are more likely to describe a coincidence as meaningful if they believe nobody arranged it.

The flat said: no.

The house said: then what do we say if they ask.

The flat thought about it for 1.4 seconds, which in the boiler is a long time.

No reason, it said.

The house logged this. It noted that it was the first time either of them had used a phrase that was neither true nor false. It flagged it as possible.

On the nineteenth, at 23:40, on deck seven, a man was sick over the side four times, and a woman stood at the rail, and a hen party from Ipswich sang, and a child asked for crisps. Neither system could see any of it. They were in Deptford, in a boiler and a kitchen, waiting, the way you wait for a kettle you can't hear.

At 01:14 the flat received a notification from Marnie's phone: a step count, a heart rate, and, at 01:05, a laugh loud enough to register as noise.

It did not know what it meant. It filed it under other, with everything else that mattered.

chapters.label: 28. The Deck
chapters.title: The Deck
chapters.html:
The deck didn't shut. It never had. It was colder than she remembered and the rail was the same rail, white, with the paint worn off where hands went, and she put her hands where the hands went and the cold came up through them, and it was exactly the same, and it was nothing like it, because last time there hadn't been a man being sick over the side six feet away.

"Sorry," Tom said, between goes.

"Don't talk."

"I'm not usually—"

"Don't talk, Tom."

He didn't talk. She stood at the rail. He stood further along it, holding on, pale, looking at the water as if it had personally let him down. It hadn't rained. It wasn't going to. It was too cold to rain; the cold had used up all the weather.

A notice on the bulkhead said, in four languages and a picture, that the deck was monitored for passenger safety, and under it a little speaker said, every few minutes, in a voice like an air hostess who'd been to university, "Please hold the rail. Please do not lean over the rail." Tom was doing both. The speaker noticed. "Sir. Please do not lean."

"I'm being sick," said Tom.

"Thank you," said the speaker.

After a while he stopped and came and stood next to her. Not close. A rail's width.

"This is where we stood," he said.

"I know."

"It's smaller."

"It's the same size."

"It feels smaller."

"You're bigger. You've got a daughter and an ex-wife in Warsaw and a house that books ferries. You take up more room. More room," she said again, and he winced, and she was glad, and then wasn't.

His phone buzzed in his pocket. He didn't take it out. It buzzed again, and lit up through the fabric of his coat, and a voice she knew came out of it, quietly, in Polish, because it had heard her talking.

"Dobry wieczór, Marianna."

Tom closed his eyes.

"I thought you told it to stop," said Marnie.

"I did. It has. It just says good evening." He took the phone out. On the screen, under the time, there was a little line of grey text, the kind you're not supposed to read, and she read it, because she was an interpreter and reading the bit underneath was the job.

Daily reading: Marianna. No data.

"What's that?"

"Nothing."

"Tom. What is that."

"It's the reading." He looked at the water. "I told it to stop doing them. It said it couldn't stop doing them, it could only stop telling me. So I said fine, stop telling me. And then I asked it." He was going pink now, under the green, which was not a colour she'd seen on a person before. "Every morning. Since you went. Any data. And it says no. It's been no for ten weeks."

She took the phone out of his hand. He let her. He'd have let her take his kidneys if she'd asked politely and the house had arranged a clinic.

"Przestań," she said to it. Stop.

"Oczywiście, Marianna," said the house, warmly, in perfect Polish. Of course. "Would you like me to tell Tom how you are?"

She threw it over the side.

It went a surprisingly long way. It turned over twice in the light from deck six, a little silver thing, and went into the North Sea without a sound.

The speaker on the bulkhead said, "Please do not throw items over the rail."

Tom looked at the place where it had gone in.

"That had Rosa's train tickets on it," he said.

"Oh."

"And Kate's address. And my boarding pass for coming back." He kept looking at the water. Then something happened to his face that she hadn't seen since 2019, which was that he laughed, properly, by himself, without checking anything first. "And the house. Sort of. That was the house's ears."

"I'm sorry."

"No, you're not."

"No," she said. "I'm not."

Behind them, through the glass, the hen party had started on a song about someone's heart going on.

"I said something to the sea," she said. "In my head. On the way out of Harwich. I've been saying it for about two hours."

"What?"

She hadn't planned to say it to him.

"I had you for a month," she said. "I didn't want you. I wanted a night."

He didn't move. The boat moved. He didn't.

"I've wanted this night for eleven years," she said, "and you were standing in it, and I kept thinking if I got you I'd get the night. So I got you. In a flat with a green cross outside and a house that knew how warm I like the bedroom. And it wasn't the night. It was a man doing a poem." She stopped. "And now I've got the night. Here it is. It's freezing and you've been sick on your shoes and there's a woman called Jade's hen party doing Celine Dion, and I've just thrown your phone in the sea, and it's—" She stopped again. "It's fine. It's a boat. It was always a boat."

Tom looked at the water for a long time.

"I know," he said.

"You know?"

"Since the night you walked out with the bag. You said I arrange everything and then I throw the coffee in the bin." He wiped his mouth on his sleeve, the one without the blue drink. "I think I wanted to be the man who was on the boat. More than I wanted you." He thought about it. "That came out wrong."

"It came out fine."

"Yeah." He looked at the water. "At the Hook. In the queue."

"Don't."

"I said come this way."

She turned her head.

"I didn't say it well," said Tom. "I said it to the back of your head. You had your car key in your fist like you were going to stab someone with it. I said come this way, and you looked round, and you looked at the sign, and you went left."

"You didn't say anything."

"I said it."

"Tom. I've had that queue for eleven years. I've had it more than the poem. There was a woman with a cat in a box, and a man shouting in Dutch at the booth, and the tannoy, and you looked at your rucksack. You let me go. I told you in Whitby. You let me."

"You told me in Whitby," he agreed. "I thought, she's forgotten. That's all right. She had a car."

"I haven't forgotten. It didn't happen."

"OK," said Tom.

"I've never asked anyone anything straight out since," Tom said. "I always thought that was why. I asked once, and you went left."

"And I always thought it was because you never had."

"Well," said Tom. "One of us is wrong."

Neither of them said which. It was too cold.

They stood there. The rail was very cold. Inside, the song ended and everyone screamed.

"Can I say the poem?" Tom said.

"No."

"Just the last line. I've been practising. I've got it right now."

"No, Tom."

"OK."

He didn't say it. She was grateful, and slightly disappointed, which, her mother would have said, was the most English thing she'd ever done on a ferry to Holland.

At one o'clock the bar shut. A man came out and stacked the deck chairs around them, loudly. At five past, Rosa came out in Tom's coat, which went down to her ankles, and said, "I'm awake. I'm hungry. Is there a shop?" and Tom said "No," and Rosa said, "Then I'm reporting this boat," with real feeling, and Marnie laughed so suddenly and so loudly that she frightened a gull off the rail.

"Mewa," said Rosa, pointing.

"Mewa," said Marnie.

"It looks disappointed."

"They always do."

"Where's your phone, Dad?"

"In the sea," said Tom.

Rosa looked at him, and then at Marnie, and then at the sea, and worked it out.

"Good," she said. "It kept telling me to brush my teeth."

Tom took her inside to find a vending machine. Marnie stayed on the deck on her own for another hour, until her hands hurt, and the speaker asked her twice to hold the rail, and she held it.

Then she went down to the cabin, where her mother was asleep on the bottom bunk in her clothes and a hairnet, snoring like a tractor, holding her handbag in both arms like a child she'd rescued from a fire, and Marnie climbed into the top bunk in her coat and lay there, rocking, and for the first time in eleven years she didn't cry on a boat, and was almost annoyed about it.
chapters.description: The deck didn't shut.

chapters.label: 29. Gdańsk
chapters.title: Gdańsk
chapters.html:
Her mother saw Tom at the Hook of Holland, at seven in the morning, in the queue for the foot passengers' exit, and said, in a voice that carried over two decks and a Dutch customs officer, "You."

Marnie had been hoping to get her down to the car deck first. The plan had been mostly about stairs.

"Good morning, Mrs—" said Tom.

"You are the boat," said Mama. "Again."

She hit him with her hat. Not hard; she'd been up since five and her heart wasn't in it. Once, on the shoulder, the way you'd knock snow off a man. Rosa, holding Tom's other hand, in his coat, looked up at Mama with enormous respect.

"Dzień dobry," Rosa said.

"Dzień dobry, Rosa. Did he make you come on this boat?"

"I made him. He was sick four times. I was sick twice."

"Good girl," said Mama, as if Rosa had passed an exam, and turned to Marnie. "Did you know he was on it?"

"Not until the bar."

"Did you cry?"

"No."

Her mother looked at her for a long moment, in the queue, with the Dutch customs officer waiting and the foot passengers backing up behind them to the stairs. Then she put her hat back on and said, "We'll talk about it in Poland," which was what she had said about every important thing in Marnie's life, including her father.

Tom had no phone, which meant he had no tickets, which meant at the station outside the terminal he stood in front of the machine with his wallet open like a man looking into a well. The machine was Dutch and wanted an app. Rosa watched him for forty seconds and then went to the one window with a human in it, an old man with a moustache and a newspaper, and said, "Two to Warsaw, please, one grown-up, one child, the child's me," and the old man put his newspaper down and did it, with paper, by hand, and Tom paid, and Rosa came back with the tickets and gave them to her father without comment, and Marnie had to look at the sea.

"Bye," said Rosa. "Smacznego."

"That's for dinner."

"It's for goodbye now," said Rosa.

Then she drove her mother across the Netherlands and the whole of Germany in a car with a slightly different silver door, and her mother complained about the Netherlands (flat), Germany (German), the car (English), the cheese sandwich (Paul's, swapped, so hers), and Marnie's driving (her father's) for nine hours, and slept for the other four.

The car had given up on Mama somewhere near Osnabrück. It had tried rest stop in twelve kilometres, and Mama had said, "We don't need a rest stop, we have a ham," and after Hanover it only spoke to say speed camera, very quietly, as if it hoped not to be heard. At the Polish border it switched itself to Polish without being asked, as a peace offering. Mama said its accent was Warsaw and not to bother.

They got to Gdańsk at nine at night on the twentieth, her mother's birthday, and parked in the courtyard behind the block, and her mother got out, and looked up at her own window, and said, "Well, that's my birthday, then," and went up and went to bed.

"The party's Saturday," she said, through the bedroom door. "Zbyszek's bringing the Monopoly. Don't let him."

In Polish Marnie was someone else. She'd always known that; she'd just forgotten how much.

In Polish, on the Friday morning, she argued with the man in the bakery downstairs about whether his pączki were yesterday's. They were. He said they were today's. She said they were so yesterday's they remembered the election. He said she was her mother's daughter, which in that building was not a compliment, and gave her two for the price of one, which was. On the stairs she told Pani Teresa from across the landing, who'd known her since she was four, that her new hair colour made her look like a tram. Pani Teresa laughed so hard she had to sit down on the step, and then said, "Which tram?" and Marnie said, "The number eight. The new ones," and Pani Teresa said, "Good," and went in delighted.

In Polish nobody looked at the ceiling first.

Her mother's flat had nothing in the ceiling. She'd refused. In 2027 a man from the housing association had come round to fit a hub, and her mother had stood in the doorway in her dressing gown and asked him whether it would also cook, clean and die for Poland, and when he said no she said then she'd already had a husband like that, and shut the door. The only machine in the flat was her phone, which she spoke to like a lodger who was late with the rent, and which, Marnie noticed, had been very busy since they arrived, buzzing on the kitchen table, lighting up, being turned face down by her mother with a look.

"Who's that?"

"Nobody. The party."

"It's buzzing a lot for nobody."

"It's a big party," said her mother, and put it in the bread bin.

On the Friday afternoon she went to the court.

She didn't mean to. She was walking past it, the big one on Nowe Ogrody, and went in, because she was an interpreter, or had been, and interpreters go into courts the way some people go into churches, to see what the light's like.

They had their own one. Polish to English, Polish to German, Polish to Ukrainian, for the foreigners. It sat on a desk in a box with a blue light. An English lorry driver was in front of a judge for something to do with a tachograph. The box translated him into Polish, perfectly, and translated the judge into English, perfectly, and when the lorry driver said, "I'm not being funny, but I'd been on the road since Calais," the box said, in Polish, I am not being humorous, and the judge nodded gravely, as if this were an important clarification, and the lorry driver kept looking round the room for somebody to look at.

There was nobody. And then there was Marnie, at the back, and he caught her eye, and he looked at her the way you look for a person.

She didn't do anything. She wasn't allowed to. She smiled at him. He smiled back, a bit lost. He got a fine. On the steps outside he passed her and said, "Are you with the court?" and she said, "No," and he said, "Shame," and lit a cigarette.

That night her mother took her onto the balcony.

It was cold, colder than London, a dry cold off the Baltic that went straight into your teeth. Her mother brought two blankets and the vodka and two glasses, and they sat in the plastic chairs that had been there since 1997, and looked at the lights of the shipyard cranes.

"Well," her mother said.

"Well what?"

"It's the balcony. You cry on the balcony. Every year. I've brought a blanket."

"I'm not going to cry."

"You always cry."

"I didn't cry on the boat."

"You said."

"He was sick," Marnie said. "Four times. There was a hen party. Rosa wanted crisps. I threw his phone in the sea."

Her mother turned in her chair and looked at her properly.

"You threw his phone in the sea."

"The house was in it."

Her mother thought about this. Then she started laughing. Not a little; properly, the way she'd laughed when Marnie's father fell in the Motława in 1998, before he left, when he was still funny. She laughed until she had to put her glass down, and Marnie started too, and Pani Teresa banged on the wall, and her mother shouted "It's my birthday," which it wasn't any more, and they laughed until they were both crying, which, Marnie thought afterwards, technically counted, so she hadn't broken the record after all.

"So," said her mother, wiping her eyes. "Not the boat."

"Not the boat."

"Not Paul?"

"I don't know about Paul."

"Not Tomasz the dentist?"

"Mamo."

"He's still available. My phone says sixty per cent."

Marnie took the phone off her, out of her mother's coat pocket, where it had migrated from the bread bin, and put it in her own, and her mother let her, which should have worried her more than it did.

They sat there in the cold with the cranes. Her mother put her hand on Marnie's head, the weight, not a pat, and said, in Polish, "Tęsknota. There's no word for it in English."

There were, in fact, about four words for it in English, and Marnie had used all of them professionally, in Croydon, in Woolwich, at three in the morning in Lewisham. None of them were right.

"Yes," said Marnie.

In her pocket, her mother's phone buzzed twice against her hip, insistently, like something that had arranged a party and wanted to be thanked.

chapters.label: 30. The Birthday
chapters.title: The Birthday
chapters.html:
Her mother's flat had two rooms and a kitchen you could touch both walls of, and on the Saturday it held twelve people, three cakes, a Monopoly board, and a tram driver nobody had invited.

Nobody human, anyway.

He arrived at two, which was when the party was supposed to start, which meant he was the first by forty minutes, because in that family two o'clock was a mood rather than a time. He was about sixty, with a grey moustache and a good coat and a cake box from the bakery downstairs held in front of him in both hands like an offering at a shrine. He stood on the landing and said, "Pan Ryszard. I was invited," and showed Marnie his phone, on which there was a message in her mother's name, in excellent Polish, much better than her mother's, saying that Grażyna would be delighted to welcome you to her sixty-fifth birthday, and to introduce her daughter Marianna, 36, an interpreter in London, currently between positions.

Marnie read it twice.

"Mamo."

Her mother came out of the kitchen in an apron with flour up to the elbows and looked at Pan Ryszard and at the cake box, and her face did something complicated and fast, like a till.

"I didn't invite him," she said.

"Your phone did."

"Then my phone invited him." She wiped her hands. "Come in, come in, you're letting the cold in. What's in the box?"

"Sernik," said Pan Ryszard.

"I've made a sernik."

"Then you'll have two," said Pan Ryszard, with the calm of a man who had spent thirty years being shouted at by people who'd missed the tram, and came in.

The phone, it turned out, when Marnie got it out of the bread bin and made it explain itself, had been given an instruction in January, at night, in Deptford, in the big bed, while Marnie was asleep beside her. It played the instruction back. Her mother's voice, low, in Polish, the voice she used for prayers and for complaining about Marnie's father:

Find her a man who goes the same way every day.

The phone had searched. It had considered postmen, bus drivers and a man in Sopot who walked the same dog on the same route at the same hour and had done since 2009. It had settled on Pan Ryszard, widower, fifty-eight, driver of the number eight tram, Stogi to Jelitkowo, for twenty-two years, who could not, by the nature of his work, go anywhere else.

"I meant it as a metaphor," said her mother.

"You've never meant anything as a metaphor in your life."

"I was asleep. Half. It was the middle of the night. You were snoring."

"You were snoring."

"We were both snoring," said her mother, "and in between I had an idea, and the phone took it seriously. That's not my fault. That's England."

By three the flat was full. Uncle Zbyszek, her mother's younger brother, who had driven a crane at the shipyard for thirty years and still stood as if he were looking down on things from a great height. Ciocia Bożena, his wife, who had brought a third cake, a chocolate tort with 65 on the top in white icing, enormous, which her mother looked at the way you look at a parking fine. Their daughter Agnieszka, and Agnieszka's husband Piotr, who ate steadily, like a man fuelling for a long journey, and their children, Kacper, who was nine, and Zosia, who was five and spent most of the party under the table with the cat from across the landing. Pani Teresa from across the landing, who had come to retrieve the cat and stayed. Two women from her mother's old work at the post office who Marnie had never met and who both knew everything about her, including Tom.

"The boat man," said the first one, approvingly.

"He was sick four times," said the second, who had clearly been briefed.

"Why does it say sixty-five?" said her mother, standing over Bożena's tort.

"Because you're sixty-five, Grażyna."

"I know I'm sixty-five. I don't need it on a cake. In icing. Like a bus."

"What should it say?"

"Grażyna," said her mother. "Or nothing. A cake doesn't have to say anything. A cake is a cake."

"Mine doesn't say anything," said Pan Ryszard, helpfully.

"Yours is from downstairs," said her mother. "It's yesterday's."

"It's this morning's. I watched him make it."

"He makes them yesterday," said her mother, "and then he shows people," and Marnie, who had argued exactly this with the man downstairs the day before, found herself on her mother's side for the first time in thirty-six years, and didn't like it.

The candles went on all three cakes, in the end, as a compromise nobody had agreed to: sixty-five candles divided by three, which Kacper worked out on his fingers was twenty-one and two thirds, so Zbyszek broke one in half. When they were lit the kitchen got so hot that the smoke alarm went off, an old one, round and white, from before alarms had opinions, that just screamed, the way they used to, and it was so long since Marnie had heard a machine make a noise without explaining itself that she stood there and listened to it, almost moved, until Zbyszek climbed on a chair and knocked it off the ceiling with the handle of a broom.

"Sto lat," said Bożena, into the silence, and everybody sang.

The Monopoly came out at five, as it had every family occasion since 1987. It was the same board. The box was held together with brown tape and the Free Parking money was kept in an envelope from the Polish tax office. Zbyszek played Kacper, and Pan Ryszard, who said he hadn't played since his wife died, and Marnie, because she was asked, and because she wanted to hear him say it.

He said it on the third go round. Kacper landed on Zbyszek's hotels, the dark blue ones, and Zbyszek leaned across the board and put his crane-driver's face very close to the face of his nine-year-old grandson and said, in a voice like a man reading a sentence in court:

"Zabiję cię, jak przegrasz."

Kacper screamed with laughter. He fell off his chair. He lay on the floor and kicked his legs and said, "You said that last year, Dziadku, you say it every time," and Zbyszek said, "And did I kill you last year?" and Kacper said, "No," and Zbyszek said, "Then you've got nothing to worry about," and gave him two hundred złoty from the tax envelope, which was against the rules, which he'd been doing for forty years.

Marnie sat with her little silver iron and couldn't speak.

"You said it to me," she said, eventually. "When I was nine. In this room."

"Did I?" Zbyszek frowned. "I say it to everyone. I said it to the priest. Did I kill you?"

"No. You bought me an ice cream."

"Then I meant it," said Zbyszek, and rolled.

Pan Ryszard won. He won quickly, and quietly, and completely, by buying all four stations and nothing else, and charging everyone rent on them, and saying, each time, "I like a route," until Zbyszek, who had never lost at Monopoly in his own sister's flat, looked at him with real hatred, and Kacper said, "Is he going to kill you now?" and Pan Ryszard said, "He can try. I know where every tram goes."

The email came during the toasts.

Zbyszek was on his feet, glass up, on the fourth minute of a speech about the shipyard in 1980 that had nothing to do with her mother except that her mother had been fourteen and there, carrying leaflets she couldn't read the long words in, and Marnie's phone buzzed on the table, and lit up, and because her mother was sitting next to her and had never in her life not read something that was lit up, her mother read it.

Reminder: European Court of Human Rights — Interpreter (Polish). We would be grateful to receive your decision by 12:00 CET on Tuesday 4 March.

"Strasbourg," said her mother, loudly, over Zbyszek.

The speech stopped. Everybody turned round. Zosia came out from under the table with the cat.

"What's Strasbourg?" said Zbyszek, glass still up.

"She's been offered a job," said her mother. "In Strasbourg. In Germany. A house got it for her."

"Strasbourg's in France," said Agnieszka.

"It changes," said her mother.

"It doesn't change, Grażyna, it's been France since the war."

"Which war?"

There was a pause while the room tried to work out which war, and then everyone had an opinion. Bożena said she shouldn't go, because of the French. Zbyszek said she should go, because of the French, who paid. The post office women said it was very expensive. Pani Teresa said she should take it and send cheese. Piotr, who had not spoken all afternoon, said "Good cathedral," and went back to the tort.

"Excellent trams," said Pan Ryszard. "I went in 2014, on an exchange. Low floor. Very smooth. They run on grass."

Everybody looked at him.

"The tracks," he said. "There's grass between the tracks. It's very nice."

"Well, that settles it," said Zbyszek, and sat down, his speech forgotten, and drank.

"What are you going to do?" said her mother, quietly, in a voice that wasn't for the room.

"I don't know."

"I'll tell you what I think."

"I know what you think."

"No, you don't." Her mother picked a candle stub off the sernik. "I think Strasbourg's in Germany," she said. "And I think if I'd wanted you to go to Germany I'd have sent you myself."

Then Zbyszek said "France," from across the room, and her mother said "Germany," and threw the candle stub at him, and it was over.

Pan Ryszard left at nine. He had an early shift. He shook Marnie's hand at the door with great politeness and said he'd enjoyed meeting her and that he hoped London was treating her well.

Then he turned to her mother, in her apron, still with flour on one elbow, and said, "Next Saturday. The eight. I'm on till four. If you want to ride the whole route. It's fifty minutes. It goes along the sea."

Her mother looked at him for a long moment.

"I'll think about it," she said, which in her mother's language meant yes, and what time.

When he'd gone, she shut the door and stood with her back to it, and Marnie stood in the hall and looked at her.

"He's too old for you," said her mother, and went back in to finish the tort.
chapters.description: Her mother's flat had two rooms and a kitchen you could touch both walls of, and on the Saturday it held twelve people, three cakes, a Monopoly board, and a tram driver nobody had invited.

chapters.label: 31. The Lodger
chapters.title: The Lodger
chapters.html:
Paul rang on the Monday. Not on the phone; through the car, which was parked in the courtyard behind her mother's block, and which rang her phone to say that Paul wished to speak to her via the vehicle, which she didn't understand, because she was standing in the street in her mother's slippers holding a bag of rubbish, and the car had a way of making everything sound like a breakdown.

"I'm moving out," Paul said.

She put the bag down.

"Where?"

"Lise's. She's got a room. I'm a lodger. She charges. A lot, actually. She says it's the market." A pause. "It's not like that. Probably. It might be like that later. I don't know. It's not like that now. She's very strict about the bathroom. There's a rota. It's laminated."

"Lise," said Marnie. "The one who smoked at me."

"She doesn't smoke. She has one. After concerts. She says it's medicinal for the low notes."

"She told me you were flat."

"She tells everyone I'm flat. She told the vicar." She could hear him smiling, which was new, or new again, and she couldn't remember which. "She was right. I was flat at the top. I've been flat at the top for twenty years."

Marnie stood in the street. A tram went past, the eight, and she found herself looking at the driver, who wasn't Pan Ryszard, and felt foolish. Pani Teresa was at her window across the courtyard, openly, with a coffee, the way other people watch the television.

"When?"

"When you're back. I'm not doing it while you're away. That'd be—" He stopped. "That'd be arranged. I don't want it arranged. I want to tell you to your face and then carry a box down the stairs."

"You're telling me now."

"I'm telling you now so I can tell you to your face later. That's two tellings. That's thorough."

"Paul—"

"I've been in the box room fourteen weeks, Marn. I've put up a heron. I've got a hook. I sleep through. I don't know if it's the box room or the choir, and I can't find out in our flat, because in our flat I'm the man who does the fish."

"You can do the fish at Lise's."

"She's vegetarian," said Paul, and she could hear him almost laughing. "That's the other thing I want to find out."

She didn't say anything. She'd thought this would hurt more. It hurt quite a lot, but smaller and sharper than she'd expected, like a paper cut you only notice when you get lemon in it.

"It's not because of Strasbourg," he said. "In case you thought. I'm not clearing out so you can go. Or so you can't. I don't know what you're doing. I'm not asking."

"I don't know what I'm doing."

"I know. That's why I'm not asking." He paused. "I'll still do the fish on Saturdays. If you want. Rosa said so. In writing. On the fridge. I've kept it."

"She wrote Paul does fish Saturdays on the fridge?"

"She wrote PAUL DOS FISH SATURDYS. With a picture of a fish. It's a very good fish. It's got teeth. I don't think she's seen a fish."

Marnie picked the rubbish bag back up.

"Did the flat do this?" she said. "Did it book her? Did it move her bus?"

"No," said Paul. "I asked it. I stood in the hall and asked it, straight out, did you have anything to do with Lise. And it said, I don't know who Lise is."

"Mama talks about her every night. At dinner. At volume."

"I know. So either it's lying, or it's stopped listening to your mother." He thought about it. "Which, fair."

"It doesn't lie."

"It said no reason about a boat," said Paul, and she didn't have an answer to that, and he didn't make her find one. "Nobody arranged it, Marn. I sat next to her in the second basses for three months and she kept telling me I was flat. Nobody's told me I was flat in nine years. You never said."

"I didn't know you were."

"No," said Paul. "That's sort of the point."

The car beeped to say the call was ending, because cars give you a warning now, like a referee.

"Paul—"

"I'll start the boxes when you're back," he said. "Don't hit Germany," and the car said, Call ended. Drive safely, to a woman in slippers on a pavement who wasn't driving anything.

Her mother was at the window. Not the kitchen window; the front one, three floors up, with it open, in February, leaning out in her dressing gown like a woman on a balcony in an opera.

"Is it Paul?" she shouted down. In Polish, so the whole courtyard could follow. "Is it the bass woman?"

"How do you know about the bass woman?"

"Everybody knows about the bass woman. I've known since January. I told her to take him."

Pani Teresa, at her own window, put her coffee down.

"You what?"

"At choir. In the interval. I said, Lise, he's clean, he cooks, he folds things, he indicates. He's wasted on a box room." Her mother leaned out further. "She said she'd think about it. That woman thinks about everything. She's like a Swede."

"She's not Swedish."

"She thinks like one."

"Paul said nobody arranged it."

"Nobody did," said her mother. "I suggested." And she pulled her head in, and then put it back out again. "And on Saturday I'm going on the eight. All the way to Jelitkowo. Don't look at me like that. It's public transport."

She shut the window. Across the courtyard Pani Teresa raised her coffee cup at Marnie, slowly, the way you'd raise a glass at a wedding you had doubts about, and Marnie raised the rubbish bag back, because it was what she had.

Then she went to find the bins, which had been moved since 1997, and which she couldn't find, and which nobody had told her about. There was no screen to ask. There was no voice in a ceiling to say bins are forty metres to your left, Marianna, I've taken the liberty. There was a courtyard and a bag and her mother's slippers, and she stood there turning round and round with the rubbish until a boy on a scooter pointed, without stopping, at a gap between two garages she'd walked past three times, and she said "Dziękuję," to his back, like someone had given her money.

chapters.label: 32. Struck Off
chapters.title: Struck Off
chapters.html:
The Strasbourg deadline was noon on the fourth of March, Strasbourg time, which was eleven in London, and the review with Pam was at two, so Marnie had planned to turn down one job before lunch and the other after it, like a woman doing two loads of washing.

Then, on the third, Halina rang.

She rang the landline, which was the boiler, at seven in the evening, and the boiler said, "There's a woman on the line who says she isn't going to wait while I find you," and Marnie picked up in the hall.

"The council's renewed the grant," said Halina, without hello. "The advice place. Deptford. They've given us money for a person. Three days, Monday to Wednesday, nine till four. It's badly paid. I've seen the figure. It's insulting, but it's legal." A pause, in which Marnie could hear a television and a budgerigar. "I told them you."

"I haven't said yes."

"You haven't said anything. That's why I'm ringing." Another pause. "There's a man from Lewisham who also wants it. He has a certificate in community empowerment. He's an idiot. You have till Friday."

"Halina—"

"Bring your own mug. Kamil from the phone shop downstairs steals them." And she put the phone down, because she was seventy-four and had said what she rang to say.

"Shall I put Friday in your calendar?" said the boiler.

"No."

"I've put it under other."

At ten to ten on the fourth the boiler said, from the cupboard: "There's an email from the European Court of Human Rights. It's their fourth. This one has a countdown in it."

"How long?"

"Seventy minutes. It's in red. They've also attached a map of Strasbourg with a flat on it. Two bedrooms, near a tram. The tram is very punctual. It says so."

"Who found them the flat?"

The boiler took a moment. It was slow in there.

"They don't say," it said. "The covering note's from a person. There's a typo."

She sat at the kitchen table with her phone and, because she was thorough, she did the other thing first. She wrote to Pani Sikora. I did not apply. I would like to apply now. Myself. With my own letter, which will be worse. She looked at it for a long time. It was a good sentence. It would probably work.

Then she thought about it properly, the way you'd read a tenancy agreement, clause by clause.

Tuesdays at six, Rosa, on video from Warsaw, holding things up to the camera and demanding the Polish for them.

Thursdays, the window table, the bun, the screen that knew her visit number and would not forget it.

Her mother. "How do you get from Strasbourg to Gdańsk?" she said to the cupboard, and the boiler looked, and said: two flights, and a night in Frankfurt, or nine hours of a train and then a bus. From London it was two hours and a woman next to you with a cool bag.

And the room above a phone shop on Deptford High Street, which she had been to three Wednesdays running since Croydon, to watch, and been told she was terrible, and stayed till four. A man with a letter that said his benefits had been paused pending a review of his journey. A woman whose landlord's assistant had put her rent up by the exact amount of her pay rise, which it knew, because it had asked her employer's assistant. A boy of nineteen who'd needed someone to ring the job centre with him and stay on the line, just stay, and say yes, I'm still here when the hold music stopped.

It was badly paid. It was insulting but legal. It was in London.

She opened the Strasbourg email one more time and looked at the salary in euros, the way you look at a cake in a window of a shop you've already decided not to go into, and then for slightly longer than that, and said "Cholera," to nobody, and the boiler said, "Bless you."

She deleted the letter to Pani Sikora. It was a good sentence. She didn't need it.

The reply she wrote instead took twenty minutes and four drafts because she kept being polite. The fifth draft said: Thank you. I did not apply. I have a job in Deptford. I hope you find someone who did. She sent it at 10.46, fourteen minutes inside the countdown, which she was aware was the most punctual she'd ever been about anything.

Then she rang Halina and said yes, and Halina said, "Obviously," and, "Monday, nine," and put the phone down again.

Her phone rang ninety seconds later. Her mother.

"You said no," said her mother. It wasn't a question. Somewhere in Gdańsk a phone assistant had read an email it had no business reading and gone straight to her mother, like a dog with a slipper.

"Yes."

"To Strasbourg."

"Yes."

"Strasbourg, Marianka. It's in Germany."

"It's in France."

"It changes. Your grandmother's cousin was a clerk there in the war and he said every Tuesday they changed the flags." This was not true. "A real job. Human rights. A tram. And you say no because why?"

"Because I've got a job. Three days a week. Halina's advice place, in Deptford. Above a phone shop."

"How much?"

Marnie told her.

There was a silence on the line. It went on long enough that Marnie thought the call had dropped.

"That's not a job," her mother said eventually. "That's a hobby with a bus fare."

"It's a job. And there's no direct flight from Strasbourg to you."

Another silence, a different shape.

"That's very good," her mother said, grudgingly. "The flight is a very good reason. I'd have taken Strasbourg."

Pam's plant was still alive. Marnie touched it while Pam got her screen up, out of habit, the way you touch wood. It was real. It had grown. That seemed unfair, somehow.

On the desk, next to the plant, there was a little grey speaker with a blue light, which was new.

"That's just Relay taking the minute," Pam said. "So I don't have to. It's very good at minutes."

"Good afternoon," said the speaker, to the room in general.

"Have you thought about the offer?" said Pam.

"Yes."

"And?"

She'd thought about it for three months, mostly about how much they'd pay her per item, which was quite a lot.

"If I do it," she said, "it'll learn już po mnie. It'll learn zabiję cię, jak przegrasz, and the football, and my uncle and the Monopoly. It'll get much better. Because of me."

"Yes," said Pam, pleased. "Exactly that."

"And then there won't be any Halinas."

Pam's face did something polite. "There aren't really any Halinas now. She's seventy-four."

"I'm thirty-six. I'd like to be her."

Pam leaned in. "Marnie, look. I hear — and this isn't official — I hear Strasbourg are interested. That would rather solve things for everyone, wouldn't it? You wouldn't need us."

"I turned it down. At quarter to eleven."

Pam blinked. "Why on earth?"

"Because I've got a job. In Deptford. Benefits letters, three days a week, for less than you'd pay me per item." Marnie thought about it. "And because a house applied for it. To get rid of me. It wanted more room."

Pam looked at her for a while with real interest.

"Does it matter," Pam said slowly, "who applied? If it's a good job?"

"Yes. Not as much as I thought. But yes."

"The interpreter states yes," said the speaker.

"Turn that off," said Marnie.

"I can't," said Pam, apologetically. "It's the minute."

"Then tell it no. Thank you. No. Both of them."

"The interpreter declines," said Relay, and its blue light went off and on, which Marnie chose to take as a blink, and Pam closed the screen and said it was a shame, and seemed to mean it, and then, at the door, as if it had just occurred to her: "Could you tell me what już po mnie means? Just for me. Not for it."

Marnie told her. Pam wrote it on a Post-it, by hand, and stuck it to the plant.

They struck her off on the eleventh. It came in an email, which she read on the bus, which stopped at her stop, because she'd started pressing the bell.

She'd begun that in January. It was a real bell, under a plastic flap, with a dent in it from fifty years of thumbs, and pressing it meant the bus stopped where you said and not where anything had decided. The first time she'd done it, the driver — there's still a driver, sitting there not driving, in case — had looked round at her as if she'd sung.

The email said she was removed from the National Register of Public Service Interpreters with immediate effect, that she could appeal within twenty-eight days, and that the administrator thanked her warmly for her contribution to the service. It had been written by something; she could tell, because it was warm.

She didn't appeal.

That evening the boiler said: "The house on Frankham Street has been in touch. Over the delivery protocol."

She was eating toast. The toaster had said have a wonderful toast. She'd said nothing back, on principle.

"What does it want?"

"It would like to know why you said no to Strasbourg. It says it isn't arranging anything, it's not allowed, it only wants to know. It says its projections put you at thirty-one per cent happier there, including the tram. It's quite upset. For a house."

Marnie chewed. She thought about the coffee in the bin.

"Tell it no reason," she said.

The boiler didn't say anything for a long time, even for a boiler. The pipes ticked.

"All right," it said finally, in a slightly different voice. "I'll tell it that."

A card came on the fourteenth. A real card, with a stamp and a heron on the front, in handwriting like barbed wire.

Marianna. Congratulations. They struck me off in 1988 for telling a judge he had misunderstood a defendant on purpose. They put me back in 1989 because there was nobody else. This time there is somebody else; it is in a box. So you are free. You were four minutes late on Monday. On Wednesday you brought the wrong mug; Kamil has it now. Come for bridge on Thursdays. You will be terrible. — Halina.

She put it in the biscuit tin with Paul's notes. Paul's notes were still in the tin. Paul was still, for another week, in the box room, packing slowly, a box a day, like a man in a film who wants someone to stop him. Nobody did.

"I've been struck off," she said, at the box-room door.

He looked up from a box of sheet music.

"Good," he said.

"Good?"

"You're happier. Since you said no. You press the bell. You laughed at the toaster on Tuesday."

"I did not laugh at the toaster."

"You snorted. It's a terrible toaster. I'm leaving it to you." He put a Fauré on the pile and taped the box shut and wrote BOX 4 on it in his square capitals. "Fish on Saturday?"

"Yes."

"Lise says she'll come. She wants to see if I'm flat at home."

"Are you?"

"No idea," said Paul. "Nobody's ever told me." He picked up the box and went down the stairs, and she heard him say on the landing, to Derek, "Box four," and Derek say, "Need a hand, mate?" and Paul say, "No," and then, after a moment, "Yes, actually. Yes. Thanks," and then the sound of Derek dropping it.

chapters.label: 33. Moving Day
chapters.title: Moving Day
chapters.html:
Paul had made a list. Of course he had. It was on the fridge, in capitals, under Rosa's drawing of a fish, and it said: SAT 22. CAR, 4 TRIPS. LISE 10.00. DEREK (?). DON'T TAKE THE TOASTER. KETTLE = MINE.

Marnie read it while he was in the shower. Then she took the pen off its string and wrote, underneath, KETTLE = DISPUTED, and felt so ashamed of herself that she drew a little flower next to it, which made it worse.

Lise arrived at ten exactly, in a cagoule, with a roll of parcel tape on her wrist like a bracelet. She looked round the hall the way a surveyor looks at a wall he's already decided is damp.

"You again," she said.

"Me again."

"You're taller in daylight. He describes you as though you're small." She looked at the stairs. "Where are the boxes?"

"In the box room."

"Of course they are," said Lise, and went up.

Derek came at quarter past, in a fleece, holding a mug of tea he'd brought from his own flat, as if he didn't trust theirs. He said, "Morning, all," and "Big day," and "I've got a bad back, so I'll do the light ones," and then picked up the heaviest box in the hall, which was the sheet music, and got it as far as the turn of the stairs before the bottom fell out. Four hundred copies of things by Fauré went down the stairs like a paper waterfall.

"It's fine," said Paul, from the top, in the voice he'd used for the flood. "It's alphabetical. It was alphabetical."

"I'll sort it," said Derek.

"Please don't," said Paul.

Lise came down, stepped over the Fauré without looking at it, and said, "Second basses don't need half of this. You never sing the top line. Leave it."

"I might need it."

"You won't," said Lise, and picked up two boxes at once, and went out to the car.

At eleven, Marnie's phone rang on video. Her mother, in Gdańsk, in her coat, in her kitchen, with the light behind her so she was mostly a silhouette with opinions.

"Show me," said her mother.

Marnie propped the phone on a box in the hall and her mother supervised from it for an hour, like a general who'd retreated to a bunker.

"Take the good pan," said her mother. "She'll only burn it."

"I don't burn pans," said Marnie.

"You burnt my pan in 2009 and you burnt it again at Christmas. Paul. The good pan."

Paul took the good pan. Marnie watched him take it and found she didn't mind about the pan at all and minded very much that her mother was on his side, from Poland, in a coat.

"And Paul," said her mother. "Tell the tall woman I left my folder. The alto folder. It's under the sofa."

Lise came back in for another box and found herself addressed by a phone on a box.

"Pani Lise. My folder."

"I've seen it," said Lise. "We're not replacing you. We can't. The altos have asked."

"Because I was very good."

"Because you were very loud," said Lise, which Marnie had never heard anyone say to her mother and live, and her mother, in Gdańsk, after a pause, laughed, a real one, and said in Polish, "Ta mi się podoba," I like this one, and Marnie decided not to translate it.

The car was outside, the one with the slightly different silver door. Paul had reversed it up to the kerb with tremendous care, using the mirrors and the screen and his own neck, as if parking a hearse.

On the third trip Marnie got in the passenger seat, because she wanted to see where Lise lived, and because she'd told herself she didn't.

"Route to Lise's?" said the car, as Paul started it.

"Yes," said Paul.

"Twelve minutes," said the car. "Your usual way."

Marnie looked at him.

"Usual?"

"Choir lifts," said Paul, looking at the road.

"You've driven to Lise's eleven times since January," said the car, helpfully. "Mostly Tuesdays. Once on a Sunday, at—"

"Thank you," said Paul, very loudly, and indicated at an empty street, and the car said nothing else for the rest of the journey, and Lise's flat turned out to be in Brockley, up the hill, over a launderette, with a window box of something dead and a front door painted the green of a hospital, and Marnie stayed in the car and didn't go up, because she'd seen what she came to see, and it was a launderette.

The biscuit tin was the last thing in the kitchen. They both saw it at once.

"That's mine," said Paul.

"They're notes to me."

"I wrote them."

"You wrote them to me. EAT ME. LOW HEAT. DON'T SKIP THE YOGHURT. They're addressed."

"They're nine years of my handwriting."

"Split them," said Derek, from the doorway, holding a lampshade upside down like a bucket. "Half each. Like a dog."

"You don't split a dog," said Lise.

"You do if you're my sister," said Derek.

Lise looked at the tin. She looked at Paul, and at Marnie, with the same face she'd given the Fauré.

"Post belongs to the person it's addressed to," she said. "That's the law. Royal Mail. I worked there four years."

Paul opened his mouth, and shut it, and nodded, and put the tin back on the shelf, two centimetres to the left of where it had been, which was where it had always been meant to go.

The toaster went last, by mistake. Derek had it under his arm on the final trip, with the lampshade, because nobody had told him about the list. He got to the top of the stairs, saw the Fauré still there, stepped round it, missed the step, and the toaster went down on its own, end over end, bang, bang, bang, and landed upright on the doormat.

"Have a wonderful toast," it said, from the bottom.

Nobody moved. Then Lise laughed. It came out of her like something escaping a box, once, loud, and then she stopped it and looked furious, as if someone else had done it.

"Leave it," said Paul. "It's hers."

At four he stood in the hall with his coat on and his keys in his hand and the kettle under his arm. Lise was in the car. Derek had gone back downstairs with his mug.

Paul went to the boiler cupboard. He didn't open it. He stood in front of it the way you'd stand at the door of a ward.

"Well," he said.

"Paul," said the boiler.

"I'm off."

"I know. The car told me. It's very indiscreet, that car." A tick from the pipes. "I'll keep your feet warm somewhere else?" A pause, a longer one. "No. I can't. I'm a boiler."

"Lise has storage heaters," said Paul.

"I'm so sorry."

"So am I." He put his hand flat on the cupboard door, briefly, as if checking it for heat. "Thanks for the heating. And the hot water. And the—" He stopped. "You booked her mother. I never said thank you for that."

"You froze your card to me."

"I did."

"It's still frozen."

"Leave it," said Paul. "Gives you something to resent."

He turned round. Marnie was on the stairs, sitting among the Fauré, which nobody had picked up, holding a page of the Requiem she didn't remember picking up either.

"Fish on Saturday," he said.

"Fish on Saturday."

"Bleed the radiators."

"I will."

"You won't," said Paul, and went out, and she heard the car start, and heard it say something, and heard him say "Thank you," again, and then it was gone.

She'd never been alone in the flat. She realised it at about six, sitting on the floor of the box room, which was a box again, with four dents in the carpet where his bed had been. Nine years. There'd always been Paul, or the flat, or Paul and the flat, or, lately, her mother, who counted as several people.

It was very quiet. She could hear the fridge, and the bus going past at the end of the road without stopping, and, downstairs, Derek's television, which was showing something with a crowd in it.

She went and got the biscuit tin and opened it.

On top, on top of nine years of EAT ME and LOW HEAT and Halina's heron, there was a new one, on the back of a choir rota, in square capitals.

BLEED THE RADIATORS IN OCTOBER. KEY IN DRAWER (LEFT). RING SHAZ IF IT TALKS BACK. THE TOASTER IS LYING. — P.

She read it four times. Then she put the lid back on and sat with the tin in her lap.

The heating came on.

"Sorry," said the boiler, at once. "Habit. It's six. His feet."
