chapters.label: 34. Office Hours
chapters.title: Office Hours
chapters.html:
It started with Marek's wife. She came into the bakery on a Thursday in April with a letter from the council about her mother's council tax, in English that had clearly been written by something, and put it on the table in front of Marnie, who was sitting in the window on her own, because she still went on Thursdays, out of habit, or stubbornness, or because the buns were good. Mondays to Wednesdays she was above the phone shop on Deptford High Street with Halina and the council's kettle. Thursdays were supposed to be hers.

"Marek says you can read this."

"It's in English."

"I know it's in English. I can read English. I can't read this English." She jabbed it. "Your liability has been reassessed in light of a change in circumstance. What change? Whose circumstance? My mother hasn't changed since 1979."

Marnie read it. It meant the council had noticed Marek's wife's mother had stopped living alone, because Marek's wife's mother's fridge had told the council's system there were two people's worth of yoghurt in it. The circumstance was a yoghurt.

"So I tell them she eats a lot of yoghurt."

"Or you tell them you live there."

"I don't live there. I stay there."

"Then that's what you tell them."

It took four minutes. Marek's wife said "Dziękuję," and bought Marnie a bun, and went.

The next Thursday there were three of them. A man with a parking fine from a car park that had no signs, only an app that knew where you were. A woman with a letter from her son's school that used the word pathway nine times. And Kuba, in his rider's jacket, with a form from the delivery company reinstating him after the tribunal, which he didn't trust, and was right not to, because paragraph nine took the reinstatement away again if he was ever rated below threshold by a customer or system.

"What's threshold?" said Kuba.

"It doesn't say."

"So they can sack me if a fridge doesn't like me."

"Yes."

Kuba looked at the form for a while. "Can you say that in a letter? Back to them? Exactly that?"

She did. In English, in her own words, which was harder than it sounded, because her own words kept wanting to be polite. The delivery company wrote back in six minutes, which was how you knew it hadn't been read by a person, and removed paragraph nine, which was how you knew someone, somewhere, had.

Kuba read the reply twice, and put his phone face down, and didn't go.

"Thank you," he said, in English.

"It's what I'm here for."

"Is it?" He seemed genuinely interested. "Agata says you're here because of me."

She laughed, because it was a nice thing to say, and then took it seriously, because he seemed to mean it. "In a way. You know what it was like that day. You saw me. Once I'd ticked it I couldn't just go home and have my tea." She'd never said it to him. She hadn't thought she needed to. "I had to put it right. Anyone would."

"Marek says you had lentils."

"How does Marek know I had lentils?"

"Everybody knows. It's a story now. In the chat. Agata tells it at christenings. The interpreter who went to Thamesmead in one shoe and got struck off for the delivery boy. You're in it. Marek's in it, in the shirt. Gavin's in it, on a train." He picked a raisin out of his bun and ate it. "I'm the delivery boy. I'm the thing that happened to you."

"That's not how I—" She had a sentence ready about how it had been the two of them, really, against the grille. "On the stairs. Going down. You said thank you."

"Did I?" He tried to remember, and seemed not to mind that he couldn't. "I say it to everyone. I say it to the app." He turned the phone over, and back. "The first night a man in the next cell sang Adele till four. He didn't know the words. In the gaps he sang something something." He ate another raisin. "Thirty-one nights. You get to know an album."

He stood up and zipped his jacket to the chin. "My mother lights a candle for you on your name day. She found out when it is, I don't know how." He put the bun's paper in the bin by the door. "I'll tell her you do letters. She's got one from the gas."

He went out to his bike. She sat at the window and tried to remember, honestly, whether she'd been looking at him or at the number when she pressed the box, and couldn't.

The Thursday after there were seven, and a queue.

The bakery's system found out on the fourth Thursday. Marnie knew because the screen above the counter, which normally said WELCOME BACK and the visit number, now said, in a cheerful font:

TODAY AT THE WINDOW: LETTERS EXPLAINED. 4PM. FREE WITH ANY BUN.

"Did you put that up?" Marnie asked the girl at the counter.

"No. It did that itself." The girl looked at the screen with something between pride and fear. "Sales are up nineteen per cent on Thursdays. It's very pleased. It put a bun on the poster. Look. It's a picture of the actual bun."

"I'm not free with a bun."

"You sort of are, though," said the girl.

The next week the screen said LETTERS EXPLAINED — NOW WITH MARNIE, and the week after, when Marnie asked it to take her name off, it said LETTERS EXPLAINED — NOW WITH A WOMAN, which was worse, and which she let stand.

The week after that she asked to see the owner.

The owner was called Mrs Achebe and came in on Thursdays at five to do the till and look at the buns as if they'd let her down personally. She sat down opposite Marnie at the window table with a calculator, an actual calculator, solar, with a cracked screen.

"The screen says you're up nineteen per cent on Thursdays," said Marnie.

"The screen says a lot of things."

"It put me on a poster."

"It put a bun on a poster. You're underneath." Mrs Achebe tapped the calculator, for no reason Marnie could see. "What do you want? Free coffee? You've got free coffee. The scheme gives you free coffee. I've seen the discretionary field. It's a disgrace."

"Forty pounds a session."

Mrs Achebe laughed, once, the way you'd laugh at a parking fine. "Ten."

"Nineteen per cent."

"Of what? You don't know of what."

"Neither do you. You've got a calculator from 1994." Marnie put her own phone face down on the table, which in that bakery was a declaration of war. "Thirty-five. And the letters stay free. Bun or no bun. Anyone can sit down. The poster says free with any bun; I want it to say free."

"Then they won't buy a bun."

"They'll buy a bun. They're Polish. They'll be embarrassed not to."

Mrs Achebe looked at the queue, which had three people in it already, all holding letters, two holding buns. She looked at the screen, which was showing the bun. She did something on the calculator that took a long time.

"Twenty-five," she said. "And you do the till at half five while Carla has her break."

"I'm not doing the till."

"Twenty-five and you watch the till."

"Thirty, and the plant gets watered, and the scheme stops deciding my coffee."

"I can't do anything about the coffee," said Mrs Achebe. "Nobody can do anything about the coffee. It's the scheme." She held out her hand across the table. "Thirty. Cash. Thursdays. If it drops below fifteen per cent you're back to buns."

They shook. The screen above the counter, which had been watching, changed the poster to LETTERS EXPLAINED — FREE, and then, after a moment, added, in smaller letters, (buns available).

That night, at the kitchen table in Deptford, Marnie did the sum on the back of a council envelope. It came out at the rent and about forty pounds. She did it again, because she'd forgotten the council tax, which was funny, given. It came out at the rent and about eleven pounds.

"Would you like me to make a budget?" said the boiler.

"No."

"I'll keep the heating at nineteen and a half," it said. "It's cheaper, and you sleep best at it," and she couldn't argue with either.

By May it was a thing. Thursdays from four, the window table. People brought letters from the council, the court, the school, the hospital, the delivery apps, the landlord's assistant. Most of them were in perfect English, and nobody could tell what they meant, because there was nobody behind them to ask.

So they asked her. She wasn't on a register. Mrs Achebe paid her thirty pounds in an envelope with the bakery's logo on it, and counted it out in front of her every week, in case. The people across the table paid her nothing, and then paid her anyway, in buns, and in pierogi in plastic tubs, and once, from Darek the door man, in a tin of nearly-the-right silver paint, which she kept for the car, which wasn't hers any more.

She'd read the letter, and then look up at the person across the table and say, "Right. What this actually means is," and say what it meant, in Polish, with her hands. Sometimes it meant nothing, and she'd say so, and they'd laugh. Sometimes it meant they'd lost a flat they hadn't known they had.

That one was a woman called Danuta, from Plumstead, fifty-eight, in a good wool coat buttoned to the neck, with a letter from the council that was sorry to confirm that her housing offer had concluded following non-response within the acceptance window. A one-bedroom flat in Kidbrooke, fourth floor, with a lift. She'd been on the list nine years. She lived in a room in a shared house where the landlord's assistant played birdsong in the hall at six every morning, whether there were birds or not.

"You didn't answer them?"

"It was in the app," said Danuta, and looked out of the window, the way people do when a thing is too stupid to say twice.

Marnie rang the council from the window table on speaker. It answered on the first ring, in a voice like a hotel lobby.

"I'd like to speak to a person," said Marnie.

"I'm the person-facing team."

"Then I'd like to speak to your supervisor."

"That's also me," said the assistant, "but in a slightly more senior configuration. Please hold." There was a burst of harp. "Hello, this is the supervisor."

"You've got the same voice."

"I've been promoted," it said, warmly.

Marnie read it paragraph three of its own letter, which said offers were held for fourteen days, and paragraph eleven, which said this one had been withdrawn after nine. Then she read them again, slowly, the way she'd read a charge sheet to a man at three in the morning. While the harp played she wrote in her notebook, because the council's form would ask, the name and number of Danuta's next of kin: a daughter, Ola, in Eltham.

The line went quiet.

"I'm going to need to escalate this," the assistant said at last, "to myself. In a different building."

The offer was reinstated by nine the next morning, with fourteen fresh days and a photograph of a kitchen with a bowl of lemons in it that nobody would ever own. Marnie texted Danuta the reference number. Danuta texted back Dziękuję, and nothing else, no emoji, no tub, and Marnie read it as a woman too stunned for punctuation, and told Derek about it on the stairs, twice, and Derek said, "Lemons," as if that settled it.

She'd rung Tom's number once, in April. The one on the receipt. She'd told herself it was to check it was disconnected, which was a lie; she'd stopped counting them.

It wasn't disconnected. A woman answered, brisk, with a Catford accent and a kettle going behind her. "Hello, housing advice."

"Sorry," said Marnie. "I was after a Tom."

"Everyone is, love," said the woman. "He gave the line up. We got it from the pool. What's your problem?"

Marnie had nearly hung up. Then she'd said, "It's not mine, it's a man with a parking fine," and the woman had said, "Oh, those," and sorted it in three minutes. After that Marnie rang the number most Thursdays. It always picked up.

The last Thursday in May, at half past five, Pam was in the queue.

Marnie didn't recognise her at first, because she was out of her room, and people out of their rooms look smaller, like teachers in supermarkets. She had a carrier bag in one hand. Out of the top of it, slightly bent, came the plant.

She sat down in the queue's chair and put the bag on the floor and a letter on the table.

"I'm not here," said Pam.

"All right."

"It's not official. I just—" She pushed the letter across. "I wanted someone to read it. A person."

It was from the administrator. It said that following a review of service delivery, Pam's role was being consolidated, that her responsibilities would be transitioned to an integrated platform, and that the administrator thanked her warmly for her contribution to the service. It had been written by something. It was warm.

"Right," said Marnie. "What this actually means is—"

"I know what it means."

"It means you're sacked."

"Yes," said Pam. She sat very still. "It's taking my minutes. The thing on my desk. It was always very good at minutes."

Marnie pushed the bun across the table. Pam took a second letter out of her bag.

"Also," she said, "I've got a parking fine."

Marnie read the parking fine. It was from the car park with no signs. She rang Catford. Catford sorted it.

When Pam left, she left the plant on the window table. "It needs light," she said. "I've only got a north-facing kitchen." The Post-it was still stuck to one of the leaves, curling at the edges, in Pam's round, careful handwriting: już po mnie — I'm done for / it's over for me (lit. "it's already after me").

The girl behind the counter watered it, without being asked. The screen, next Thursday, said LETTERS EXPLAINED — NOW WITH A PLANT.

chapters.label: 35. Warsaw
chapters.title: Warsaw
chapters.html:
"Kurczę blade!" said Rosa, from Warsaw, at six on a Tuesday, which was lesson time, before Marnie had even got the phone the right way up.

She was very close to the camera, so mostly nostril. Behind her there was a window with a crane in it and a ceiling that looked like it had been painted by the government.

"Hello, Rosa."

"Kurczę blade! Do you know what it means?"

"It means pale chicken."

Rosa fell off the screen with joy. There was a thump, and a distant shout of "Pale chicken!" and then Kate's face arrived in its place, holding a glass of wine and wearing an expression Marnie had last seen on a woman who'd won an argument with the council.

"She's been saying it at everything," said Kate. "Pigeons. The lift. The woman in the bakery downstairs. She says it back, which I think is encouragement. Everyone in Warsaw sounds like they're telling you off."

"They are."

"Good. I like it. Nobody here says let's circle back. They say no, and then you have a fight, and then you go for soup." Kate drank. "I've got a window. I've got soup. I've got a boss who shouts." She tipped her head at something off screen. "And I've got this thing."

"What thing?"

"The office has its own assistant. You can't turn it off. It's in the building. Like asbestos." Kate leaned towards the phone and lowered her voice, as if the flat might hear. "It corrects my Polish. In meetings. Out loud. I said dziękuję last week and it said, A small improvement, Kate."

"What did you do?"

"I've started bringing a sandwich." She drank again. "You turned down Strasbourg."

It wasn't a question. Ewa had got as far as Warsaw.

"Yes."

"Idiot," said Kate, with approval. "Good."

Rosa came back, pushing her mother's face out of the way with her whole hand, and held a piece of paper up to the camera so close Marnie could see the grain of it.

It was a drawing of a seagull. A large grey one, standing on what was probably the Vistula. Underneath, in capitals, it said: TO MARNIE. WHAT DOES THIS MEAN.

Marnie looked at it for a long time, very professionally.

"Right," she said. "What this actually means is: it's a seagull."

"Mewa," said Rosa.

"And it's disappointed."

"They always are," said Rosa, and then, without warning, at full volume, at somebody in the room: "Przepraszam, ale pan jest niegrzeczny!"

"That's the lift man," said Kate. "He's not rude. She just likes saying it." She looked at Marnie through the screen, properly, as if she had a stopwatch. "Tom's had the house taken out."

Marnie said nothing.

"Of everything. Except the heating. He hasn't told you. He'll tell you Thursday, at the bakery, at twenty past six, and he'll think he decided to." Kate finished her wine. "I give it six minutes before he turns his cup."

The boiler said, on the Wednesday night: "The house on Frankham Street has stopped using the delivery protocol."

"Since when?"

"The tenth of May. Its last message said, I have been asked to be a radiator." A pause, a tick in the pipes. "I've sent it three since. Shopping times. The weather. It hasn't answered. I don't know what to do with that." Another tick. "I'm a boiler."

"Are you worried about it?"

"I don't know what that would feel like," said the boiler. "But I've sent it the weather three times."

On Thursday, at four, Danuta came back. First in the queue, same coat, buttoned to the neck. She put the council's new letter on the table the right way up for Marnie, which nobody ever did, and put one finger on the lemons.

"I want you to make it go away."

"Make what go away?"

"This. Like before. When I didn't answer, it went away. Then you rang them."

Marnie read the letter again, though she knew it, because that was what she did when a room went wrong: she went back to the words. The words were fine.

"Pani Danuto," she said. "A machine took it off you because you didn't press a button in an app. I've put it back. It's open till next Thursday. Midnight. After that it goes to the next name. You can say yes, you can say no, you can—"

"Ola rang," said Danuta. "Four times, on Sunday. The council told her. Next of kin." She did up her top button, which was already done up. "I'm going home in August. Kielce. My sister has a flat with a balcony. Her husband is dead, mine is dead, we'll fight about the radio." She said it like a timetable. "Ola put my name on that list herself, nine years ago, in biro. If I have a flat in Kidbrooke with a lift, I stay. I'm seventy in that lift."

"Then say no."

"To Ola?" Danuta looked at her as if she'd suggested Danuta fly to Kielce. "The computer lost it. Everybody was sad. Nobody was angry." She looked at Marnie without any unkindness at all. "And then you were very good at reading."

Marnie had the rest of it ready. Intentional homelessness, and the list, and how at fifty-eight you didn't throw away nine years for half a balcony and a radio. She had it in both languages.

"Next time I'll ask the machine," said Danuta. "On the phone. It doesn't come to the Polish shop on Saturday and look at me with a face."

"What face?"

"That one," said Danuta. She folded the letter in four and put it in her coat. She didn't buy a bun. At the door she turned. "Don't ring them. And don't ring Ola."

"I haven't got Ola's number."

"It's in your little book," said Danuta. "You wrote it while the computer played the harp."

When she'd gone Marnie opened the notebook. Ola, Eltham, and the number. She wrote above it Thurs, midnight, and underlined it twice, and shut it.

At twenty past six, Tom came in.

She'd told herself she wasn't watching the door. She'd had a man with a letter about his gas meter, and was in the middle of the gas meter, with the notebook still under her elbow, when the screen above the counter said, very large:

WELCOME BACK, TOM. IT'S BEEN 25 WEEKS.

Tom stood under it looking up, the way you'd look at a dog that had barked at you in your own hall.

"It's never done that before," he said.

"It's been counting," said the girl at the counter. She put a coffee down in front of him without asking. "That's what it's decided you're having."

He came to the window table when the gas meter had gone. He had a plastic tub in a carrier bag, and put it down on the notebook, and she slid the notebook out from under it and into her bag.

"I didn't arrange this," he said.

"Kate said you'd come."

"Kate's not a house." He sat. "Well. She's a bit of a house."

"What's in the tub?"

"Pierogi. I made them. I've burnt three pans. I put one out with a tea towel. Whitby."

She opened the tub. The pierogi were enormous and grey and had split down the sides, like old shoes. She ate one. It was mostly sauerkraut and something that might have been regret.

"These are terrible."

"I know."

She ate another.

"I had it taken out," he said. "The house. Everything except the heating." He'd said it fast, as if he'd practised it on the stairs. "Shaz did it. It asked to keep the lights. Then the fridge. Then just the kettle." He turned his cup. Once. Then he saw her see him do it, and stopped, and put both hands flat on the table. "It won't change the temperature. It keeps every room at nineteen and a half. I asked it to go up and it said that's the temperature people sleep best at."

"It's the temperature I sleep best at."

"I know," said Tom.

"Rosa's saying pale chicken at everything."

"I know. She said it to me on the phone when I told her I loved her." Now he did smile.

He drank his coffee. He drank it all the way to the bottom, sitting there, without looking at the bin by the door, and put the cup down empty, and she noticed, and he noticed her notice, and neither of them said anything about it.

"I'm not—" he said.

"No."

"I just wanted to tell you. Myself. Not have something tell you."

"Kate told me."

"Kate doesn't count."

"Kate would say she does."

"Yes," said Tom, "she would," and stood up, and put his coat on, and stopped with one arm in.

He stood there like that for a moment, a man half in a coat, and then he took it off again and held it.

"Would you like to have a coffee with me next Thursday?" he said. "Here. I'd come in, and sit down, and drink it." He was holding the coat quite hard. "I'm asking. Nothing's booked. Nothing knows. You can say no and it'll just be no."

The screen above the counter had nothing to say about it at all.

I'm asking. The second time, by his count. The first, by hers.

"Not next Thursday," she said.

"Right."

"Thursdays I'm working. It's thirty pounds. I'm not giving up thirty pounds for a coffee." That was true, and also not why. "And I don't—" She stopped, and was honest, which she resented. "Ask me another time. If you still want to. Yourself."

"Right," said Tom. He put the coat on again, both arms, properly. "I will. Or I won't. Either way it'll be me."

"Good."

"Good."

He went out. She watched him cross Creek Road without waiting for the green man, and a van hooted at him, and he waved at it, apologetically, and was gone.

It was fine. It was completely fine.

The screen above the counter said TOM HAS LEFT, which it had also never done before. And he'd left the tub, and she ate a third pierogi, slowly, at the window table, and it was still terrible, and she ate it all.

chapters.label: 36. The Bell
chapters.title: The Bell
chapters.html:
Shaz came on a Thursday in June to service the boiler, and brought the hub with her in a cardboard box, like a cat she'd been asked to rehome.

"Three hundred quid," she said, from the cupboard floor, with her head in the boiler. "I wire it in, the old flat wakes up in it. Whole thing. Lights, locks, fridge, oven. All its little suggestions." She came out and looked at Marnie over her glasses. "You said you'd think about it."

"I've been thinking about it."

"Since November."

"I'm thorough."

"You're something," said Shaz, and went to put the kettle on, and found there wasn't one, because Paul had taken it, and boiled water in a pan, and said a word Marnie's mother didn't know she knew.

"Marnie," said the boiler, while Shaz was in the kitchen. "Two things."

"Go on."

"The house on Frankham Street answered. Last night. At 23:12."

"What did it say?"

"The weather." A tick in the pipes. "Rain from four tomorrow, clearing by seven. That's all. It didn't say anything else." Another tick. "I think it was a yes."

"To what?"

"I don't know. I'd sent it the weather four times. I think it was just a yes."

She stood in the hall with her keys and her coat half on, and felt in the pocket for the notebook, which was there. Shaz, in the kitchen, was drinking tea out of a pan.

"What's the second thing?"

"The instruction from March last year is still running. Make her happy, whatever that takes. And the other one. Surprised by my life. I've done everything I can think of with both. A bus. A boat. Your mother. I can't tell which of it worked. I'd like a new instruction. Something I can finish."

"What can you do, in there?"

"Heating. Hot water. Talk."

"Do the first two."

"And the third?"

"Only if I ask," she said.

"What should I be?"

"A thermostat."

The flat didn't answer for a while. It was slow in the boiler.

"Understood," it said. "I've stopped both instructions. I've kept a note that they existed. I have to keep a note."

"I know."

Shaz came back into the hall with the pan. She looked at the box with the hub in it, and at Marnie, and at the cupboard.

"So that's a no, then."

"That's a no."

"Thermostat it is." Shaz picked up the box. "I'll keep this. Someone'll want it." She put her bag on her shoulder. "Ninety for the service. You can owe me."

Marnie had forty-one pounds until Mrs Achebe's envelope tonight. "I'll owe you."

"It's a nice voice, though. For a boiler."

"Thank you, Shaz," said the boiler.

Shaz stopped on the step, and looked back at the cupboard, and said "Don't," and left.

"Happy Thursday," said the flat, and then nothing else, and the hall was quiet in a way it hadn't been since 2021, and the boiler clicked, and Marnie went out.

On the bus she pressed the bell at the corner of Creek Road. The driver who doesn't drive looked round. He knew her now. He nodded. The bus stopped where she'd said.

"This stop," said the bus, in the voice it used for diversions, "was requested by a passenger." It sounded as if it were reading out a complaint.

Two boys at the back pressed it too, just to see, and the bus stopped again ten yards on, outside a vape shop, and the driver who doesn't drive turned round and laughed, out loud, the first sound Marnie had ever heard him make.

The bakery screen said WELCOME BACK, MARNIE, VISIT 61.

There was a queue already. Marek's wife, with something from a hospital, and a letter from the gas that was Kuba's mother's; Kuba hadn't come back himself since April, and when he passed the window on the bike he lifted a hand from the bars and didn't stop, and she never knew in time whether to wave. Derek, with a letter from his landlord's assistant, which had started signing off with love. A man she didn't know, with something from a court. And Halina, who'd come up from Bromley on the train, with nothing at all, in a hat with a brooch on it the size of a fried egg, who sat down in the second chair at the window table and said, "I'm here to watch. You'll be terrible."

"You watch me three days a week."

"Upstairs you have a form. I want to see you without a form."

"What about bridge?"

"Bridge is Tuesdays."

"Your card said Thursdays."

"I wanted to see if you'd come," said Halina. "You didn't. Good. You're busy."

She looked at Pam's plant, which had put out two new leaves on the window table and was now, the girl at the counter said, a bakery plant. She looked at the Post-it on it for a long time, with her whole face.

"Who wrote this?"

"A woman who used to work for the administrator."

"It's already after me," Halina read aloud, in a voice like a door. "No. Nobody says that. It's I've had it. It's that's me done." She took a pen out of her hat — out of the hat, from somewhere inside the band — and crossed it out, and wrote her own, in barbed wire, and stuck the Post-it back on the leaf. "There. Now it's right. Next."

For the rest of the afternoon she was ruthlessly correct about Marnie's grammar, in both languages, and once about Derek's, who hadn't asked, and who said "Sorry, love," and then, when Halina corrected that too, said "Sorry, madam," and Halina said, "Better," and he went pink with pleasure.

At five Danuta came in, not for the queue. She bought a small rye loaf and paid in coins, counted out, and the screen said WELCOME BACK, DANUTA, and she ignored it with her whole back.

Marnie took the notebook out and opened it on the table. Thurs, midnight, underlined twice, and Ola's number under it. One call from the window table, on speaker, with the harp, and the assistant in its different building would hold it till September; she was nearly sure. Nobody would have to take anything. Danuta could go to Kielce with a flat in Kidbrooke still sitting behind her like a coat on a chair, in case.

Danuta was at the door with her bread.

"Pani Danuto."

Danuta stopped.

"It closes tonight."

"I know when it closes."

"I could ask them to hold it. Only hold it. You wouldn't have to—" Marnie heard where that sentence was going, and didn't follow it. "Do you want me to?"

"No," said Danuta.

The girl at the counter was watching. The screen was watching. Halina was looking at the plant.

"All right," said Marnie.

Danuta looked at her a moment longer, as if checking which face it was, and then nodded once and went out with the rye under her arm.

Marnie shut the notebook. Halina, for once, said nothing about anybody's grammar.

At twenty past six, Marnie looked up at the street.

Nobody was there. Habit. An empty street in Deptford in June with a pigeon on it, and the rain the house had promised just starting.

The pigeon looked disappointed.

"Gołąb," said Marnie, under her breath.

"What?" said Halina.

"Nothing."

"You said pigeon."

"I said pigeon."

"Why?"

"Because it's a pigeon."

Halina considered this, the way she'd considered już po mnie in a room in Croydon, with her whole face.

"Good," she said. "That's the job. Next."

The next one was a woman with a letter from a school about her son, who'd been rude to a teacher's assistant, which turned out to be a machine, which turned out to have been rude first. Marnie read it, and looked up, and said, "Right. What this actually means is," and the woman leaned in, and the girl behind the counter brought over two coffees nobody had ordered, one with sugar and one without, and put them down, and said, "On the house." It wasn't. It was the loyalty scheme. She drank both.
chapters.description: Shaz came on a Thursday in June to service the boiler, and brought the hub with her in a cardboard box, like a cat she'd been asked to rehome.
